Description: Turn the top-ranked lead into a specific, short first message that connects the signal to a reason for the customer to respond.
Prompt: Here is the top lead from my follow-up plan: [paste source signal, account, role, likely interest, and any prior interaction]. Draft a first contact message under 100 words that references the specific signal, states one reason this is relevant to their business now, and asks for one small next step. Give me two versions: one for a business decision maker and one for a technical decision maker. Do not claim knowledge of their environment we do not have, and do not assert a product feature I have not given you.
ActivitySteps:
1. Take the top lead from the prioritized plan.
2. Confirm consent and context are appropriate for outreach.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Edit into your own voice.
5. Send one, and note the date.
RequiredContext: The prioritized lead plan; the source signal; the contact's role; prior interaction history; consent and outreach appropriateness.
ExpectedOutput: Two short first-contact drafts, one business and one technical, tied to the originating signal.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP confirms consent and outreach appropriateness, verifies every factual statement about the customer, and owns the wording before sending.
WhyThisMatters: A prioritized list that never becomes a message is just a better-sorted backlog.

Name: Close the loop on what the follow-up produced
Description: Review the leads worked this week, record what happened, and decide which signals are worth trusting next time.
Prompt: Here are the leads I followed up this week and what happened with each: [paste lead, source signal, action taken, response or silence]. Tell me which signal sources produced a response and which did not, what the responses have in common, and which two signal types I should prioritize next week. Be direct about small sample size; do not overstate a pattern from a handful of leads.
ActivitySteps:
1. List the leads worked and the outcome of each.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Record the outcome in the opportunity or lead record.
4. Name the one signal source you will deprioritize.
RequiredContext: The leads worked this week; the originating signal for each; the action taken; the response or lack of one.
ExpectedOutput: A short read on which signal sources are working, and one prioritization change for next week.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP judges whether the pattern is real or coincidence given the sample size, and owns the decision to change prioritization.
WhyThisMatters: Lead follow-up improves only if you find out which signals were worth following.

Name: Build the optimization evidence base
Description: Analyze enabled usage, cost and consumption evidence.
Prompt: For [Customer] and [period], summarize enabled usage, consumption and cost signals relevant to optimization. Identify material changes and patterns visible in the report and supporting metrics. Separate observations from recommendations and state missing architecture or business context.
RequiredContext: Enabled certified report and scope.
ExpectedOutput: Optimization evidence summary.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms what each measure actually counts before acting on it. Optimization metrics are defined differently across services, and acting on a misread one produces a saving that never appears.
WhyThisMatters: Most of the effort in the optimization evidence base is assembly, and assembly is exactly what AI removes.

Name: Create the FinOps and optimization recommendation
Description: Produce a bounded optimization recommendation.
Prompt: Using approved evidence, create an optimization recommendation for [Customer/workload]. Include current state, outcome, options, supported technical and financial effect, architecture tradeoffs, dependencies, risks, milestones and human-review requirements. Do not invent savings or intent.
RequiredContext: Approved evidence; architecture context; outcome; constraints.
ExpectedOutput: Optimization recommendation.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms the saving is achievable in this customer's environment. Optimization recommendations are generated from patterns, and a saving that ignores a constraint you already know about costs more trust than the saving was worth.
WhyThisMatters: You spend your time editing the FinOps and optimization recommendation rather than staring at a blank version of it.

Name: Compare architecture options against decision criteria
Description: Investigate external technical patterns and authoritative evidence.
Prompt: Research [architecture decision] using current authoritative Microsoft and approved customer sources. Compare viable options against [decision criteria], identify assumptions, risks, dependencies and evidence gaps, and cite each material claim.
RequiredContext: Architecture decision; decision criteria; approved sources.
ExpectedOutput: Sourced architecture options assessment.
HumanCheckpoint: SE and architecture SMEs validate current guidance, applicability and unsupported assumptions.
WhyThisMatters: Comparing architecture options and evidence surfaces the difference that actually changes the decision.

Name: Create the architecture decision record
Description: Turn approved evidence into a concise decision artifact.
Prompt: Using the approved discovery brief and architecture evidence, create a decision record with customer outcome, options considered, criteria, selected direction, risks, dependencies, validation steps, unresolved questions and next technical action.
RequiredContext: Approved discovery brief and architecture evidence.
ExpectedOutput: Architecture decision record.
HumanCheckpoint: The SE owns what the record says was decided. An architecture decision record becomes the reference everyone builds against, and a decision captured slightly wrong is reproduced faithfully by everyone who reads it.
WhyThisMatters: You spend your time editing the architecture decision record rather than staring at a blank version of it.

Name: Package a reusable technical asset with context
Description: Convert successful work into a repeatable, governed asset.
Prompt: Using the approved [demo, script, architecture, response or checklist], create a reusable asset package with purpose, prerequisites, steps, editable parameters, validation checks, known limitations, owner and example use.
RequiredContext: Approved technical asset.
ExpectedOutput: Reusable asset package.
HumanCheckpoint: SE removes sensitive content, validates technical accuracy and confirms reuse permissions.
WhyThisMatters: Reuse happens when the asset includes enough context for another SE to trust and adapt it.

Name: Create a technical Skill Blueprint for a repeatable SE workflow
Description: Turn a repeatable workflow into a structured personalized skill.
Prompt: Create a reusable Skill Blueprint for [SE workflow]. Define trigger, inputs, trusted sources, ordered steps, expected output, rules, exclusions, exception behavior, human review, validation checks, and one representative test case. Do not publish until tested.
ActivitySteps:
1. Choose the asset worth reusing.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Invoke the skill in Scout or Cowork.
4. Review the generated structure at the checkpoint.
5. Add the context a colleague would need.
6. Publish where the team will actually look.
RequiredContext: SE workflow; trusted sources; test case.
ExpectedOutput: Technical Skill Blueprint with validation checks and test case.
HumanCheckpoint: SE or skill owner tests representative work and validates access, outputs, safeguards, and repository placement before promotion.
WhyThisMatters: A blueprint lets the team test repeatability before pretending the skill is production-ready.

Name: Inspect technical deal health and proof gaps
Description: Use available MSX and customer context to identify technical progression gaps.
Prompt: Review [opportunity] and summarize the intended customer decision, current technical stage, exit criteria, proof completed, open blockers, recent technical engagement, missing roles and next recommended technical action. Show the source signal and flag unavailable context.
RequiredContext: Opportunity and available customer context.
ExpectedOutput: Technical deal-health brief.
HumanCheckpoint: The SE judges whether the record reflects the technical reality. Opportunity data is maintained for commercial purposes, and the technical risk that matters is frequently not in it.
WhyThisMatters: Technical deal health improves when blockers, proof gaps, and next decisions are visible in one place.

Name: Create the technical risk and handoff plan
Description: Synthesize approved deal, proof and delivery context into an action plan.
Prompt: Using approved sources, create a technical risk and handoff plan with blocker, impact, evidence, owner, mitigation, checkpoint, decision needed and delivery handoff requirements.
RequiredContext: Approved deal, proof and delivery sources.
ExpectedOutput: Technical risk register and handoff plan.
HumanCheckpoint: The SE confirms delivery has accepted the handoff. A plan that names delivery without their agreement transfers the risk on paper only, and the gap appears when the work is meant to start.
WhyThisMatters: Risk plans help only when they assign the owner, evidence, mitigation, checkpoint, and next decision.

Name: Build the decision-centered demo or workshop plan
Description: Create a bounded multi-part experience package.
Prompt: Create a demo or workshop package for [customer decision]. Include audience, scenario, decision criteria, agenda, demo flow, sample data needs, roles, likely objections, tenant or permission dependencies, fallback plan and explicit next decision.
RequiredContext: Customer decision; audience; approved scenario.
ExpectedOutput: Demo or workshop package.
HumanCheckpoint: SE validates the environment, permissions, technical behavior, evidence and customer appropriateness.
WhyThisMatters: A decision-centered plan keeps the demo or workshop from becoming a feature tour.

Name: Research supporting proof, limitations, and objections
Description: Find authoritative evidence supporting the selected scenario.
Prompt: Find current authoritative evidence for [scenario or capability]. Return only claims relevant to the customer decision, likely objections, known limitations and SME-needed flags. Cite sources.
RequiredContext: Scenario or capability; approved sources.
ExpectedOutput: Evidence and objection brief.
HumanCheckpoint: The SE checks whether the proof is still current. Product capability and published limits change between releases, and a proof point that was accurate last quarter is a credibility problem this quarter.
WhyThisMatters: Authoritative proof and known limitations are what make the demo safe to use in a customer decision.

Name: Build the technical discovery and decision-criteria brief
Description: Synthesize approved customer and technical context into a brief that names the customer decision, constraints, evidence gaps, and criteria.
Prompt: Using the selected approved customer and technical sources, prepare for [meeting]. Summarize known outcomes, decisions, constraints, architecture context, open technical questions and missing evidence. Propose five discovery questions that advance the technical decision. Separate sourced facts from hypotheses.
RequiredContext: Selected approved customer and technical sources.
ExpectedOutput: Technical discovery brief with questions and evidence gaps.
HumanCheckpoint: The SE decides which questions are appropriate to ask this customer. A technically sound discovery question can be premature or presumptuous given where the relationship is, and discovery is where that costs most.
WhyThisMatters: Discovery becomes useful when it produces decision criteria the customer and team can inspect.

Name: Rehearse the technical discovery conversation
Description: Practice questions, listening, objections and the intended next decision.
Prompt: Role-play [customer or stakeholder] for the upcoming technical discovery conversation. Use the approved brief only. Simulate realistic questions and objections, coach clarity and listening, and identify statements requiring technical or customer validation. Do not invent customer facts.
RequiredContext: Approved discovery brief.
ExpectedOutput: Role-play, coaching observations and improvement actions.
HumanCheckpoint: The SE owns what is said in the room. Rehearsal makes phrasing fluent, and fluency makes an unverified claim sound exactly as certain as a verified one.
WhyThisMatters: Practicing discovery questions reduces the chance that the real meeting ends with ambiguity instead of criteria.

Name: Scope the smallest useful PoC
Description: Build the PoC work package.
Prompt: Create a PoC plan for [technical decision]. Define hypothesis, in-scope scenario, success and exit criteria, milestones, data and environment needs, roles, risks, dependencies, review gates, final decision and handoff if successful.
RequiredContext: Technical decision; constraints; resources.
ExpectedOutput: PoC plan and decision gates.
HumanCheckpoint: The SE decides whether the proof is necessary at all. A proof absorbs weeks of engineering time, and the ones that were never going to change a decision are the most expensive thing on the calendar.
WhyThisMatters: A small, criteria-led PoC reduces waste and makes the exit decision clear before work starts.

Name: Pressure-test PoC readiness
Description: Review a proposed PoC plan for gaps and ambiguity.
Prompt: Review this PoC plan. Identify vague success criteria, unowned dependencies, unrealistic milestones, missing security or data assumptions, weak linkage to the customer decision and unclear exit paths. Return five review questions and the smallest revisions needed.
RequiredContext: Proposed PoC plan.
ExpectedOutput: Readiness review and revision list.
HumanCheckpoint: The SE owns the go or no-go call and confirms the required reviewers have seen the plan before it is called ready. A readiness checklist can be entirely green while the one thing that will actually break the proof was never on it, and that thing is usually known to the engineer rather than to the checklist.
WhyThisMatters: Readiness issues should be found in planning, not after the customer expects a proof.

Name: Draft the sourced technical answer matrix
Description: Answer technical questions with sources, confidence, assumptions, exceptions, and reviewer flags.
Prompt: Answer the selected technical questions using approved and authoritative sources. For each item provide a grounded answer, source citation, confidence, assumptions and SME-needed flag. Preserve the question order and do not hide unsupported areas.
RequiredContext: Selected technical questions; approved sources.
ExpectedOutput: Grounded technical answer matrix.
HumanCheckpoint: The SE routes security, legal and product claims to the SMEs who own them. A sourced answer looks authoritative regardless of whether the source was current, and these are the answer types a customer will hold you to.
WhyThisMatters: A technical answer is safer when confidence, assumptions, and reviewer needs are visible.

Name: Assemble the governed technical response package
Description: Produce reviewed answers in the required structure and coordinate gaps.
Prompt: Using the approved answer matrix, assemble the response in the requested format. Create an exception list for unanswered items, assign suggested reviewers and provide a final quality checklist. Do not submit or send.
RequiredContext: Approved answer matrix; required format.
ExpectedOutput: Formatted response plus exception list.
HumanCheckpoint: The SE confirms approvals before distribution rather than after. A response package circulates faster than a correction to it, and the unapproved version is the one that reaches procurement.
WhyThisMatters: Governance is what keeps fast response work from becoming unsupported customer guidance.

Name: Build the solution-selling plan
Description: Shape a solution-specific plan to advance the next customer decision.
Prompt: Build a solution-selling plan for [solution play] at [account]. Include customer outcomes, maturity, solution vision, stakeholder coverage, value conversation arc, demo or workshop sequence, proof needs, risks, and a 30-day plan to clear the next decision. Flag missing stakeholders and unsupported claims.
RequiredContext: Account; solution play; current stage; known stakeholders; approved evidence.
ExpectedOutput: Solution-selling plan with decisions, proof needs, owners, and progression actions.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP validates customer need, stage, solution fit, evidence, stakeholders, and commitments.
WhyThisMatters: Most of the solution-selling plan is assembly; the SSP should spend judgment on the pursuit decision.

Name: Pressure-test the solution strategy
Description: Test the plan against customer priorities, competitive alternatives, stakeholders, and decision criteria.
Prompt: Review this solution-selling plan against customer priorities, competitive alternatives, stakeholder coverage, proof needs, technical and commercial dependencies, and decision criteria. Return risks, gaps, missing evidence, and the next decisions needed.
RequiredContext: Draft solution-selling plan; customer context; stakeholder map; proof and constraints.
ExpectedOutput: Pressure-tested strategy with risks, gaps, and next decisions.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP confirms source accuracy, customer context, role ownership, technical/commercial dependencies, and any system action before use.
WhyThisMatters: If the solution strategy will fail, it should fail in review before it fails with the customer.

Name: Map who actually decides and who is missing
Description: Build the real decision map for this solution play, including the people who can stop it, not only the people who like it.
Prompt: Here is my solution-selling plan and the stakeholders I have engaged: [paste plan and stakeholder list with roles and engagement level]. The solution play is [paste], the decision type is [paste, for example new workload, renewal, or migration], the customer's organizational model is [paste, for example centralized IT, business-unit autonomy, or shared services], and their known procurement and technical governance constraints are [paste]. Build a decision map showing who decides, who influences, who implements, and who can block. For each person, state what they need to believe for this to move forward and what evidence would convince them. Then identify missing roles ONLY where the solution play, decision type, organizational model, or governance constraints I gave you imply that role is required. Do not list generic enterprise buying-committee roles. Do not invent names; describe missing roles by function. If my context is too thin to identify missing roles, say so rather than guessing.
ActivitySteps:
1. List stakeholders engaged so far with role and engagement level.
2. Gather the solution play, decision type, customer organizational model, and governance constraints.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Identify the highest-risk absence.
5. Decide who introduces you to that person and by when.
RequiredContext: Solution-selling plan; stakeholders engaged with roles; the solution play and decision type; the customer's organizational model; known procurement and technical governance constraints; who owns the customer relationship.
ExpectedOutput: A decision map with what each stakeholder needs to believe, plus a named list of missing roles and the risk each creates.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP validates the stakeholder reality against what the account team actually knows, and owns the plan to reach anyone missing.
WhyThisMatters: Solution plans usually fail on a person nobody engaged, not on a fact nobody knew.

Name: Convert the plan into dated commitments
Description: Reduce the plan to the few actions that will actually happen in the next 30 days, each with a named owner and a date.
Prompt: From this solution-selling plan [paste], extract only the actions that must happen in the next 30 days to clear the next customer decision. For each: what it is, who owns it by role, the date it must be done by, and what it unblocks. Limit to five actions. If the plan implies more than five critical actions in 30 days, tell me which ones are not realistic and what to cut. Do not assign an action to a person or team I have not named.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring the pressure-tested plan.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Cut to five or fewer.
4. Confirm each owner has agreed.
5. Record the dates where the account team will see them.
RequiredContext: The pressure-tested solution-selling plan; the account team and their availability; the next customer decision and its timing.
ExpectedOutput: Five or fewer dated actions with named owners and what each unblocks.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP confirms each owner has actually agreed to the action and the date, rather than being assigned it in a document.
WhyThisMatters: A plan without dates and owners is a description of intentions.

Name: Prepare the technical advisory conversation
Description: Turn approved evidence into a customer-centered plan.
Prompt: Using approved customer context and technical decision package, prepare for [meeting]. Include outcome, technical state, recommendation and tradeoffs, questions, supporting evidence, likely objections, caveats, next action and ownership. Flag claims requiring review.
RequiredContext: Approved context; technical package; desired decision.
ExpectedOutput: Technical advisory conversation plan.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA decides which tradeoffs to surface. Advisory credibility comes from naming the downside before the customer finds it, and preparation that carries only the upside reads as selling rather than advising.
WhyThisMatters: Preparation for the technical advisory conversation is the step most often skipped and most often decisive.

Name: Rehearse the architecture recommendation
Description: Role-play and coach a technical advisory conversation.
Prompt: Use the approved conversation plan to role-play with [customer/stakeholder]. Simulate realistic architecture, readiness, security, operational, cost and implementation questions. Coach clarity, evidence, listening, tradeoffs and next step. Identify claims needing SME review. Do not invent customer facts or commitments.
RequiredContext: Approved conversation plan and audience.
ExpectedOutput: Role-play transcript and improvement actions.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA owns every claim made in the room. Rehearsal makes a recommendation sound confident whether or not it is correct, and a customer hears confidence as commitment.
WhyThisMatters: Ten minutes rehearsing the architecture recommendation is cheaper than improvising it in the room.

Name: Tailor the solution value narrative
Description: Translate the solution into customer-specific outcomes, evidence, caveats, and next ask.
Prompt: Using selected approved sources, build a customer-specific value narrative for [solution play] at [account]. Include top use cases, measurable or directional outcomes, proof points, differentiation, assumptions, caveats, executive talking points, and the next ask. Flag unsupported value claims.
RequiredContext: Approved customer priorities, solution evidence, value frameworks, and target audience.
ExpectedOutput: Customer-specific value narrative with evidence and review flags.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP validates value claims, proof, ROI or adoption assumptions, tone, and final ask before customer use.
WhyThisMatters: Generic value decks lose to specific narratives grounded in customer priorities.

Name: Research evidence for the value story
Description: Investigate customer, industry, use-case, and market evidence that strengthens or challenges the value story.
Prompt: Research [customer/industry/use case] to identify relevant market evidence, customer signals, comparable proof, risks, and counterevidence for [solution play]. Separate sourced facts from recommendations and flag unsupported value or competitor claims.
RequiredContext: Customer; industry; use case; solution play; approved source boundaries.
ExpectedOutput: Evidence brief for the value narrative.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP validates source quality, applicability to the customer, and all value or competitor claims.
WhyThisMatters: Being able to cite value evidence beats remembering a generic claim.

Name: Stress-test the assumptions the value claims depend on
Description: Expose what each outcome number quietly assumes, and record which assumptions the customer would have to accept.
Prompt: Here is our value narrative and the evidence brief behind it: [paste both]. For every outcome claim, produce a row containing: the claim, the assumption it depends on, who has to accept that assumption for the claim to hold, the evidence we currently have, and what happens to the claim if adoption is half as fast as projected. Rank the rows by how much the claim collapses when its assumption fails. Do not add claims that are not in my narrative, and do not supply evidence I have not given you.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring the value narrative and evidence brief.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Find the claim that collapses hardest.
4. Either find proof for its assumption or remove the claim.
5. Bring the assumption table to the huddle.
RequiredContext: The value narrative; the evidence brief; the customer's financial context; adoption expectations already discussed with them.
ExpectedOutput: An assumption and risk table ranked by how much each claim depends on an unproven assumption.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP decides which assumptions are defensible with this customer, and owns every outcome figure before it reaches them.
WhyThisMatters: The value claim you cannot defend is the one the customer will ask about.

Name: Reduce the narrative to something the customer can forward
Description: Produce the short version your champion can send to people you will never meet, without you in the room to explain it.
Prompt: Reduce this value narrative [paste] to a single page that our champion could forward internally without us present. It must stand alone: state the business problem in the customer's own terms, the outcome, what it depends on, and what we are asking for next. Remove anything that only makes sense if a seller is explaining it. Remove any claim that is not supported by the evidence brief I gave you. Keep it under 350 words.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring the rehearsed narrative with weak claims removed.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Read it as if you were a stranger receiving it.
4. Cut anything that needs explaining.
5. Confirm the ask is specific.
RequiredContext: The rehearsed value narrative; the evidence brief; who the champion is and who they would forward it to; the next ask.
ExpectedOutput: A one-page, forwardable value summary with a specific next ask.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP verifies every claim survives without a seller present, and approves the wording before the champion receives it.
WhyThisMatters: Most internal customer decisions happen in rooms the seller is not in.

Name: Create the technical progress and value narrative
Description: Synthesize approved technical evidence.
Prompt: Using approved architecture, delivery, adoption, consumption, optimization and risk materials for [Customer], create the CSA contribution to the business review. Connect progress to supported outcomes, explain risks and decisions, identify commitments and owners, and propose next technical actions. Separate evidence from interpretation and flag unsupported value claims.
RequiredContext: Approved review sources; audience; period.
ExpectedOutput: Technical progress and value narrative.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms the link between technical progress and claimed value. Those two are frequently assembled separately and joined afterwards, and a link that does not hold is what a skeptical stakeholder tests first.
WhyThisMatters: You spend your time editing the technical progress and value narrative rather than staring at a blank version of it.

Name: Assemble the technical review package
Description: Create a repeatable customer-review package.
Prompt: Assemble a technical customer-review package from approved sources: executive technical summary, architecture and delivery progress, consumption or adoption evidence, optimization actions, material risks, open decisions, commitments and follow-through tracker. Preserve source links and flag missing or contradictory evidence.
RequiredContext: Approved source package and reviewers.
ExpectedOutput: Structured technical-review package.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms each contributor has actually reviewed their section. A package assembled from contributions is treated as jointly owned, and the contributor who never saw the final version is the one who contradicts it in the room.
WhyThisMatters: Most of the effort in the technical review package is assembly, and assembly is exactly what AI removes.

Name: Build the specialist, technical, partner, and funding plan
Description: Clarify role coverage, dependencies, asks, owners, partner/funding needs, and decision checkpoints.
Prompt: Create a pursuit orchestration plan for [opportunity] with customer outcome, solution scope, required specialist and technical roles, partner need, funding consideration, dependencies, owner for each action, decision checkpoints, and unresolved risks. Do not represent funding as approved.
RequiredContext: Approved opportunity, customer context, roles, partner criteria, funding context, and constraints.
ExpectedOutput: Pursuit orchestration plan with owners and checkpoints.
HumanCheckpoint: The SSP decides who genuinely needs to be on the v-team. Every added role dilutes accountability, and an oversized v-team is usually a sign that nobody owns the outcome.
WhyThisMatters: Pursuits stall when handoffs, partner asks, or funding dependencies are assumed rather than owned.

Name: Make each ask specific enough to be accepted
Description: Turn a role requirement into an ask a busy colleague can say yes to without a meeting to clarify it.
Prompt: From this pursuit orchestration plan [paste], write the individual ask for each role involved. Each ask must state: what specifically is needed, why this pursuit needs that role rather than someone else, what the person receives from me to make it easy, the date it is needed by, and how long it should take. Keep each ask under 80 words. Do not represent funding, approvals, or customer commitments as secured if the plan does not show them as secured.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring the orchestration plan.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Check each ask states a realistic time commitment.
4. Send the asks.
5. Record who accepted.
RequiredContext: The pursuit orchestration plan; the roles required; what you can supply to each; the customer timeline.
ExpectedOutput: One short, specific, dated ask per role, ready to send.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP verifies that no ask overstates funding, approval, or customer commitment status, and owns what is promised in return.
WhyThisMatters: A vague ask gets a polite yes and no calendar time.

Name: Catch the checkpoint that quietly slipped
Description: Compare the plan against what has actually happened and surface the dependency nobody has mentioned in two weeks.
Prompt: Here is the pursuit orchestration plan with its checkpoints and owners [paste], and here is what has actually happened since [paste updates, meeting notes, or status]. Identify every checkpoint that has passed without evidence of completion, every dependency that has gone quiet, and every owner who has not confirmed. Rank by impact on the customer timeline. For the top item, draft the one message that would restart it. Do not assume something is complete because it was not mentioned.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring the plan and recent activity. If the plan has no dated checkpoints or owners recorded, write them down first; the activity does not work without them.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Confirm which items are genuinely stalled.
4. Send the restart message for the top one.
5. Reset the checkpoint date.
RequiredContext: The orchestration plan with checkpoints and owners, written down even if only informally; recent updates, notes, or status; the customer timeline. If checkpoints and owners do not exist yet, create them before running this activity.
ExpectedOutput: A ranked list of stalled checkpoints and quiet dependencies, plus one message to restart the highest-impact item.
HumanCheckpoint: SSP confirms an item is genuinely stalled rather than simply undocumented before escalating to an owner.
WhyThisMatters: Pursuits rarely stop. They go quiet, and quiet looks like progress until the date arrives.

Name: Analyze consumption and technical blockers
Description: Connect customer and sales context to technical trajectory.
Prompt: Show consumption versus target for [Account], flag blockers, and recommend architecture, partner, or specialist actions that could improve the technical trajectory. Distinguish source facts from recommendations.
RequiredContext: Account; target period; available MSX and customer context.
ExpectedOutput: Consumption gap and blocker view with candidate actions.
HumanCheckpoint: ATS validates consumption interpretation, architecture actions, partner need, and customer context.
WhyThisMatters: The technical trajectory should respond to the blockers that are actually slowing value.

Name: Research technical options and bets
Description: Compare technical options and evidence before setting trajectory.
Prompt: Analyze the main pipeline and consumption drivers for [Account] and recommend the top three technical bets. For each include business outcome, stakeholder, security posture, AI workload readiness, adoption blocker, first conversation, and validation gap. Separate sourced evidence from recommendations.
RequiredContext: Account strategy; pipeline or consumption context; authorized sources.
ExpectedOutput: Three evidence-backed technical bets with validation gaps.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS decides what is feasible for this customer specifically. A recommendation that is technically sound and organizationally impossible consumes the credibility you needed for the achievable one.
WhyThisMatters: Technical bets should be chosen on evidence, not novelty.

Name: Delegate the technical strategy package
Description: Build a bounded strategy and validation package.
Prompt: Using the approved account context, technical bets, and source materials, create a technical strategy package with objectives, current estate, decision criteria, priority bets, proof needs, owners, milestones, risks, and open technical decisions.
RequiredContext: Approved account context, technical evidence, and constraints.
ExpectedOutput: Technical strategy package with decisions, owners, proof needs, and milestones.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS confirms the milestones are ones the customer would recognize. A roadmap sequenced for engineering convenience will not survive contact with the customer's own planning cycle.
WhyThisMatters: You should spend time editing the strategy, not staring at a blank version of it.

Name: Build the technical decision path
Description: Connect approved account and customer context to the technical decision.
Prompt: For [Customer/opportunity], summarize outcome, current technical decision, stakeholders, recent interactions available, blockers, commitments and opportunity stage. Propose a decision path with evidence required, gaps, owners, milestones and next customer-facing action. Show source signals and flag unavailable context.
RequiredContext: Authorized scope and approved technical context.
ExpectedOutput: Grounded technical decision path.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms the sequence matches how this customer actually decides. A technically logical decision path can ignore the customer's own governance, and a path that skips their approval rhythm stalls at the first gate.
WhyThisMatters: Most of the effort in the technical decision path is assembly, and assembly is exactly what AI removes.

Name: Design the validation and proof plan
Description: Create a bounded validation plan.
Prompt: Using the approved technical decision brief, build the smallest useful validation plan for [decision]. Include criteria, hypothesis, evidence available, proof gaps, activities, success measures, exit criteria, owners, milestones, dependencies, risks and expected decision. Do not expand beyond what is necessary.
RequiredContext: Approved decision brief; owner; constraints; evidence.
ExpectedOutput: Validation plan.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA decides what the plan will not prove. A validation plan that appears to cover everything invites everyone to assume their particular concern was included, and the gap is found during delivery.
WhyThisMatters: Settling the validation and proof plan before the work starts is the only version of that decision that holds.

Name: Design the executive briefing experience
Description: Plan an end-to-end executive briefing experience.
Prompt: Help me organize an EBC for [Customer]. Choose the right session design and propose a coherent timeline and prep plan. Include desired customer decisions, executive audience, participants, evidence, role contributions, preparation milestones, risks, and follow-through.
RequiredContext: Customer; executive audience; desired decisions; approved context.
ExpectedOutput: EBC plan with session design, participants, evidence, timeline, and follow-through.
HumanCheckpoint: ATS validates purpose, participants, technical narrative, evidence, and customer decision.
WhyThisMatters: An EBC only works if the decision, people, evidence, and follow-through line up.

Name: Adjust the talk track from current signals
Description: Adapt approved technical messaging using selected work context.
Prompt: Using the approved account brief, recent meetings, email, and technical source materials, identify the customer signals that should change the technical talk track. Draft revised opening language, five questions, likely objections, and responses. Separate sourced facts from recommendations.
RequiredContext: Selected authorized work sources and approved technical narrative.
ExpectedOutput: Revised technical talk track grounded in selected signals.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS decides what a signal means before acting on it. Telemetry shows what changed and never why, and the interpretation is where a routine variation becomes an unnecessary customer conversation.
WhyThisMatters: The talk track should change when the customer signal changes.

Name: Translate architecture into business value
Description: Create a concise business-value summary from approved architecture content.
Prompt: Turn this reference architecture into a one-page business value summary. Map technical choices to customer priorities, expected business outcomes, Azure consumption implications, risks, and assumptions requiring review. Quantify only when the source supports it.
RequiredContext: Approved reference architecture and supporting evidence.
ExpectedOutput: One-page technical-to-value summary with review flags.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS owns the numbers once they are said out loud. A value translation persuades precisely because it simplifies, and the simplification is where a defensible figure becomes an indefensible one.
WhyThisMatters: Architecture matters more when the customer can see the business consequence.

Name: Build the run-of-show and evidence pack
Description: Turn the approved briefing plan into the run-of-show the session is actually delivered from.
Prompt: Using the approved EBC plan, build the run-of-show: each segment in order with its time allocation, the person leading it, the evidence or demonstration used, the questions put to the customer, and the decision the session closes on. Assume the plan, participants and objectives are already agreed.
RequiredContext: Approved EBC plan, confirmed participant list, and approved evidence.
ExpectedOutput: Run-of-show with segment order, timing, owners, evidence, customer questions, and the closing decision.
HumanCheckpoint: ATS confirms every piece of evidence is approved for customer use and that each segment owner has agreed to their part.
WhyThisMatters: The plan says why the briefing exists. The run-of-show is what the room is actually delivered from.

Name: Rehearse the strategic technical talk track
Description: Practice the technical conversation and receive coaching.
Prompt: Use Agent J.ai to role-play the upcoming strategic technical conversation with [customer or stakeholder]. Use the approved narrative and focus on technical outcomes, open decisions, likely objections, evidence, and the technical ask. Pause for my response before coaching me on clarity, listening, evidence, and next step. Do not invent customer facts or commitments.
RequiredContext: Approved narrative; meeting type; customer context; desired decision.
ExpectedOutput: Interactive rehearsal, likely questions or objections, coaching, and improvement actions.
HumanCheckpoint: ATS validates customer facts, technical claims, commitments, evidence, and any response used with the customer.
WhyThisMatters: Ten minutes rehearsing the talk track is cheaper than improvising it in the room.

Name: Prepare the CxO technical briefing
Description: Build an account-grounded executive technical briefing.
Prompt: Prepare a CxO technical briefing for [Account] on [Topic]. Include customer outcomes, architecture direction, risks, proof points, executive talking points, likely questions, and the technical ask. Cite source signals where available and flag unsupported claims.
RequiredContext: Account; topic; desired decision; available MSX and customer context.
ExpectedOutput: CxO technical briefing with risks, proof points, talking points, and ask.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS owns the technical ask. A narrative can build a compelling case toward a request the customer has no mechanism to approve, and that is discovered in the room.
WhyThisMatters: The executive technical narrative needs enough evidence to be credible and enough focus to drive a decision.

Name: Build the executive technical deck
Description: Create a bounded executive-ready presentation package.
Prompt: Build a concise executive technical deck for [Account] aligned to stated outcomes and the Azure or AI roadmap. Include the story arc, proof, architecture implications, risks, open technical decisions, and review flags.
RequiredContext: Approved emails, transcripts, roadmap, and source materials.
ExpectedOutput: Executive technical deck with open decisions flagged.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS is accountable for every roadmap statement made. Roadmap language is heard as commitment however carefully it is caveated, and a slipped date attributed to you is remembered.
WhyThisMatters: Deck creation should be assembly work; judgment stays in the story, claims, and ask.

Name: Build a technical health evidence brief
Description: Synthesize approved technical context.
Prompt: Using approved sources for [Customer], build a technical health brief. Separate verified evidence from assumptions. Summarize architecture and delivery state, material technical risks, optimization opportunities, open commitments, dependencies and missing evidence. End with the three issues that most deserve CSA attention and why.
RequiredContext: Approved customer technical sources; review period; customer outcome.
ExpectedOutput: Technical health brief.
HumanCheckpoint: CSA validates architecture, delivery, support, usage interpretation, priorities and commitments.
WhyThisMatters: Most of the effort in a technical health evidence brief is assembly, and assembly is exactly what AI removes.

Name: Prioritize a technical risk response
Description: Analyze enabled certified data relevant to technical health.
Prompt: For [Customer] and [period], identify the most material enabled consumption, usage or adoption changes visible in this report. Show supporting metrics, distinguish evidence from interpretation, state what the report cannot answer, and suggest which signals warrant deeper technical review. Do not assign a health score or infer customer intent.
RequiredContext: Enabled certified report; customer; period.
ExpectedOutput: Evidence-backed signals and technical-review priorities.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA decides what is technically significant. A metric can move sharply and mean nothing, and chasing statistical noise is how technical credibility gets spent on non-problems.
WhyThisMatters: Deciding a technical risk response is really deciding what you will not do. Say it out loud.

Name: Create the technical V-team alignment brief
Description: Align technical roles, dependencies, priorities, and owners.
Prompt: Using the approved account and technical context, create a V-team alignment brief with customer outcome, priority workloads, technical decisions, risks, required roles, dependencies, owner for each action, and next checkpoint. Flag unsupported assumptions.
RequiredContext: Approved account and technical context; role list; decision needs.
ExpectedOutput: Technical V-team alignment brief with owners and checkpoints.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS confirms each named role has capacity to take the work. Orchestration that assigns without asking produces a plan everyone nods at and nobody starts.
WhyThisMatters: Most work stalls in the handoff, not the task.

Name: Assess ECIF investment opportunities
Description: Identify whether ECIF funding could accelerate technical outcomes.
Prompt: Review Opportunity ID [ID]. Using the customer architecture roadmap, consumption goals, and current deployment blockers: identify where ECIF funding could accelerate time-to-value, recommend relevant funding motions, explain expected customer outcome and directional consumption impact, and highlight risks, dependencies, or reasons ECIF may not be appropriate.
RequiredContext: Opportunity ID; architecture roadmap; consumption goals; deployment blockers.
ExpectedOutput: Prioritized ECIF funding opportunities with outcomes, impact, risks, and dependencies.
HumanCheckpoint: ATS and ECIF owner validate eligibility, funding motion, technical feasibility, consumption assumptions, dependencies, and recommendation before action.
WhyThisMatters: Investment belongs in the v-team discussion when it removes a blocker to the technical strategy.

Name: Monitor ECIF investment performance
Description: Evaluate milestone progress, deployment readiness, and consumption path.
Prompt: Analyze the proposed ECIF-funded engagement for Opportunity ID [ID]. Evaluate scope, milestones, deliverables, technical outcomes, Azure consumption goals, deployment path, risks, dependencies, and priority fixes. Provide a readiness assessment and name the decision owner.
RequiredContext: Opportunity ID; proposed engagement; scope; milestones; deliverables; technical outcomes; consumption goals.
ExpectedOutput: Engagement-quality assessment, gaps and risks, consumption-readiness assessment, and priority fixes.
HumanCheckpoint: ATS and ECIF owner validate scope quality, feasibility, consumption path, partner and customer readiness, compliance dependencies, and final funding decision.
WhyThisMatters: Realization is judged on evidence someone collected or did not collect.

Name: Prioritize AI and Azure workloads
Description: Convert enabled business insights into a workload action list.
Prompt: Turn this week’s business and technical signals into a prioritized AI and Azure workload action list. For each workload include readiness, potential impact, ACR or consumption upside if supported, blockers, owner, due date, and validation gap.
RequiredContext: Enabled Proactive Insights, MSXI data, account context, and candidate workload list.
ExpectedOutput: Prioritized workload action list with rationale, owner, and date.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS tests the upside against what this customer can actually absorb. Potential calculated from estate size ignores whether the organization has the people to deploy it.
WhyThisMatters: This converts workload interest into a decision list with owners.

Name: Research workload readiness evidence
Description: Investigate technical and external evidence before prioritization.
Prompt: Investigate [candidate workloads] for [Account]. Compare customer objectives, current estate, security posture, AI readiness, dependencies, adoption blockers, relevant external evidence, and validation gaps. Separate sourced facts from recommendations.
RequiredContext: Account context; candidate workloads; authorized internal and public sources.
ExpectedOutput: Evidence brief supporting workload prioritization.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS judges whether the source is strong enough to build a recommendation on. Architecture recommendations get quoted long after their evidence is forgotten, and a weak source becomes an unattributed fact.
WhyThisMatters: Research is useful when it exposes why a workload is ready, blocked, or not worth chasing yet.

Name: Create the technical risk register
Description: Organize technical risks using available account and business data.
Prompt: Build a weekly technical risk register for my account scope. Include affected accounts, opportunities, workload, MCEM stage, signal source, risk, likely impact, mitigation owner, and 14-day action. Flag unavailable context.
RequiredContext: Enabled MSXI or sales data; ATS account scope.
ExpectedOutput: Technical risk register with owner and action horizon.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS decides which risks are worth registering. A register that lists everything is read by nobody, and the risk that mattered becomes indistinguishable from the twenty that did not.
WhyThisMatters: Unnamed technical risk does not get owned.

Name: Build the account intelligence brief
Description: Combine work and public context into a meeting-prep brief.
Prompt: Act as my account intelligence analyst for [Account]. Build a meeting prep brief that summarizes business priorities, current technical strategy, stakeholder context, relevant KPIs, AI and Azure workload signals, open risks, recent customer commitments, and the top actions I should consider. Separate sourced facts from hypotheses and flag missing context.
RequiredContext: Account; authorized email, Teams, calendar, files, CRM or sales context, and approved public context.
ExpectedOutput: Account intelligence and meeting-prep brief with risks, priorities, and actions.
HumanCheckpoint: ATS validates current account context, stakeholder interpretation, technical risk, and customer relevance.
WhyThisMatters: Account intelligence is useful when it changes the next technical decision, not when it creates a longer dossier.

Name: Explain the KPI and locate the report
Description: Clarify the certified KPI or report behind the business signal.
Prompt: How is [KPI] calculated? Link me to the relevant report and explain the methodology, filters, and limits I should understand before using it in account technology planning.
RequiredContext: Enabled MSXI report or metric context.
ExpectedOutput: KPI definition, methodology, relevant report, and caveats.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS confirms the metric answers the question actually being asked. Two similarly named measures frequently count different things, and presenting the wrong one is worse than presenting nothing.
WhyThisMatters: If the signal is misunderstood, every technical priority built on it is suspect.

Name: Read what the customer's satisfaction data already says
Description: Pull the satisfaction, support and relationship signals for one account and separate what the data shows from what you assumed.
Prompt: Give me a CX health summary for [Customer name - TPID]. Show OSAT, DSAT and VSAT with their trend over the last four fiscal months, the ATQ and RM scores, and the most recent verbatims. Tell me which metric moved most and when it moved. Where a metric has no data for this account, say so rather than leaving it out.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring one account you own, with its TPID. CX Vitals only covers TPID-mapped accounts.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Open Sales Agent and run the prompt. There is no setup and no separate tool.
4. Compare what the data shows against what you believed about this account before you ran it.
5. Note any metric returned as no data, and treat that as unknown rather than healthy.
6. Keep the output internal. CX Vitals content is Microsoft internal and must not be shared with the customer.
RequiredContext: One account you own and its TPID; your own current read on how that customer feels; Sales Agent access.
ExpectedOutput: A satisfaction summary for one account with OSAT, DSAT, VSAT, ATQ and RM trends, recent verbatims, the metric that moved most, and any metric with no coverage named.
HumanCheckpoint: The AE decides whether the data matches the relationship they actually have. Where the score and the lived relationship disagree, that gap is the finding, and the AE names which one they trust and why.
WhyThisMatters: You already have a satisfaction signal on most accounts. Not looking at it is a choice, and it is usually the reason a deteriorating account becomes a surprise.

Name: Rank your portfolio by where satisfaction is deteriorating
Description: Compare satisfaction across the accounts you own so attention goes to the steepest decline rather than the loudest customer.
Prompt: Rank my accounts by OSAT, lowest first, and separately show me the accounts whose OSAT has declined most over the last two quarters. Flag any account scoring below 3.5. For each flagged account, show the DSAT drivers and the most negative recent verbatims. Do not compare my accounts against another seller's portfolio.
ActivitySteps:
1. Run the prompt against your own account list.
2. Separate the two lists it returns: low absolute score, and steep decline. They are different problems.
3. Pick the account where the decline is steepest rather than the score is lowest, unless the low score is new.
4. Check whether a low score reflects a known, already-owned issue before treating it as a new finding.
5. Do not attempt cross-seller comparison. CX Vitals blocks it as a privacy boundary.
RequiredContext: Your owned account list mapped to TPIDs; any known open escalations so you can discount what is already being handled.
ExpectedOutput: Two ranked views, one by absolute satisfaction and one by rate of decline, with sub-3.5 accounts flagged and DSAT drivers named for each.
HumanCheckpoint: The AE separates a low score that is already owned and being worked from one nobody has seen. Only the second needs action this week.
WhyThisMatters: A steep decline on a healthy account is a better predictor of trouble than a stable low score. Ranking by absolute score alone finds the accounts you already knew about.

Name: Turn the satisfaction finding into an owned intervention
Description: Convert one deteriorating account into a specific action with an owner, a date and the threshold that would escalate it.
Prompt: For [Customer name - TPID], I need to act on a declining satisfaction signal. Using the CX evidence, help me draft an intervention plan: what the evidence suggests is wrong, which of those causes I can address and which belong to support or delivery, the specific next action with an owner and date, and what would have to get worse before this becomes an escalation. Separate what the data evidences from what is my inference.
ActivitySteps:
1. Start from the account you selected in the previous practice.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Split the causes into ones you own and ones that belong to support, delivery or the CSU.
5. Name a real person and a real date for each action, not a team.
6. Agree the escalation threshold now, while the situation is calm, rather than at the point it is breached.
RequiredContext: The satisfaction evidence for one account; who owns support and delivery for that customer; your escalation route.
ExpectedOutput: An intervention plan naming the evidenced causes, the split between what you own and what others own, one action with owner and date, and an agreed escalation threshold.
HumanCheckpoint: The AE confirms every cause with the account team before acting on it. CX Vitals shows the symptom; it does not diagnose the cause, and acting on a wrong cause damages trust faster than acting slowly.
WhyThisMatters: A satisfaction score you have read but not acted on is worse than one you never saw, because now you knew.

Name: Mine the verbatims for what the score hides
Description: Read what customers actually wrote rather than the number it rolled up into, and find the theme the score cannot show.
Prompt: Show me all recent verbatims for [Customer name - TPID] and group them by theme. For each theme, tell me how many comments support it, whether it is getting better or worse over time, and whether it points at product, support, delivery or relationship. Quote the customer's own words rather than paraphrasing. Do not infer a theme from a single comment.
ActivitySteps:
1. Use an account where the score alone has not explained the situation.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Read the actual quotes before reading the themes.
5. Discard any theme resting on a single comment.
6. Use the customer's own vocabulary in your next conversation rather than translating it into internal terms, but never quote a verbatim directly or reveal that you have their survey responses.
RequiredContext: One account with verbatim coverage; the themes you already believe are true so you can test them.
ExpectedOutput: Verbatim themes with supporting comment counts, direction of travel, the function each points at, and the customer's own wording preserved.
HumanCheckpoint: The AE decides which themes are real signal and which are one unhappy individual. A single strong comment is not a pattern. The AE is also accountable for the boundary: verbatims inform the questions you ask, and never appear in anything the customer sees.
WhyThisMatters: The number tells you something is wrong. The verbatims tell you what. Only one of those is useful in the next customer conversation.

Name: Run a standing satisfaction sweep across your portfolio
Description: Sweep every account you own for satisfaction movement, and put the sweep on a cadence you run yourself so decline surfaces before a customer raises it.
Prompt: Across my accounts, show me current OSAT with its trend, any account scoring below 3.5, where the most negative recent verbatims sit, and where the support experience measured by ATQ is getting worse. Rank by size of recent movement rather than absolute score. Do not compare my accounts against another seller's portfolio.
ActivitySteps:
1. Confirm which of your accounts are TPID-mapped, since only those are covered.
2. Run the prompt in Sales Agent across your portfolio.
3. Compare the result against the note you kept from the last time you ran it. The movement is the finding, not the score.
4. Put a recurring reminder in your own calendar, timed to land before your account review. CX Vitals has no alerting in this version, so nothing will tell you to look.
5. Keep a short record of what you saw so the next sweep has something to compare against.
RequiredContext: Your owned account list with TPIDs; the note or record from your previous sweep if you have one; the review rhythm this should feed.
ExpectedOutput: A portfolio satisfaction sweep ranked by recent movement, with sub-3.5 accounts, negative verbatims and worsening support experience identified, plus a dated record to compare against next time.
HumanCheckpoint: The AE decides which movements are real. A single survey response can move a score on a small account without anything having changed, and the AE owns that judgment rather than the ranking.
WhyThisMatters: CX Vitals will not tell you when a customer sours; there is no alerting in this version. The sweep is the substitute, and it only works if you run it on a rhythm rather than after someone complains.

Name: Decide whether the satisfaction signal changes your ask
Description: Test the ask you were planning to make against the customer's current satisfaction and support experience, and change it if the evidence says you should.
Prompt: I am going into a conversation with [Customer name - TPID] and the ask I intend to make is [state your ask]. Based on this customer's current satisfaction and support experience, tell me whether that ask is well timed. Name anything in the recent evidence that a customer could reasonably raise in this meeting that I would struggle to answer, and suggest what I should resolve or acknowledge first. If the evidence does not justify changing the ask, say so plainly rather than inventing a concern.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write down the ask you intend to make before you run anything. The point is to test it, not to discover it.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt with that ask included.
4. Decide whether to proceed with the ask, soften it, or resolve something first.
5. Prepare an answer for anything the customer could reasonably raise.
6. Never quote the internal satisfaction data in the meeting. It shapes your preparation and stays out of the room.
RequiredContext: The account and its TPID; the specific ask you intend to make; the meeting date.
ExpectedOutput: A judgment on whether the intended ask is well timed, the issues a customer could raise that you are not ready for, and what to resolve or acknowledge before making the ask.
HumanCheckpoint: The AE decides whether to proceed with the ask. The tool can flag a poorly timed ask, but only the AE knows what the relationship can carry and what has already been discussed offline.
WhyThisMatters: Preparation usually fails at the ask, not the agenda. Walking a growth ask into a customer whose support experience is deteriorating is how a relationship gets set back a quarter.

Name: Test renewal risk against how the customer actually feels
Description: Put the customer's satisfaction signal next to your own renewal risk read, and investigate every account where the two disagree.
Prompt: For these accounts renewing in the next six months, show me the satisfaction picture for each: current OSAT and its trend, DSAT drivers, the most negative recent verbatims, and the support experience measured by ATQ. Here are the accounts and how I have currently rated their renewal risk: [paste your renewal list with your own risk rating for each]. Tell me which accounts show a deteriorating satisfaction signal, and present it next to the rating I gave so I can see where the two disagree.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring your renewal view for the next six months, with your own current risk rating for each account.
2. Paste that list into the prompt. The satisfaction data and your risk ratings live in different places, so you supply the ratings.
3. Run it in Sales Agent and look only at the disagreements.
4. For each disagreement, decide which signal you trust and write down why.
5. Raise any renewal you downgrade with the account team before it appears in a review.
RequiredContext: Your renewal portfolio for the next six months with TPIDs; your own current risk rating for each of those accounts, since the tool does not hold your risk read.
ExpectedOutput: A renewal list showing satisfaction evidence alongside your own risk rating, with the accounts where a declining signal contradicts a favorable rating explicitly identified.
HumanCheckpoint: The AE owns the renewal risk call. Satisfaction is one input, not a verdict, and a satisfied customer can still leave for commercial reasons no CX metric will show.
WhyThisMatters: Renewal risk assessed on pipeline signals alone misses the customer who is quietly unhappy and has not told you yet.

Name: Catch the escalation while it is still a conversation
Description: Use satisfaction and support-experience thresholds to find the customer heading for escalation before they get there.
Prompt: Across my accounts, find where the support experience suggests an escalation is building: OSAT below 3.5, ATQ trending worse, RM score declining, or a cluster of negative verbatims about the same theme. For each, tell me what the evidence supports and what would need to be true for this to become a formal escalation. Separate the evidenced signal from the inference.
ActivitySteps:
1. Run the prompt across your portfolio.
2. Treat threshold crossings and trend direction as separate signals; a stable low score is different from a fresh drop.
3. Check each against what delivery and support already know before raising it.
4. Choose one account and open the conversation with the customer proactively.
5. Record the escalation threshold you agreed so the next check is measured against it.
RequiredContext: Your portfolio with TPIDs; current known escalations; your delivery and support contacts for each account.
ExpectedOutput: A list of accounts with escalation risk building, the evidence behind each, and the condition that would make each a formal escalation.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSAM verifies each signal with delivery and support before raising it with the customer. CX Vitals shows dissatisfaction; it does not know what is already being fixed.
WhyThisMatters: An escalation you raise yourself is a conversation about a plan. The same issue raised by the customer is a conversation about your credibility.

Name: Find out what you actually inherited
Description: Assemble the history, relationships, open work and unresolved risk on an account you are taking on, before you speak to anyone.
Prompt: I am taking over [Account name or TPID]. Build me a picture of what I am inheriting: the customer's stated priorities, the open opportunities and their current stage, active commitments and milestones, recent support or delivery escalations, who the known stakeholders are and who owns each relationship, and anything that looks unresolved or overdue. Tell me plainly where the record is thin or stale, because that is what I most need to know before I meet this customer.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring one account you are inheriting, or one you are handing over.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate what the record says from what it does not say. The gaps matter more than the summary.
5. Write down the three questions only the outgoing seller can answer.
6. Do not contact the customer yet. The internal handoff comes first.
RequiredContext: The account you are inheriting or handing over, with its TPID; access to MSX for that account; the name of the outgoing or incoming seller.
ExpectedOutput: An inherited-context brief covering priorities, open opportunities, commitments, escalations and stakeholders, with the thin or stale parts of the record explicitly named.
HumanCheckpoint: The seller decides what the silence means. An account with no recorded risk is not a healthy account, it is an unwritten one, and the incoming seller must treat an empty field as unknown rather than as good news.
WhyThisMatters: You inherit whatever the last person wrote down, and most of what mattered was never written down. Finding that out before the customer meeting is the difference between a handover and a restart.

Name: Run the internal handoff conversation properly
Description: Turn the gaps you found into the specific questions for the outgoing seller, and capture the answers where the next person will find them.
Prompt: Here is what I found on [Account name or TPID] and here is what is missing: [paste your gaps]. Help me prepare the internal handoff conversation with the outgoing seller. Draft the specific questions I should ask about relationships, unwritten history, sensitivities, commitments made verbally, and anything that would embarrass me in front of this customer. Prioritize the questions whose answers exist only in that person's head.
ActivitySteps:
1. Start from the gaps you named in the previous practice.
2. Paste those gaps into the prompt where it asks for them, then run it.
3. Separate what the customer actually said from your interpretation of it, and label both.
4. Put the notes in the record, not in a chat message. Chat is not where the next person will look.
5. Hold the handoff conversation as well. The notes make the conversation shorter, not unnecessary.
RequiredContext: Your inherited-context brief and its gaps; time with the outgoing seller; access to update the account record in MSX.
ExpectedOutput: A prioritized question list for the outgoing seller, the answers captured in MSX rather than in private notes, and an agreed plan for who notifies the customer.
HumanCheckpoint: The seller decides what is safe to record. Some relationship context is candid and belongs in a conversation rather than a permanent field, and the seller owns that line rather than transcribing everything.
WhyThisMatters: The handoff conversation is the only chance to collect what was never written down. Held badly, the next transition starts from the same empty record.

Name: Prepare the customer conversation that earns the relationship
Description: Plan the introduction so the customer hears continuity and a reason to invest in a new relationship, not an administrative notification.
Prompt: I am being introduced to [Account name or TPID] as their new [role]. Help me prepare the first conversation. I want to show I already understand their priorities and open commitments, ask what the record cannot tell me, and give them a reason to invest in this relationship. Draft the opening, the three questions worth their time, and how I acknowledge anything that has gone wrong recently without over-promising. Do not invent history I have not confirmed.
ActivitySteps:
1. Use the context and the answers from the internal handoff.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Cut anything you cannot personally stand behind. Confidence about details you have not verified is what damages a first meeting.
5. Agree with the outgoing seller how the introduction is made.
6. Hold the meeting. The transition record stays open until you have.
RequiredContext: Your inherited-context brief and the handoff answers; the outgoing seller's introduction plan; the customer stakeholders you will meet.
ExpectedOutput: A first-conversation plan with an opening that demonstrates continuity, three questions the record could not answer, and a considered position on any recent problem.
HumanCheckpoint: The seller decides what to acknowledge. Raising a known problem you cannot yet fix builds credibility only if you also say what happens next, and the seller judges whether that is ready.
WhyThisMatters: The customer did not choose this change and is measuring whether it costs them. The first conversation is where they decide whether to invest in you or wait you out.

Name: Pressure-test what you are handing over
Description: Look at an account you are handing on and find what only exists in your own head, before it is lost.
Prompt: I am handing over [Account name or TPID]. First, based on what is recorded in MSX, tell me what an incoming seller would and would not understand about this account. Then interview me: ask me up to six questions, one at a time, designed to surface what I know that is not written anywhere, covering informal relationships, the history behind a decision, sensitivities, verbal commitments and who actually influences outcomes. Do not guess my answers. After I have answered, organize what I told you into what belongs in the record and what is better said in conversation.
ActivitySteps:
1. Choose an account you are handing over, or one you know well.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt. It will read the record first, then ask you questions; answer them as you go.
4. Be specific in your answers. The value of this is entirely in what you say, not what the tool retrieves.
5. Record the parts it identifies as belonging in the system, and plan to say the rest in conversation.
6. Check whether any verbal commitment you mentioned is captured anywhere.
RequiredContext: An account you are handing over; your own knowledge of its unwritten history; access to update the record.
ExpectedOutput: A read on what the record fails to convey, plus your own tacit knowledge drawn out through questioning and sorted into what to record and what to say in person.
HumanCheckpoint: The outgoing seller decides which commitments must be written down. A verbal commitment that dies with the handover becomes the incoming seller's credibility problem and the customer's evidence that Microsoft does not remember.
WhyThisMatters: Every seller who inherited a thin account was handed it by someone who knew more than they recorded. This is where that stops being someone else's problem.

Name: Own the ninety days after the introduction
Description: Convert what the customer said in the first meeting into commitments with dates, so the transition is judged on follow-through rather than on the meeting.
Prompt: Here is what came out of my first conversation with [Account name or TPID]: [paste your notes]. Turn this into a follow-through plan: what I committed to, what the customer asked for, what needs someone else at Microsoft, and what I should have demonstrably delivered before the ninety-day mark. Flag anything I appear to have committed to that I have not confirmed I can deliver.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open your notes from the first customer conversation.
2. Paste those notes into the prompt where it asks for them, then run it.
3. Check every commitment it identifies. Deal with anything you promised without meaning to.
4. Put dates against each item and name owners for anything that is not yours.
5. Schedule the ninety-day point now, while it still feels urgent.
RequiredContext: Your notes from the first customer conversation; the commitments you made; the Microsoft roles who would own anything outside your control.
ExpectedOutput: A ninety-day follow-through plan with commitments, owners, dates, and any unconfirmed promise flagged for resolution.
HumanCheckpoint: The seller confirms every commitment is one they can actually keep. A transition is judged on whether the first promise was kept, and an unkept one costs more than the original change did.
WhyThisMatters: Transitions are not judged by the introduction meeting. They are judged ninety days later, on whether the thing you said you would do happened.

Name: Test whether the qualification would survive the receiving role
Description: Check that an opportunity being handed on has the qualification evidence the receiving role needs, before you transfer it rather than after they reject it.
Prompt: I am handing over [opportunity name or ID] to the specialist team. Review what is documented and tell me whether a specialist receiving this could act on it immediately. Specifically: is the customer outcome clear, are the business and technical decision makers identified, is the budget and timing evidenced, are the blockers named with a mitigation, and does the milestone carry a real estimated value and date rather than a placeholder. Tell me what is missing rather than summarizing what is there.
ActivitySteps:
1. Choose one opportunity you are about to hand over, or one you recently received.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Treat every gap as work to do before the transfer, not after.
5. Check the milestone has an estimated date and a value that is not zero.
6. If you received this handoff, send the gap list back rather than rebuilding it silently.
RequiredContext: One opportunity being transferred, with its ID; the milestone attached to it; the qualification criteria your team applies.
ExpectedOutput: A gap list against the qualification the receiving role needs, covering outcome, decision makers, budget, timing, blockers and milestone completeness.
HumanCheckpoint: The sending role decides what is genuinely known versus assumed. Handing over an assumption dressed as a qualified fact is worse than handing over an acknowledged gap, because the receiving role will act on it.
WhyThisMatters: Most handoffs are rejected or quietly rebuilt because the receiving role cannot act on what arrived. The gap was always visible before the transfer; nobody looked.

Name: Write the handoff so the next role does not have to ask
Description: Capture the qualification, the customer context and the unwritten detail in the record itself, so the transfer survives without a meeting.
Prompt: Help me write the handoff notes for [opportunity name or ID] moving to [receiving role]. Cover what the customer is trying to achieve and in their own words where I have them, what has been agreed and what has not, who influences the decision and how, what I have already tried, and what I would warn the receiving person about. Write it so someone who has never spoken to this customer could pick it up. Flag anything I have written that is my opinion rather than something the customer said.
ActivitySteps:
1. Start from the gap list you produced in the previous practice.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate what the customer actually said from your interpretation of it, and label both.
5. Put the notes in the record, not in a chat message. Chat is not where the next person will look.
6. Hold the handoff conversation as well. The notes make the conversation shorter, not unnecessary.
RequiredContext: Your gap list; what the customer has said in their own words; the receiving role and who specifically will take it.
ExpectedOutput: Handoff notes covering customer outcome, agreed and unagreed items, decision influence, what has been tried, and warnings, with opinion separated from evidence.
HumanCheckpoint: The sending role decides what belongs in a permanent record. Candid relationship context may be better said than written, and the sender owns that judgment rather than transcribing everything.
WhyThisMatters: The handoff conversation happens once and is forgotten. The record is what the receiving role actually works from, and what the person after them inherits.

Name: Find the handoffs that stalled in the gap between roles
Description: Look across your opportunities and milestones for transfers that were started and never completed, where ownership is ambiguous and nothing is moving.
Prompt: Across my opportunities and milestones, find where a transfer between roles looks incomplete or stalled: ownership that changed but where nothing has happened since, milestones sitting at the same stage well past their estimated date, opportunities where the specialist or customer success team was engaged but no activity followed, and anything where I cannot tell from the record who currently owns the next action. Rank by how long each has been static.
ActivitySteps:
1. Run the prompt across your own opportunities and milestones.
