Name: Open the conversation without revealing how you found them
Description: Prepare a first approach informed by the customer's likely situation, without referencing the internal engagement data that surfaced them.
Prompt: I am making first contact with a customer who surfaced through an internal engagement signal. Here is what I know: [paste the account, the solution area, and what I have established about their situation]. Prepare an opening built on their likely business situation and what companies like them are typically working through. Do NOT reference or allude to anything they viewed, clicked, downloaded or attended, and do not imply I know what they have been looking at - that information is internal and referencing it damages trust. Give me the question I should lead with, what I should not assume, and what would tell me quickly that this is not an evaluation after all. Keep it usable in a short call or message, and do not write me a pitch.
ActivitySteps:
1. Take a signal you have decided to pursue.
2. Paste the account, solution area and situation into the prompt where it asks. Do not paste the engagement detail itself; you are not trying to reference it.
3. Read the opening back and check it does not hint at how you found them. If it would sound like surveillance to the customer, it is wrong regardless of how it was generated.
4. Check the opening question is genuinely open. If it can be answered yes or no, it will be.
5. Confirm the contact exists in MSX before relying on any drafting help, and note that outreach drafting in Sales Home is English only during preview.
RequiredContext: The account and its solution area; what you have established about their situation; a contact that exists in MSX if you intend to draft outreach.
ExpectedOutput: An opening grounded in the customer's likely business situation with no reference to internal engagement data, the assumptions to avoid, and what would show this is not a real evaluation.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS is accountable for what the customer hears. Internal engagement data is exactly that - internal - and an opening that reveals how closely someone has been tracked costs the relationship far more than the signal was ever worth.
WhyThisMatters: The signal tells you who to call. It does not give you anything you can say. Openings that leak how the seller found the customer are the fastest way to make a first conversation the last one.

Name: Read what the signals are telling you about your solution area
Description: Look back at recent signals in your solution area for what customers consistently react to, and what that says about where demand is forming.
Prompt: Here are the engagement signals in my solution area recently: [paste the list, with the topic or offer, the account profile, and whether each went anywhere]. Tell me what customers are consistently engaging with, which topics or offers generate engagement that goes nowhere, and whether the pattern differs by customer size or industry. Separate what this genuinely supports from what would be over-reading a small sample. I want to know where demand is actually forming, so be direct if the honest answer is that there is not enough here to say anything.
ActivitySteps:
1. Pull the recent signals in your solution area from Sales Accelerator or your own records.
2. Mark each as converted, still open, or went nowhere. The last group is the useful half.
3. Paste the list into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Check whether any pattern holds across customer sizes or is driven by a handful of accounts.
5. Test one finding against what you have actually heard in customer conversations, then bring it to your qualification progression discussion.
RequiredContext: Recent engagement signals in your solution area with topic, account profile and outcome; your own recollection of recent customer conversations to test findings against.
ExpectedOutput: What customers consistently engage with, what generates engagement that does not convert, whether patterns hold across customer profiles, and an honest statement where the sample is too small.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS tests the pattern against real conversations. A pattern in engagement data can be an artifact of what marketing happened to send, and the specialist is the only one positioned to know the difference.
WhyThisMatters: You see more signals in your solution area than anyone else does. What consistently fails to convert is intelligence nobody else in the territory can give.

Name: Decide what genuinely belongs with a partner
Description: Work out which of your opportunities a partner would actually serve better, rather than which ones you have least time for.
Prompt: Here are opportunities and plan priorities I am considering routing to a partner: [paste the list, with what each involves, the account, and why I am considering routing it]. For each, help me judge whether a partner genuinely serves this better or whether I am routing it because I lack capacity. Consider what the work actually needs, whether it is the kind of deployment or solution a partner typically leads, and what the customer would experience either way. Be direct where the honest answer is that I am offloading rather than orchestrating. Do not assume routing is the right answer just because I raised it.
ActivitySteps:
1. List the opportunities you are thinking about routing, with why for each.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Be honest in the ones where the real reason is capacity. That is sometimes the right call, but it should be a decision rather than a story.
4. Check whether the customer has an existing relationship with a partner already. That usually settles it.
5. Pick one to route properly, and take the others off the routing list rather than leaving them ambiguous.
RequiredContext: The opportunities or plan priorities you are considering routing; what each involves; the account and any existing partner relationship; your honest reason for considering it.
ExpectedOutput: A judgment per opportunity on whether a partner genuinely serves it better or whether it is a capacity decision, with what the customer would experience either way.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides what to route. You remain accountable for account-level orchestration after the handoff, so routing something a partner cannot serve well does not remove the problem from you, it just delays it.
WhyThisMatters: Partner-led is structural in this segment, not overflow. Routing by capacity rather than by fit is how customers end up with a partner who was never the right answer.

Name: Package it so the partner can actually act
Description: Write the referral notes a partner needs to pick the work up, keeping internal detail out of the draft from the start.
Prompt: I am sending a referral to an external partner. Here is what I can share: [paste ONLY the customer objective, what stage the conversation is at, what has been discussed, and what I want the partner to do. Do not paste financial figures, seat or license counts, individual names or contact details, or anything copied out of an internal system]. Draft the referral notes from what I have given you. Write for an external audience throughout: no financial or seat-level detail, no personally identifiable information, and nothing phrased as if it came off an internal screen, even if I have accidentally included some. If what I have given you is too thin to be worth sending, say so plainly rather than padding it out.
ActivitySteps:
1. Take the opportunity you decided to route.
2. Before pasting anything, remove financial figures, seat and license counts, individual names and contact details, and anything copied from an internal screen. Keeping it out is the control; nothing downstream will reliably catch it.
3. Paste what remains into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Read the draft yourself against your team's data-sharing rules. Do not treat the model as having cleared it - it cannot see what is identifying about your account and it will not tell you it is unsure.
5. Send it through Accept and Send to Partner, which creates the lead in Partner Center and notifies both the partner Referrals Admin and the named partner seller. Note the date, because the acceptance window starts now.
RequiredContext: The opportunity and customer objective; what has been discussed; what you want the partner to do; your team's data-sharing rules; the named partner seller.
ExpectedOutput: Referral notes covering the customer objective, conversation stage, history and your specific ask, written for an external audience, or a plain statement that there is not enough to send.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE clears the draft, and does so personally. The model cannot audit its own output for disclosure and must not be relied on to try; what makes a detail identifying is usually account context only you hold. The real control is what you decline to paste in the first place.
WhyThisMatters: Most referrals fail because the partner cannot tell what they are being asked to do. The rest fail because something crossed that should never have left - and by the time it is in the draft, the exposure has already happened.

Name: Find the referrals that are about to run out of time
Description: Check your open referrals against the acceptance and conversion windows before the system closes them for you.
Prompt: Here are my open partner referrals: [paste the list from the Partner Timeline view on each plan priority, with the date sent, whether the partner has accepted, and the date of acceptance where it happened]. The windows are 14 days for the partner to accept or decline before the lead expires, and 60 days after acceptance to qualify, convert to a co-sell opportunity, or mark it lost, after which the system marks it lost automatically. Work out from the dates which are close to either boundary, which have already passed one, and which I have not given you enough information to judge. For each one at risk, tell me whether the next move is mine or the partner's.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open the Partner Timeline view on your plan priorities to see where each referral stands.
2. Copy the list into the prompt where it asks, with dates sent and accepted, then run it.
3. Deal with anything inside a few days of a boundary first. After the boundary the system decides for you.
4. Separate the ones waiting on the partner from the ones waiting on you. Chasing the wrong one wastes the days you have left.
5. For anything the partner has gone quiet on, raise it at the weekly partner meeting rather than sending another email into silence.
RequiredContext: Your open referrals from the Partner Timeline view with dates sent and accepted; the partner sellers involved; your weekly partner meeting or PDM contact.
ExpectedOutput: Your open referrals sorted against the acceptance and conversion windows, with those near or past a boundary named, and the next move identified as yours or the partner's.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides what to chase. An expiring referral is sometimes worth letting go, but that should be a choice rather than something you discover after the system has closed it.
WhyThisMatters: These windows close on their own. A referral that expires unaccepted and one you deliberately withdrew look identical afterwards, and only one of them was a decision.

Name: Look at your last few stalled referrals for a common cause
Description: Take a small number of referrals that went nowhere and find what they had in common, rather than attempting a portfolio review.
Prompt: Here are the last few referrals I sent that expired unaccepted or stalled after acceptance: [paste up to five, with the partner, the type of work, and what happened to each]. Looking only at these, tell me what they appear to have in common: the same partner, similar kinds of work, or a similar point at which they stopped. Be explicit that a handful of referrals cannot establish a trend, and tell me what I would need to look at to know whether this is a real pattern. Give me one thing worth testing rather than a diagnosis.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring up to five referrals you remember going nowhere. Five you can recall accurately beats twenty you half-remember.
2. Note the partner, the work and what happened for each.
3. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Treat whatever it finds as a hypothesis, not a finding. Five referrals cannot tell you about your territory.
5. If the same partner appears more than once, that is a PDM conversation rather than something to solve one referral at a time.
RequiredContext: Up to five referrals you remember stalling, with the partner, the type of work and the outcome of each; your PDM contact for partner performance issues.
ExpectedOutput: What the small set appears to have in common, an explicit caveat that a handful cannot establish a trend, and one thing worth testing next.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides whether the apparent pattern is real. A few referrals with the same partner may be a performance problem or may be the partner you route most to, and only you know which.
WhyThisMatters: It is easy to conclude that partners do not follow up. Looking hard at three or four you actually remember gets you closer to the truth than a review nobody has time to run.

Name: See where your pinned-partner deals actually sit
Description: Build a stage-by-stage picture of the partner deals you track, and find where the picture and the evidence disagree.
Prompt: Here are the pinned-partner deals I track: [paste the list from Partner Center, with the co-sell stage of each, when it last moved, and what the partner last reported]. The co-sell stages run Created and Accepted at 10 percent, Qualified at 20, Developed at 40, Proposed at 60, Negotiated at 80 and Won at 100. For each deal, tell me what the stage claims is true and what would need to be true for that stage to be genuine. Identify deals whose stage has not moved for a long time relative to the others, and deals where the reported stage looks ahead of what the partner has actually described. Do not assume a stage is accurate because it is recorded.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Partner Center and pull the current stage of each pinned-partner deal you track. The agent cannot see Partner Center, so this list has to come from you.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks, with when each last moved, then run it.
3. Look for stages that are ahead of what the partner has actually described. Optimistic stage-setting is the most common distortion.
4. Pick the deal with the longest gap since it last moved.
5. Take that one into your next partner meeting rather than raising all of them at once.
RequiredContext: Your pinned-partner deals and their current co-sell stage from Partner Center; when each last moved; what the partner last reported; your partner meeting cadence.
ExpectedOutput: A read on each deal covering what its stage claims, what would make that stage genuine, which have not moved, and which look stage-inflated.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS judges whether a stage is real. Partners set their own stages and have every reason to be optimistic, and the specialist who knows the deal is the only one who can tell an advancing deal from an advancing number.
WhyThisMatters: Partner deals rarely fail loudly. They sit at a stage that looks respectable while nothing underneath it moves, and nobody asks because the number is not obviously wrong.

Name: Work out what is actually blocking the stalled one
Description: Establish why a partner deal has stopped between stages and who is genuinely able to move it.
Prompt: A pinned-partner deal has stopped moving between stages. Here is what I know: [paste the deal, its current stage, how long it has been there, what the partner has told me, and anything I know from the customer side]. Help me work out what is most likely blocking it: partner capacity or skills, a customer-side decision, a technical dependency, a commercial or licensing issue, or the partner deprioritizing it. For each possibility, tell me what evidence would confirm or rule it out, and which role would own it - partner seller, partner development manager, the account executive, or me. Name the role rather than a person, since you cannot know the individuals. Do not guess at a cause the evidence does not support.
ActivitySteps:
1. Take the deal with the longest gap from the previous practice.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Rule out causes before acting on one. Treating a partner capacity problem as a customer problem loses weeks.
4. Map each named role to the actual person on this deal.
5. If the cause is partner performance rather than this specific deal, that belongs with the PDM, not in another deal conversation.
RequiredContext: The stalled deal, its stage and how long it has been there; what the partner has reported; anything you know from the customer side; your PDM and account executive contacts.
ExpectedOutput: Ranked likely causes with the evidence that would confirm each, the owning role for each, and the cause you have chosen to act on.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS confirms the cause before escalating. A deal stalled because the partner lacks capacity and one stalled because the customer went quiet need completely different interventions, and guessing wrong costs the deal a cycle it may not have.
WhyThisMatters: A stalled partner deal has one cause and several plausible stories. The stories are usually more comfortable than the cause.

Name: Prepare the partner conversation with one specific ask
Description: Turn a stalled deal into a partner conversation that produces a commitment rather than an update.
Prompt: I am taking a stalled deal into a conversation with the partner. Here is the situation: [paste the deal, its stage, what I believe is blocking it, and what I am able to offer to help]. Help me prepare the conversation: how to raise it as a shared problem rather than an inspection, the one specific thing I am asking them to commit to, what I will do in return, and how we will both know within a short period whether it moved. Do not invent support or resources I have not told you I can offer. Keep it to a single ask; a conversation with four asks produces none.
ActivitySteps:
1. Take the stalled deal and its likely cause.
2. Decide what you can genuinely offer before you run anything, and include it. If you do not, it will invent something you cannot deliver.
3. Paste the situation into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Cut it down to one ask. This is the step people skip and it is the one that decides whether anything happens.
5. Raise it in the deal clinic or partner rhythm rather than as a separate escalation, so it lands as working the deal rather than checking up on them.
RequiredContext: The stalled deal and its stage; what you believe is blocking it; what you are genuinely able to offer; your partner meeting or deal clinic cadence.
ExpectedOutput: A conversation plan framing the stall as a shared problem, with one specific ask, what you will do in return, and how both sides will know shortly whether it moved.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides how hard to push. Partners choose where to put their capacity, and a conversation that feels like an audit moves this deal at the cost of the next five.
WhyThisMatters: Partner conversations default to status updates, which change nothing. A single specific ask with something offered in return is what turns a rhythm into progress.

Name: Look at where your recent deals stopped
Description: Take a small number of recent partner deals and check whether they stopped at the same stage.
Prompt: Here are a few partner deals I have tracked recently and what happened to each: [paste up to five, with the partner, the stage each reached, and whether it progressed or stalled]. Looking only at these, tell me whether they stopped at a similar stage and what is different about any that got through. Be explicit that this is too small a set to establish a pattern, and tell me what I would need to see to know whether it is real. Give me one thing worth watching for rather than a conclusion.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring up to five recent partner deals from Partner Center. The agent cannot see Partner Center, so this comes from you.
2. Note the partner, the stage reached and the outcome for each.
3. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Treat any apparent stage boundary as something to watch for, not as a finding. Five deals cannot tell you where your portfolio stalls.
5. If it does keep recurring, raise it in your partner rhythm as something to look at earlier, not as a scorecard.
RequiredContext: Up to five recent partner deals with the partner, the stage reached and the outcome; your partner rhythm or deal clinic.
ExpectedOutput: Whether the small set stopped at a similar stage, what differs about any that progressed, an explicit caveat about sample size, and one thing worth watching for.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides whether a repeated stage is a real bottleneck. It may equally be the stage where optimistic early staging finally meets reality, and telling those apart needs someone who saw the deals.
WhyThisMatters: Chasing individual stalled deals is endless. Noticing that several stopped at the same point is what turns it into something you can change upstream.

Name: Explain the consumption movement before you react to it
Description: Take the accounts whose consumption has moved sharply and work out which movements actually mean something.
Prompt: Here are the accounts in my portfolio whose consumption has moved sharply: [paste the list, with the account, the direction and rough size of the movement, and anything I already know about what changed]. For each, give me the plausible explanations and what would distinguish them: a genuine change in usage, a workload landing or completing, a migration or seasonal pattern, a billing or reporting artifact, or something going wrong. Tell me which movements look like they need a human and which look self-explanatory. Do not treat a sharp move as automatically bad, and do not treat a rise as automatically good.
ActivitySteps:
1. Pull the accounts in your portfolio with significant consumption movement. If you have no other filter, a swing of around a quarter month on month in either direction is a reasonable place to start.
2. Paste the list into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Separate the movements you can already explain from the ones you cannot. Only the second group is work.
4. Watch for rises that are not good news, such as a workload running hotter than the customer intended.
5. Carry forward only the accounts where the explanation genuinely needs a person.
RequiredContext: Your portfolio and its consumption movement; the direction and rough size of each move; anything you already know about workloads landing, migrating or completing.
ExpectedOutput: Each significant movement with its plausible explanations, what would distinguish them, and a split between movements needing a human and movements that explain themselves.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what a movement means. Consumption data shows the shape of a change but not its cause, and a decline during a planned migration and a decline from a failing deployment look identical in the number.
WhyThisMatters: Movement in a consumption number tells you something changed, not what changed. Chasing the movement rather than the reason is how a month's attention gets spent on accounts that were always going to be fine.

Name: Decide where you go and what the partner takes
Description: Split the accounts that need attention into the few you will work yourself, the ones a partner is better placed to take, and the coverage gap that is left.
Prompt: Here are the accounts from my portfolio that need attention, and here is roughly what capacity I have: [paste the accounts with what each appears to need, and say honestly how many I can realistically work myself this month]. Help me split them into the ones where my own technical involvement changes the outcome, and the ones a partner is better placed to take. For each, say what makes it that category. Do not distribute them evenly to make the list look covered. Then tell me how much of what needs attention is left over once my capacity and the partner's are accounted for, and help me describe that gap in terms of what it would take to close it. Do not name individual accounts in that summary; I need the size and shape of the gap, not a list.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring the accounts that survived the previous practice, and be honest about your capacity.
2. Paste both into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Push back on any split that quietly assumes you have more capacity than you said.
4. For the partner group, check the partner actually has coverage and capability for that workload before routing.
5. Take the leftover gap to your manager as a capacity question rather than carrying it privately. Coverage at this ratio is set above you, and it can only be solved where it was set.
RequiredContext: The accounts needing attention and what each appears to need; your genuine capacity this month; which partners cover your workloads and where they have capability; your next manager conversation.
ExpectedOutput: Your accounts split into personally worked and partner-routed with the reason for each, plus a description of the remaining coverage gap in terms of scale and what would close it.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA owns the split and decides what to escalate. At this coverage ratio some demand will exceed what you and your partners can absorb, and the useful response is a capacity conversation with your manager rather than a private list of accounts you are not reaching.
WhyThisMatters: Coverage at scale is a series of choices about what not to do. Made explicitly it is a strategy you can defend and escalate; made by default it is whichever account shouted loudest getting the time.

Name: Design an intervention that works after you leave
Description: Take a stalled milestone and build the fix around the fact that you will not be back on this account for some time.
Prompt: Here is a stalled committed milestone on one of my accounts: [paste the milestone, the workload, what has been deployed, what usage looks like, and who is involved on the customer and partner side]. I cover a large portfolio, so assume I get one substantive intervention here and will not be back on this account for months. Work out what stands between this and real usage, then design the intervention around that constraint: what I must do myself while I am engaged, what has to be handed to the partner or the customer to carry on without me, what would tell them it is going wrong after I have gone, and who they escalate to. Reject any option that only works if I stay involved. Name roles rather than individuals, since you cannot know the people.
ActivitySteps:
1. Take one account you decided to work yourself, and one stalled milestone on it.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Separate deployed from used. A milestone can be technically complete and commercially worthless.
4. Check every step of the plan against whether it survives you leaving. Anything that needs you next month is not a plan, it is a delay.
5. Name the person who carries it and the signal that tells them it is failing, then tell them both, before you disengage.
RequiredContext: One stalled committed milestone and its workload; what has been deployed; what usage shows; the customer and partner people involved; a realistic view of when you would next touch this account.
ExpectedOutput: What stands between the milestone and real usage, an intervention split into what you do now and what is handed on, the failure signal the carrier should watch for, and the escalation route once you have disengaged.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what can safely be handed over. Handing work to a partner or a customer who cannot carry it is worse than not intervening at all, because everyone then believes it is covered, and at this coverage ratio nobody will check for months.
WhyThisMatters: At a large coverage ratio the intervention that only works while you are watching is not an intervention. The test of the fix is whether it is still working the month after you moved on.

Name: Look for the thing several declining accounts share
Description: Take a small number of accounts whose consumption has fallen and check whether the cause is the same one.
Prompt: Here are a few accounts in my portfolio where consumption has declined recently: [paste up to five, with the workload, roughly when the decline started, and what I know about each]. Looking only at these, tell me whether they appear to share a cause, such as the same workload, a similar point after deployment, the same partner, or a similar customer profile. Be explicit that a handful of accounts cannot establish a pattern, and tell me what I would need to look at to know whether it is real. Give me one thing worth testing rather than a conclusion.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring up to five accounts you have seen declining. Five you can describe accurately beats twenty you cannot.
2. Note the workload, roughly when each started declining, and anything you know about the cause.
3. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Treat any shared cause as a hypothesis. Five accounts cannot tell you about a portfolio of this size.
5. If it does look systemic, that is worth raising in your rhythm, because a shared cause is the only kind you can fix at this coverage ratio.
RequiredContext: Up to five declining accounts with the workload, roughly when the decline began, and what you know about each; your team rhythm for raising systemic findings.
ExpectedOutput: Whether the small set appears to share a cause, an explicit caveat about sample size, and one thing worth testing next.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA judges whether an apparent shared cause is real. Several accounts declining on the same workload may be a product problem or may simply be the workload you sold most of last year.
WhyThisMatters: One-by-one intervention does not scale to this many accounts. A cause shared across several of them is the only kind of finding that changes more than one outcome.

Name: Find what your design assumes that you never wrote down
Description: Surface the technical context sitting in your head that a partner would need and does not have.
Prompt: Here is a solution design I have been working on: [paste the design, the customer situation, and the constraints as I understand them]. A partner who was not in any of the discovery conversations is going to build this. Read it the way they would and tell me what they could not work out from what is written: decisions I have made without recording why, customer constraints I know but have not stated, dependencies I am assuming are handled, and anything where I have used shorthand that only makes sense internally. Be specific about what is missing rather than telling me to add more detail. If a section would leave a competent engineer guessing, say which section and what they would guess wrong about.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring a design you are working on that a partner will deliver.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks, along with the constraints as you understand them, then run it.
3. Look hardest at the decisions you made without recording the reason. Those are what get reversed by someone who did not know why.
4. Add the missing context rather than removing the part that needs it.
5. Check whether any gap is something the customer told you verbally. Those never make it across unless you write them down.
RequiredContext: A design a partner will deliver; the customer situation and constraints as you understand them; the decisions you made and why.
ExpectedOutput: The specific gaps a partner would hit, covering unrecorded decisions, unstated constraints, assumed dependencies and internal shorthand, with what they would get wrong in each case.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what genuinely needs recording. Only the person who was in the room knows which constraint was casually mentioned and turns out to be load-bearing, and that is exactly the kind of thing that never reaches the partner.
WhyThisMatters: The design in your head is always more complete than the one on the page. The gap between them is where delivery goes wrong, and it is invisible to the person who wrote it.

Name: Check the design against who is actually going to build it
Description: Test whether the partner you have in mind can deliver this design, and change the design if they cannot.
Prompt: Here is the design and here is what I know about the partner who will deliver it: [paste the design, and what I know about this partner's capability, capacity, and what they have built before]. Tell me where the design and the partner do not match: capability the design assumes that I have no evidence this partner has, parts that would be straightforward for them, and parts where a different approach would reach the same customer outcome with less risk. Where I have not told you enough about the partner, ask rather than assuming they can do it. Do not simply lower the ambition of the design; if a simpler approach genuinely costs the customer something, say so.
ActivitySteps:
1. Start from the design you worked on in the previous practice.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks, with what you actually know about the partner, then run it.
3. Answer its questions about the partner rather than letting it assume. The agent has no view of partner capability.
4. Decide whether to change the design or change the partner. Both are legitimate; carrying on with a mismatch is not.
5. If you change the design, note what the customer gives up. That is a conversation someone will need to have.
RequiredContext: The design; what you know about the partner's capability, capacity and delivery history; who to talk to if a different partner is needed.
ExpectedOutput: Where the design and the partner do not match, what would be straightforward, lower-risk alternatives that reach the same outcome, and what the customer gives up if the approach changes.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE judges partner capability. There is no system view of what a given partner can actually build, only what they have been certified for, and the difference between those two is usually discovered during delivery.
WhyThisMatters: A design is only as good as the team that will build it. Engaging the partner after the design is fixed means either a rebuild or a disappointed customer.

Name: Diagnose something a partner built
Description: Work out what is wrong with a deployed solution you did not build, when the person who built it made decisions nobody recorded.
Prompt: A solution a partner built is not working as intended. Here is what I have: [paste the symptoms, the intended design, what the partner has told me about how they actually built it, and what the customer is experiencing]. Help me work out where to look. Separate the possibilities into where the build has diverged from the intended design, where the design itself was wrong for this environment, where something in the customer's environment has changed since it was delivered, and where the solution is working as built but not as the customer expected. For each, tell me what evidence would confirm it and what I should ask the partner. Do not assume the build matches the design; that is the thing I am testing.
ActivitySteps:
1. Bring a partner-delivered solution that is not working as intended.
2. Paste the symptoms and both the intended design and what you know of the actual build into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Establish what was actually built before diagnosing why it fails. The design tells you the intent, not the implementation.
4. Ask the partner the specific questions rather than requesting a general update. A general update returns a general answer.
5. Separate a broken build from a design that was wrong. Those go to different people and confusing them costs a cycle.
RequiredContext: The symptoms and what the customer is experiencing; the intended design; whatever the partner has said about how they actually built it; your contact at the partner.
ExpectedOutput: Candidate causes separated into build divergence, design error, environment change and expectation mismatch, with the confirming evidence for each and the specific questions to put to the partner.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether this is a build problem or a design problem before raising it. Telling a partner their build is wrong when the design was wrong damages a relationship you will need on the next twenty deals, and the two look identical from the symptoms.
WhyThisMatters: You get called when something a partner built stops working, and you will not have the decisions they made along the way. Working out what was actually built is most of the diagnosis.

Name: Work out whether the partner can run this proof instead of you
Description: Decide whether a proof genuinely needs your hands on it, or whether the partner can run it with the right preparation from you.
Prompt: A proof of concept is going ahead and I need to decide whether I run it or the partner does. Here is the situation: [paste what the proof has to demonstrate, what I know about this partner's capability with this technology, what the customer expects, and my own read on whether the customer needs to see Microsoft in the room]. I cover a territory, so my time on one proof is time off everything else. Help me decide: which parts genuinely need me, which the partner could run with preparation, and what I would have to give them for that to work. If my read is that the customer needs Microsoft present, take that as given rather than arguing with it, and tell me the smallest presence that satisfies it.
ActivitySteps:
1. Take a proof that is going ahead, and the partner assessment from the previous practice.
2. Decide your own read on whether the customer needs Microsoft in the room before you run anything. The agent cannot judge that and should not try.
3. Paste the situation into the prompt where it asks, including that read, then run it.
4. Be honest about what the partner would need from you. A proof handed over without preparation comes back as an escalation.
5. If you hand it over, agree in advance what they tell you and when, so you find out it is going wrong before the customer does.
RequiredContext: What the proof must demonstrate; what you know of the partner's capability with this technology; what the customer expects; your own judgment on whether Microsoft needs to be present.
ExpectedOutput: A split of the proof into what needs you, what the partner can run with preparation, what you must give them, and the reporting you have agreed if you hand it over.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE judges whether the customer needs Microsoft in the room. That is a read on the relationship rather than on the technology, the seller is the only one who has it, and getting it wrong either burns a week of territory time or loses the customer's confidence in the proof.
WhyThisMatters: At territory coverage the proofs you personally run are the ones you are not spending elsewhere. Deciding what genuinely needs your hands, rather than defaulting to running everything, is what makes the coverage work.

Name: Split the territory into covered, partner-covered and neither
Description: Produce an honest three-way coverage read across the whole territory rather than a list of the accounts already front of mind.
Prompt: List every account in my territory and group them three ways: accounts where I have had direct activity recorded this quarter, accounts with an open partner referral or co-sell opportunity of any status, and accounts with neither. For the second group, show the referral or co-sell record and whatever status field it currently carries, without interpreting what that status means. For the third group, show the account name, its segment, any open opportunity, and the date of the most recent recorded activity of any kind.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Replace nothing - it runs against the territory already assigned to you in MSX.
3. Read the third group first and count it.
4. For every account in the second group, open the Partner Timeline view on the plan priority and confirm whether the referral was actually accepted. A sent referral is not coverage.
5. Move anything not accepted into your uncovered count.
6. Note the accounts where the most recent activity date surprises you.
RequiredContext: Your assigned territory in MSX. Your open partner referrals and their acceptance status from the Partner Timeline view.
ExpectedOutput: A three-way coverage read across the full territory with the uncovered accounts named and counted, not estimated.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides what counts as coverage, and confirms partner acceptance in the Partner Timeline before counting an account as covered. The agent can see that a referral exists but not whether a partner picked it up, and an unaccepted referral is an account you have told yourself is handled.
WhyThisMatters: Most territory reads start from the accounts already in mind, which is exactly the set that is already covered. Starting from the whole list is what surfaces the accounts nobody has touched.

Name: Test the plan priorities that were assigned to you
Description: Work the preloaded plan priorities against their window and decide which ones genuinely fit the territory rather than working them in the order they arrived.
Prompt: Show my open plan priorities with the date each was created, the account it sits against, and any recorded activity on that account since. For each, state what the priority is asking me to do and whether anything in the account record suggests it is already underway, already lost, or still untouched. Flag any where the account has had no activity at all.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Check each priority against the fourteen-day window from its creation date.
3. Separate the ones that fit your territory strategy from the ones that arrived because a model scored them.
4. Decide explicitly which ones you are not going to work, and record the reason.
5. Take the one closest to expiring into an action today.
RequiredContext: Your open plan priorities in MSX Plans, with their creation dates.
ExpectedOutput: Plan priorities sorted by remaining window with an explicit worked-or-declined decision recorded against each.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides which priorities are worth the window. A priority that was generated for you is not evidence that the account is ready, and declining one deliberately is a legitimate answer that a priority left to expire silently is not.
WhyThisMatters: Preloaded priorities carry a fourteen-day SLA and expire whether or not anyone looked. A declined priority and an ignored one are identical in the data and completely different in practice.

Name: Prepare the uncovered accounts for a partner conversation
Description: Turn the uncovered part of the territory into something a partner can act on, inside the rules that govern what may be shared.
Prompt: For these accounts [paste the uncovered accounts from your coverage read], summarize what would help a partner decide whether to take them on: industry, size band, the workloads already in place, any open opportunity and its stage, and the reason the account is uncovered. Write it as a briefing for someone outside Microsoft. Do not include contact names, contact details, seat counts, spend figures or anything that reads as an export from our systems.
ActivitySteps:
1. Take the uncovered accounts from your coverage read._x000D_
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [paste the uncovered accounts from your coverage read] with your actual list._x000D_
3. Read the output specifically for anything CELA rules exclude: personal data, seat-level or financial detail, or anything that looks like a screenshot or export._x000D_
4. Remove anything that crosses that line before the partner conversation._x000D_
5. Decide which accounts you are genuinely offering rather than offering everything at once.
RequiredContext: Your uncovered accounts from the coverage read. The CELA rules on what may be exchanged with a partner.
ExpectedOutput: A partner-ready briefing on the uncovered accounts with the data-sharing boundary respected before anything leaves Microsoft.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE owns what crosses the boundary to a partner and checks the output against the CELA rules before the conversation, not after. A model asked for a helpful summary will include contact and commercial detail because it is helpful, and the sender is the only control on that.
WhyThisMatters: Partner-led coverage is structural in this segment, so the uncovered part of the territory is usually a partner conversation rather than a personal to-do list. The constraint is that partner exchange is governed.

Name: Build the coverage position you will defend at Territory Health
Description: Prepare the coverage argument for the bi-weekly review, including the part that does not look good.
Prompt: Using my coverage read, draft the position I will take into a territory health review: how many accounts I am working directly, how many sit with a partner and are confirmed accepted, how many are covered by neither, and what I am doing about the third group. State plainly where the coverage is thin. Identify the two questions a manager is most likely to ask about this position and what evidence would answer them.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Check the numbers against your own coverage read rather than accepting them.
3. Decide which gap you are going to raise yourself rather than waiting to be asked.
4. Prepare the specific support ask that follows from it.
RequiredContext: Your completed coverage read. The territory health review cadence for your pod.
ExpectedOutput: A defensible coverage position with the thin areas surfaced deliberately and a specific support ask attached.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides which gap to raise first. Bringing your own worst number to a review is a judgment about credibility that pays off over quarters, and no analysis can make that call for you.
WhyThisMatters: The bi-weekly territory health review runs with the full v-team present. The coverage position is going to be discussed whether or not you prepared it.

Name: Separate propensity from evidence across your solution area
Description: Split the accounts your solution area is pointed at into those where something has actually happened and those where only a model says it should.
Prompt: For the accounts in my solution area, list each one with any recorded engagement: opportunities open in my solution area, recent activity, and any engagement signal that has come through. Group them into accounts with recorded engagement in my solution area, accounts with recorded engagement elsewhere but not in mine, and accounts with none. Show what the engagement actually was rather than only that it existed.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Read the third group and compare it against where you have been spending time.
3. For the second group, note whether the engagement elsewhere gives you a route in.
4. Identify any account you are actively supporting that appears in the third group.
RequiredContext: Your solution area. The territories and accounts you support.
ExpectedOutput: Solution-area accounts split by whether engagement is recorded in your area, elsewhere, or nowhere.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what counts as engagement in their area. A model can only see what was recorded, and the strongest signal in this segment is often a conversation the DAE had that never made it into a field.
WhyThisMatters: Propensity models produce long lists that all look equally promising. The accounts that convert are the ones where something has already started, and that distinction is visible in the record.

Name: Find the blocker that repeats across your accounts
Description: Look across every territory you support for the objection or dependency that keeps recurring, because a pattern is a solution-area problem while a single instance is an account problem.
Prompt: For the open opportunities in my solution area across all the territories I support, show each one with its stage, the date it last moved, and any recorded blocker, objection or competitor. Group the ones that have not moved stage in over a month by what the record says is blocking them. Show me which blockers appear on more than one account and how many accounts each one affects.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt._x000D_
2. Read the grouped blockers before the individual accounts._x000D_
3. Identify any blocker appearing on three or more accounts - that is a solution-area problem, not a deal problem._x000D_
4. Decide whether it needs a reusable answer, a specialist, or an escalation._x000D_
5. Take the single-account blockers back to the relevant DAE separately.
RequiredContext: The territories you support. Your solution area. The blockers and objections recorded against your open opportunities.
ExpectedOutput: Stalled opportunities grouped by recorded blocker, with the recurring blockers separated from the account-specific ones and a decision on the largest pattern.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether a repeated blocker is genuinely one problem or several that were described in similar words. Free-text blocker fields are written by different people in different territories, and only the specialist who knows the solution area can tell a real pattern from a vocabulary coincidence.
WhyThisMatters: A blocker on one account is that account's problem. The same blocker on five accounts is a solution-area problem with a reusable answer, and only the role that sees across territories is positioned to notice.

Name: Prepare one account for qualification progression
Description: Take an account with both propensity and evidence and build the case you would put in front of the weekly qualification progression.
Prompt: For [account name], assemble what is known: the workloads already in place, any open opportunity and its stage, the engagement recorded in my solution area, and the decision criteria captured so far. Identify what is missing before this could be treated as a qualified opportunity in my solution area, and state which of those gaps a customer conversation would close and which need internal work.
ActivitySteps:
1. Choose an account that appeared in the propensity-with-evidence group._x000D_
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [account name] with that account._x000D_
3. Separate the gaps that need the customer from the gaps that need the DAE or a specialist._x000D_
4. Decide the single question you most need answered._x000D_
5. Take it into the weekly qualification progression for your solution area.
RequiredContext: One account with recorded engagement in your solution area. The qualification criteria your solution area applies.
ExpectedOutput: A qualification case for one account with the gaps separated into customer-facing and internal, and the single most important question named.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides which gap actually blocks qualification. A gap list treats everything as equally missing, and the specialist is the one who knows which single answer would change the decision.
WhyThisMatters: Qualification progression runs weekly and rotates by solution area. Arriving with a specific question is materially different from arriving with a status update.

Name: Test whether you and the DAE are reading the same territory
Description: Find the accounts where the solution-area view and the account view disagree, because that gap is usually where the work is.
Prompt: For the territory I support, list the accounts with an open opportunity in my solution area. Separately, list the accounts with any activity recorded in the last thirty days. Show which accounts appear in the second list but not the first. For each of those, state what workloads are already in place and whether anything in the record suggests an opening for my solution area.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Look specifically at accounts with recent activity where your solution area has nothing open.
3. Pick one and work out whether that is a genuine gap or a correct exclusion.
4. Raise it in your next conversation with the DAE.
RequiredContext: The territory you support. Your solution area.
ExpectedOutput: The accounts where the account view and the solution-area view disagree, with one investigated.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether a disagreement is a gap or a correct exclusion. The DAE may have excluded your solution area for a reason that was never written down, and asking is faster than inferring.
WhyThisMatters: The DAE and the DSS read the same territory through different lenses, and the accounts that appear in one view but not the other are where the two roles most often lose each other.

Name: Assess what the partner has actually delivered, not agreed to
Description: Build the capacity picture from what has moved rather than from what was promised in the last planning session.
Prompt: For [partner name], list the co-sell opportunities and referrals currently associated with them: the stage of each, the date it last moved, and how long it has been at its current stage. Separate the ones progressing from the ones static for more than a month. Do not infer partner capacity or intent from the pattern; just show me what has moved and what has not.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [partner name] with your partner._x000D_
2. Read the static group and note how long the oldest has been sitting._x000D_
3. Check the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center directly for anything approaching the fourteen-day accept or sixty-day convert window._x000D_
4. Form your own read on whether the pattern is capacity, incentive or attention.
RequiredContext: One partner you work with. Their associated co-sell opportunities and referrals in MSX. Partner Center or the Partner Timeline view for partner-side status.
ExpectedOutput: A movement-based read on one partner separating progressing work from static work, with the oldest static item identified.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS interprets what the pattern means. Movement data shows what happened and not why, and capacity, incentive and attention produce very similar-looking stalls while needing completely different conversations.
WhyThisMatters: Partner capacity assessed from the planning conversation reflects intent. Assessed from what actually moved, it reflects reality, and the two are often a long way apart.

Name: Build the joint plan inside the data rules
Description: Assemble the joint plan content that can legitimately be shared, and find what you were about to include that cannot.
Prompt: Draft a joint planning input for a partner covering these accounts [list the accounts]. For each, include the industry, the size band, the workloads in place, the open opportunity and its stage, and the specific help being asked of the partner. Write it for an audience outside Microsoft. Exclude contact names and details, seat counts, spend or consumption figures, and anything that reads as an export or screenshot from our systems.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [list the accounts] with the accounts in scope._x000D_
2. Put the output side by side with the account records you drew from._x000D_
3. Go field by field through what you can see in MSX and check whether each one made it into the draft. Do not ask the model what it left out - if it missed the instruction, it cannot tell you it missed it._x000D_
4. Remove anything CELA rules exclude: personal data, seat or spend detail, anything resembling an export._x000D_
5. Decide what genuinely needs to be in the plan versus what you were including out of habit.
RequiredContext: The accounts in scope for the joint plan. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
ExpectedOutput: A joint planning input that respects the data-sharing boundary, with the excluded material listed explicitly rather than silently dropped.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS checks the draft against the source records before it leaves Microsoft, rather than asking the model to confirm its own compliance. A model told to exclude something will usually comply and will occasionally rephrase it instead, and it cannot report an instruction it did not register.
WhyThisMatters: Partner exchange is governed by CELA rules covering personal data, exports and commercial detail. The failure mode is not malice; it is a helpful summary that includes one field too many.

Name: Find where the plan asks more of the partner than it looks like
Description: Test the joint plan for the operational load it actually places on the partner, and take the economics to the PDM rather than guessing at them.
Prompt: I am building a joint plan with a partner covering [describe the accounts and the ask]. Working only from what I have described, analyze the operational shape of what I am asking: which parts require significant partner effort before any revenue is realized, which depend on the partner holding skills or capacity I have not confirmed, which have long lead times, and which would compete for the same people at the same time. Do not speculate about partner incentives, margins, programs, or compensation - you do not have access to those and I will confirm them separately. Return the operational load analysis only.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [describe the accounts and the ask] with your plan._x000D_
2. If the output mentions incentives, margin, rebates or program tiers, discard those lines - it does not have that data._x000D_
3. Take the operational load analysis into your PDM conversation and ask the economic question there: does this plan pay the partner enough to prefer it over what else they could be doing._x000D_
4. Pick the one conflict most likely to matter and raise it directly with the partner.
RequiredContext: Your draft joint plan and the specific ask it makes of the partner. Access to your PDM for anything incentive, margin or program related.
ExpectedOutput: An operational load analysis of what the plan asks of the partner, with the economic question routed to the PDM rather than answered by the agent.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS owns the economic judgment and takes it to the PDM. Partner incentive and program detail is outside what this agent can see, so anything it offers on margin or compensation is invention wearing a confident sentence, and the operational analysis is the only part worth carrying forward.
WhyThisMatters: Plans fail where they ask a partner to do something that pays less than the alternative. The operational load is visible in the plan itself; the economics are not, and guessing at them is how a joint plan gets built on a false premise.

Name: Set the trigger that tells you the plan has stopped being true
Description: Decide in advance what observable change would mean the joint plan needs revisiting, rather than discovering it at the quarterly review.
Prompt: For this joint plan [summarize the plan and its key assumptions], help me define what I should watch to know it is drifting. For each key assumption, suggest an observable change that would indicate it is no longer holding, where that change would be visible, and how soon it would realistically show. Distinguish changes I can see in our own systems from changes I would only learn from the partner directly.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [summarize the plan and its key assumptions] with your plan._x000D_
2. Separate the signals visible in MSX from the ones that require a partner conversation._x000D_
3. Choose one trigger you will genuinely check rather than several you will not._x000D_
4. Set the date and put it in the partner rhythm.
RequiredContext: Your agreed joint plan and its underlying assumptions. Your partner meeting cadence.
ExpectedOutput: One named trigger with a place to observe it and a date to check it, tied into the existing partner rhythm.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides which single trigger is worth committing to. A monitoring plan with six triggers gets checked once, and choosing the one that would actually change your behavior is the judgment that makes it survive.
WhyThisMatters: Joint plans degrade quietly. The quarterly review is where drift is usually discovered, which is one quarter after it could have been corrected.

Name: Find out who is already in this account
Description: Establish who holds the relationship before preparing, because at this account load it is often not you.
Prompt: For [account name], show me who is already engaged: every recorded contact and when they were last spoken to, which Microsoft roles have recorded activity, any partner referral or co-sell record attached, and any open support or delivery interaction. Then summarize the products and workloads in place, open opportunities and their stage, and the agreement dates on record. List what is missing as questions rather than filling it.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account.
2. Read the who-is-engaged section first. If a partner or another role holds the relationship, your conversation is a different conversation.
3. For any partner involvement, check the Partner Timeline view for what has actually happened.
4. Decide whether you should be preparing alone or with whoever already has the relationship.
RequiredContext: One upcoming customer conversation and the account it concerns. The Partner Timeline view if a referral exists.
ExpectedOutput: A picture of who already holds the relationship, alongside the account facts and the open questions.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides whether to walk into this alone. At roughly fifty accounts the relationship often sits with a partner or another role, and arriving without them turns a useful conversation into one the customer has to repeat.
WhyThisMatters: In a partner-led segment the person the customer already trusts is frequently not you. Finding that out before the meeting is cheaper than finding out during it.

Name: Work out what this customer has already been told
Description: Find the history that will shape the conversation, including commitments made by people who are no longer involved.
Prompt: For [account name], I am proposing [describe what you are proposing]. Show me the relevant history: what has been bought and when, what was deployed and whether it was used, any support issue raised and how it ended, opportunities that were opened and lost and the reason recorded, and any commitment logged against the account. Based only on that record, what is this customer likely to raise? For each, state what in the history suggests it. Do not invent customer sentiment that is not in the record.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections._x000D_
2. Read the lost opportunities and closed support issues first - that is where the resistance usually comes from._x000D_
3. Check whether any commitment in the record was made by someone who has since left the account._x000D_
4. Prepare for the one piece of history most likely to come up.
RequiredContext: Your intended proposal and the account. The account's purchase, deployment, support and lost-opportunity history.
ExpectedOutput: The account history most likely to shape the conversation, with the specific objection it implies.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides which history still matters to this customer. Territories change hands and a commitment made two sellers ago is still a commitment to the customer, while a support issue that looks severe in the record may have been forgotten entirely.
WhyThisMatters: At this account load you are often inheriting a history you were not present for. The customer remembers it and will assume you do too.

Name: Name the ask and the fallback ask
Description: Define what decision you want out of the conversation and what you will settle for, before you are in it.
Prompt: For my conversation with [account name], I want [describe the outcome you want]. Help me sharpen this into a primary ask that names a specific decision and owner, and a fallback ask that is genuinely different rather than a smaller version of the same request. For each, state what the customer would need to believe to agree to it.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account and intended outcome.
2. Test whether the fallback concedes on a different axis or just asks for less.
3. If it is just a smaller version, write a different one yourself.
4. Decide which you are opening with.
RequiredContext: Your intended outcome for the conversation and the account it concerns.
ExpectedOutput: A primary ask naming a specific decision and owner, and a genuinely distinct fallback ask.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE judges whether the fallback is genuinely different. A fallback that concedes on the same axis gives the customer one decision to decline rather than two to choose between, and only the person who knows the relationship can tell whether the second ask is real.
WhyThisMatters: A conversation without a defined ask produces a good discussion and no decision, which at this account load means you will not get back to it for a month.

Name: Write a follow-up that works when a partner is also in the motion
Description: Record what was decided so that everyone involved, including a partner, can act on it without asking you.
Prompt: Draft a follow-up for my conversation with [account name]. Here is what happened: [paste your notes]. Structure it as what was decided, what was agreed as a next step with an owner and a date, and what remains open. Where a step belongs to someone other than me, name the role rather than assuming I will do it. Keep strictly to what was said - do not promote a discussion into a decision or add commitments that were not made. Produce a customer-facing version and a short internal note; keep commercial detail out of the customer version.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write your rough notes first, before opening anything._x000D_
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [account name] and [paste your notes]._x000D_
3. Check every commitment against what was genuinely said._x000D_
4. Check the customer-facing version for anything commercial that should only be internal._x000D_
5. If a partner owns a next step, send them the internal note only after checking it against the CELA rules._x000D_
6. Send it, then ask Sales Agent to record what changed on the opportunity - a forecast comment or a revised close date. It will show a confirmation card before writing anything._x000D_
7. Read the card before confirming. On a phone between meetings this is the step most easily tapped through, and it is the only check there is.
RequiredContext: Your notes from the conversation. Whether a partner or another role owns any next step.
ExpectedOutput: A customer-facing follow-up and a separate internal note, with steps owned by role rather than defaulting to you.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE confirms each recorded decision was actually taken, and checks what goes to the customer separately from what goes internally, before either is sent. When Sales Agent offers to write the update, the confirmation card is the last moment before your reading of the conversation becomes the account's official version of it.
WhyThisMatters: When a partner or another role owns the next step, a follow-up written only for you produces a decision nobody actions. Naming the owner is what makes it move.

Name: Separate what you can see from what you are assuming
Description: Establish the real state of a deal where part of the motion is happening outside your systems.
Prompt: For [opportunity name or ID], show what the MSX record actually contains: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and its owner, the close date and whether it has been changed, any co-sell or referral record attached and its recorded status, and the date of the most recent activity of any kind. Do not infer progress from the stage, and do not describe what the partner is doing - the record shows only what has been entered here. Where a field is empty, say so rather than filling it.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your opportunity.
2. List separately what you know from a conversation rather than from the record.
3. The co-sell record shows what exists in MSX, not what the partner is doing. For that, open the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center.
4. Mark anything you have not confirmed in the last two weeks as unknown.
RequiredContext: One live deal, ideally one where a partner is involved in the transaction.
ExpectedOutput: A deal state showing what the record evidences, what is empty, and what is known only from conversation.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides what counts as known. A stage in MSX records what someone last entered rather than what is happening, and when a partner is transacting, the most important movement is the movement you cannot see from here.
WhyThisMatters: A deal a partner is closing looks the same in our systems as a deal that has quietly died. The distinction has to be made deliberately.

Name: Name the next decision and who actually makes it
Description: Find the specific decision that moves the deal and the person with authority to make it.
Prompt: For [opportunity name or ID], based on the current stage and what is recorded, what is the next decision this deal needs? State who would make it on the customer side, what they would need in order to make it, and what is currently missing. Distinguish decisions the customer makes from decisions Microsoft or a partner makes. Where the record does not identify a decision maker, say so.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your opportunity.
2. Check whether the named decision maker is someone you have actually spoken to.
3. If the decision sits with a partner, work out whether you can influence it or only ask about it.
4. Define the single thing that would unblock it.
RequiredContext: One live deal and its current stage. Any known stakeholders on the customer side.
ExpectedOutput: The next decision named with its owner, what they need, and whether it sits with the customer, Microsoft or the partner.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE judges whether the named decision maker is real. A contact recorded as a decision maker was entered by someone at some point, and in a partner-led motion the person who actually decides is often someone the partner knows and we do not.
WhyThisMatters: Deals stall because the next decision is fuzzy rather than because it was refused. Naming it is most of the work of unsticking it.

Name: Prepare the specific ask for the partner
Description: Turn the gaps in your view into one clear question the partner can answer quickly.
Prompt: I have a deal at [account name] where a partner is involved in the transaction. Here is what I know and what I do not: [paste your deal state]. Help me draft a short, specific message to the partner asking for what I actually need to know. Keep it to two or three questions. Do not include internal commercial detail, seat counts, spend figures or anything that reads as an export from our systems.
ActivitySteps:
1. Take your deal state from the first activity._x000D_
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections._x000D_
3. Check the draft against the CELA rules - no personal data, no seat or spend detail, nothing resembling an export._x000D_
4. Cut it to the two questions you most need answered._x000D_
5. Send it through your normal partner channel.
RequiredContext: Your deal state showing what is unknown. The CELA rules on what may be shared with a partner.
ExpectedOutput: A short partner message asking two or three specific questions, checked against the data-sharing boundary before sending.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE owns what crosses to the partner and checks it before sending. Even when instructed to exclude commercial detail, a model may reintroduce it while making the message clearer, and the sender is the only control on that.
WhyThisMatters: Partners answer specific questions quickly and general status requests slowly, if at all. The difference is whether you did the thinking before asking.

Name: Test the close date against the evidence
Description: Work out whether the date in the system is a forecast or a hope.
Prompt: For [opportunity name or ID], the close date is currently recorded as [date]. Based on the stage, the recorded next step, the decision still outstanding and the most recent activity, what would have to happen between now and that date for it to close on time? List the steps in sequence with realistic elapsed time for each. If a partner referral or co-sell motion is part of this deal, account for the fourteen days a partner has to accept a referral before it expires and the sixty days to convert it before it is automatically marked lost. Identify the first step that has not started.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your opportunity and its close date._x000D_
2. Compare the total elapsed time against the days remaining._x000D_
3. If a referral is in flight, check its actual age in the Partner Timeline rather than assuming the window is still open._x000D_
4. Decide whether to move the date or compress a step, and do one of them._x000D_
5. If you are moving it, ask Sales Agent to change the close date in the same chat. It will show a confirmation card with the old and new values before writing._x000D_
6. Check the new date is the one your own arithmetic produced rather than the one that felt comfortable, then confirm.
RequiredContext: One live deal with a close date on record. Its current stage and outstanding decisions.
ExpectedOutput: A backward plan from the close date showing the first step not yet started and whether the date is achievable.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE owns the close date and changes it when the arithmetic does not support it. A date that survives because nobody recalculated it is the most common cause of a forecast miss, and the confirmation card is worth reading precisely because moving a date is easy now - the ease is the risk, not the safeguard.
WhyThisMatters: Close dates get set optimistically and then inherited. Working backwards from the date is the fastest way to find out it was never going to happen.

Name: Sort the renewal book by risk instead of by date
Description: Reorder a book worked in date order into one worked in risk order.
Prompt: List my accounts with a renewal or agreement end date in the next twelve months. For each, show the date, the products and workloads in place, any open support or delivery issue and whether it was resolved, any open opportunity, and whether the deployed estate is smaller than what was purchased. Flag the ones carrying an unresolved support issue or a gap between purchased and deployed.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Look first at the accounts flagged for unresolved issues or a purchased-versus-deployed gap.
3. Those two things are what a customer brings up at renewal, whatever the date says.
4. Reorder your book on that basis rather than on date.
RequiredContext: Your accounts with agreement or renewal dates in the next twelve months.
ExpectedOutput: A renewal book sorted by the evidence a customer would raise at renewal, rather than by date.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides what constitutes renewal risk in this book. An unresolved issue may have been forgotten and a deployment gap may be deliberate, and only someone who knows the account can tell a real risk from a data artifact.
WhyThisMatters: A book worked in date order means the renewal you reach last is the one you had most time to fix. Sorting by risk inverts that.

Name: Work out which renewals you can actually evidence
Description: Test across the renewal book which accounts you could defend with evidence today, because you will not have time to build it for all of them.
Prompt: For these accounts approaching renewal [list your at-risk renewals], show for each what the record evidences about value delivered: workloads deployed and when, usage recorded where it exists, support issues raised and resolved, and any milestone or success activity logged. Group them into accounts where a value story could be told from the record today, accounts where something is missing, and accounts where there is essentially nothing. Do not fill gaps with inference.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list with your at-risk renewals._x000D_
2. Read the third group first - those are the ones that need work now, whatever their dates._x000D_
3. For the middle group, identify the single missing piece._x000D_
4. Decide which accounts you can realistically build evidence for before their dates, and which you cannot.
RequiredContext: Your at-risk renewal accounts. Their deployment, usage and support history as recorded.
ExpectedOutput: The renewal book grouped by whether a value story can be evidenced today, with the accounts that cannot be evidenced identified first.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides where to spend the evidence-building effort. At this book size you cannot build a value story for every renewal, so choosing which ones go undefended is a real decision that gets made either deliberately or by running out of time.
WhyThisMatters: Value evidence takes time to assemble and the book is larger than the time available. Knowing which renewals you cannot defend is as useful as knowing which you can.

Name: Find the expansion already inside the renewal
Description: Test whether the account has an obvious next step that is easier to land than a new pursuit.
Prompt: For [account name], based on what is deployed and what is not, identify the expansion steps that would be a natural progression from the current estate. Consider specifically: security and compliance add-ons where the customer is on a base tier, moves from standalone products to suite licensing, upgrades from a lower to a higher suite tier, and Copilot attach where the underlying suite is already in place. For each, state what in the current estate makes it a logical next step and what would need to be true for the customer to want it. Do not present these as qualified opportunities and do not assume eligibility or pricing.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your renewal account.
2. Discard anything that does not build on something already deployed.
3. Test the most plausible one against what you know of the customer's plans.
4. Decide whether it belongs in the renewal conversation or as a separate pursuit.
RequiredContext: One renewal account and its current deployed estate.
ExpectedOutput: Expansion hypotheses grounded in the deployed estate, with the most plausible one tested against customer context.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides which expansion is real, and routes eligibility and pricing to the Commercial Executive rather than assuming them. A logical next product is not a wanted one, and the record does not know what the customer has budgeted or been burned by before.
