WhyThisMatters: Expansion inside a healthy renewal is materially easier than a new pursuit, and the evidence for it is usually already sitting in what the customer has deployed.

Name: Work out what the Commercial Executive needs from you
Description: Prepare the renewal handoff so the commercial work can start before the structure is already fixed.
Prompt: For [account name] with a renewal approaching, assemble what a Commercial Executive would need to begin: the current agreement type and end date, what is deployed against it, the expansion or reduction being contemplated, any known customer constraint, and the timeline pressure. Identify what is missing that only I can supply.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your renewal account.
2. Fill the gaps that only you can answer before sending anything.
3. Send it to your CE with the date you need a view by.
4. Do not wait for the renewal quarter to do this.
RequiredContext: One renewal account approaching its date. Its agreement type and deployed estate.
ExpectedOutput: A renewal briefing the CE can act on, with the seller-only gaps filled before it is sent.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides when to bring the CE in, and does it before the commercial shape is already fixed. Commercial Executives own enrollment mechanics and renewal structure, and engaging them after a structure has been discussed with the customer removes most of the options they would have had.
WhyThisMatters: The CE can change the shape of a renewal if they are involved while it is still a question. Once a structure has been floated with the customer, they are correcting rather than designing.

Name: Find the accounts that changed direction
Description: Look for movement rather than for low numbers, and cross-check it against the consumption view the agent cannot see.
Prompt: Across my accounts, show me the ones where something has changed recently: opportunities that moved stage or stalled, support issues opened, activity that stopped, or renewal dates approaching without recent contact. For each, show what changed and when. Do not rank them by size or attempt to score their health; just show me what moved.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt._x000D_
2. Read the accounts that went quiet before the ones with visible problems._x000D_
3. Open your consumption or usage view separately. The agent cannot compute month-on-month consumption movement, so this comparison is yours to make._x000D_
4. Mark any account where consumption has moved by roughly a quarter in either direction - that scale of swing is the segment's standing trigger for a look._x000D_
5. Separate movement with an obvious explanation from movement without one.
RequiredContext: Your assigned accounts and their recent activity, opportunity and support records. Separately, whatever consumption or usage view you have access to - the agent cannot reach it.
ExpectedOutput: The accounts where something changed in MSX, cross-referenced by hand against consumption movement, with the changes described rather than scored.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE distinguishes a change that matters from a change that is normal for that account, and does the consumption comparison manually because the agent cannot. A quiet quarter is a warning at one customer and the usual pattern at another, and nothing in the record encodes which.
WhyThisMatters: A low number tells you where an account already is. A change tells you where it is going, and that is the one you can still do something about.

Name: Find out whether it is one account or a pattern
Description: Test whether the movement you found is specific to that account or showing up across several, because the two need completely different responses.
Prompt: Several of my accounts are showing [describe the movement you found]. For the accounts in my portfolio, show me which others have the same characteristics: the same workloads, a similar deployment stage, the same recorded issue type, or the same agreement structure. For each match, show what it has in common and what is different. Do not conclude that a shared characteristic is a shared cause.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [describe the movement you found]._x000D_
2. If several accounts share the pattern, this is not an account problem and escalating it one account at a time will not fix it._x000D_
3. If it is genuinely isolated, treat it as a single-account intervention._x000D_
4. Decide which of the two you are dealing with before choosing what to do.
RequiredContext: The movement you identified across your portfolio. Your full account list with workloads and agreement structures.
ExpectedOutput: A read on whether the movement is isolated or shared across accounts, with the common characteristics identified.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE judges whether a shared characteristic is a shared cause. Accounts on the same workload can decline for entirely unrelated reasons, and treating a coincidence as a pattern sends an escalation that wastes everyone's time.
WhyThisMatters: At this portfolio size the same problem usually shows up in several accounts at once. Handling it one account at a time is the single most expensive mistake available here.

Name: Decide what is yours and route the rest
Description: Separate the accounts where your own involvement changes the outcome from the ones that need somebody else.
Prompt: I have these accounts showing problems: [list the accounts and what is happening at each]. For each, show the coverage arrangement on record - whether there is a Unified support agreement, an assigned customer success or technical role, or an active partner relationship. Using that, help me think through who would own the intervention each account needs and what evidence they would need to act without coming back to me. Where the coverage arrangement is not recorded, say so rather than guessing.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list with your accounts._x000D_
2. Read the coverage arrangement first - it determines who owns the intervention before the problem does._x000D_
3. Unified accounts route differently from non-Unified, and partner-led accounts differently again._x000D_
4. Assemble the evidence the receiving role needs, then route._x000D_
5. Record that you routed it, so it is not silently yours again in a month.
RequiredContext: The accounts showing movement and your read on each. The coverage arrangement on record for each account.
ExpectedOutput: Each account routed according to its actual coverage arrangement, with the evidence the receiving role requires.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides which account is genuinely theirs, using the coverage arrangement rather than instinct. Coverage is a property of the account rather than of you, so the same problem at two accounts routes to two different owners, and taking on the technical intervention yourself means the accounts that needed you go unattended.
WhyThisMatters: At this account load the failure mode is not missing a problem. It is taking on a problem that belonged to somebody else and losing the week.

Name: Check whether last month's interventions actually worked
Description: Close the loop on the accounts you already acted on, because nothing in the working week will tell you whether anything changed.
Prompt: For these accounts where I intervened recently [list the accounts and what you did], show what has happened since: any change in opportunity stage, new or resolved support issues, activity recorded and by whom, and whether the next step logged at the time was completed. For each, show what has moved and what has not. Do not judge whether the intervention succeeded.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write down what you actually did at each account and when, before opening anything._x000D_
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list._x000D_
3. Look for interventions where nothing has moved at all - those either failed or never started._x000D_
4. Decide for each whether to escalate, try something different, or accept it and stop spending time there.
RequiredContext: The accounts you intervened at recently and what you did. The activity and opportunity record since.
ExpectedOutput: A read on which recent interventions produced movement and which did not, with a decision on each of the latter.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides whether an intervention has failed or simply needs longer. The record shows movement rather than progress, and an intervention that quietly did nothing will stay on your list indefinitely unless someone decides to stop.
WhyThisMatters: Interventions get started and rarely get checked. At this account load the ones that silently failed are indistinguishable from the ones still in flight until somebody looks.

Name: Sort the book by where commercial options are still open
Description: Order a renewal book by how much commercial room remains rather than by how soon each date arrives.
Prompt: List the accounts in my book with an agreement end date in the next eighteen months. For each, show the date, the agreement type, the products and quantities on the agreement, whether a partner is associated with the account, and the most recent recorded activity. Group them by how far out the date is: more than twelve months, six to twelve months, and under six months.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Work the first group before the third. The renewals over twelve months out are the only ones where structure is genuinely still open.
3. Mark which are partner-transacted - your role differs on those.
4. Pick the earliest-dated agreement in the first group that carries real value.
RequiredContext: Your book of agreements with end dates and agreement types. Partner association where it exists.
ExpectedOutput: A renewal book grouped by remaining commercial room, with the partner-transacted agreements marked.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides where commercial room genuinely remains. Time to the date is a proxy for optionality rather than the thing itself, and an agreement eighteen months out whose customer has already committed a budget is more closed than one at six months that has not.
WhyThisMatters: Almost all the commercial value a CE adds depends on arriving while the structure is still a question. A book worked in date order guarantees arriving last at the ones with most room.

Name: Establish what the agreement actually says versus what is happening
Description: Compare the commercial commitment on paper against the deployed reality, because the gap is the renewal conversation.
Prompt: For [account name], show the current agreement position: the agreement type and end date, the products and quantities committed, what is actually deployed against them, and any amendment or exception recorded. Highlight where deployed quantities differ from committed quantities in either direction. Do not interpret licensing entitlement or eligibility - show what is recorded and flag what needs an authoritative answer.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [account name] with your renewal._x000D_
2. Read the over-deployment and under-deployment separately - they are opposite commercial problems._x000D_
3. Route anything touching entitlement, eligibility or pricing to the authoritative source. Do not accept the agent's reading of it._x000D_
4. Decide which gap changes the renewal structure.
RequiredContext: One renewal account and its agreement record. Access to the authoritative licensing source for anything about entitlement.
ExpectedOutput: The committed position against the deployed position, with the gaps identified and the entitlement questions routed rather than answered.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE owns the commercial interpretation and routes entitlement and eligibility to the authoritative source rather than accepting a generated reading. A confidently wrong licensing answer is discovered at signature, and by then it has been built on.
WhyThisMatters: Under-deployment is a renewal risk and over-deployment is a compliance exposure. Both are visible long before the date, and neither surfaces on its own.

Name: Work out what changes when the partner holds the renewal
Description: Establish where your influence sits on a renewal a partner will transact, and what they need from you.
Prompt: For [account name], a renewal where a partner transacts, show what is visible from here: the agreement position, the partner associated with the account, any co-sell or referral record, and the recorded activity on both sides. Then help me separate the parts of this renewal I can decide, the parts I can only recommend, and the parts I will not see at all. Do not describe partner-side activity - the record shows only what has been entered in MSX.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [account name] with a partner-transacted renewal._x000D_
2. Treat the third category as the important one - what you will not see is what will surprise you._x000D_
3. Check the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center for the partner-side picture; the agent cannot reach it._x000D_
4. Decide the one thing the partner needs from you that they do not currently have.
RequiredContext: One partner-transacted renewal. The partner associated with it. Partner Center or the Partner Timeline view for partner-side status.
ExpectedOutput: The renewal separated into what you decide, what you recommend, and what is not visible to you, with one partner need identified.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides what to escalate to the partner conversation rather than working around it. In CSP the partner owns the customer commercial relationship, and a CE who tries to run the renewal directly damages the relationship that will actually deliver it.
WhyThisMatters: Treating a partner-transacted renewal like a direct one produces advice nobody asked for and a partner who stops sharing information. The boundary is worth being explicit about.

Name: Check whether the agreement allows a mid-term change at all
Description: Establish what this agreement type actually permits before anyone takes an expansion idea to the customer.
Prompt: For [account name], show the agreement type, its start and end dates, any anniversary or true-up mechanism recorded, the amendment history, and any co-term arrangement. Based only on what is recorded, describe what changes have previously been made mid-term on this agreement and when in its cycle they happened. Do not state what the agreement type permits in general and do not assess eligibility - I will confirm that with the authoritative source.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [account name] with the account._x000D_
2. Read the amendment history first. What has already been done mid-term is the most reliable evidence of what can be._x000D_
3. Confirm the mechanism with the authoritative licensing source before telling anyone it is available. The agent does not reliably know which amendments an agreement type allows._x000D_
4. Give the account team a clear yes, no, or confirm-first, with the date it would need to happen by.
RequiredContext: One account with an agreement in place, including amendment history and any true-up or anniversary mechanism. The authoritative source for what the agreement type permits.
ExpectedOutput: A read on whether a mid-term change is mechanically available on this agreement, evidenced by amendment history and confirmed with the authoritative source.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE confirms the mechanism with the authoritative source before anyone acts on it. Prior amendment history is evidence rather than permission, and an expansion promised on an agreement that cannot carry it until renewal costs credibility with the account team and the customer at once.
WhyThisMatters: Account teams generate expansion ideas continuously. The commercial question is not whether the idea is good but whether the paper allows it now, and that answer is worth days if it arrives early.

Name: Separate what you decide from what you recommend
Description: Map your actual authority on a deal a partner will transact, before spending effort on the parts you do not hold.
Prompt: For [opportunity name or ID], where a partner will transact, show the deal position recorded in MSX: stage, products, quantities, any co-sell or referral record, the account's existing agreements, and the partner associated. Then help me categorize the commercial elements into ones Microsoft decides, ones the partner decides, and ones the customer decides. Where the record does not make ownership clear, say so rather than assuming.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your opportunity.
2. Look hardest at the middle category - that is where effort gets wasted.
3. For anything you decide, confirm it against current approved guidance rather than the agent's reading.
4. Pick the single element where your input changes the outcome most.
RequiredContext: One live deal a partner will transact. The account's existing agreements. The partner associated with it.
ExpectedOutput: Commercial elements separated by who actually decides them, with the one element worth your effort identified.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides where their input actually changes the outcome. Advising on an element the partner owns is effort that produces friction rather than a different deal, and only someone who knows the partner relationship can tell which is which.
WhyThisMatters: Commercial effort in this segment gets spent on decisions that belong to somebody else. Mapping authority first is the cheapest work available.

Name: Compare the structures the partner could actually sell
Description: Test commercial options against what is transactable through this route rather than what would be optimal directly.
Prompt: For [opportunity name or ID], the customer needs [describe the commercial requirement]. Based on the account's existing agreements and what is recorded, lay out the commercial structures that could meet it. For each, state what it requires from the customer, what it requires from the partner, and what has to be true about the existing agreement for it to work. Flag anything that depends on policy, eligibility or pricing that I need to confirm with the authoritative source rather than assume.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections._x000D_
2. Discard any structure the partner cannot transact through their route, whatever its merits._x000D_
3. Route every policy, eligibility and pricing flag to the authoritative owner before comparing._x000D_
4. Choose the structure that is best among the transactable ones, not best in the abstract.
RequiredContext: One live deal and the customer's commercial requirement. The account's existing agreements. The authoritative source for policy, eligibility and pricing.
ExpectedOutput: Commercial structures compared on what is actually transactable through this route, with the policy questions routed rather than assumed.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE judges what the partner can genuinely transact, and confirms every policy and eligibility question with the authoritative owner before comparing options. A structure that is commercially elegant and cannot be sold through this route is a recommendation that wastes a cycle for everyone.
WhyThisMatters: Structures get compared on commercial merit and then discovered to be untransactable through the route in play. Applying that filter first changes which option wins.

Name: Give the partner what makes the right structure easy to sell
Description: Turn your commercial recommendation into something the partner can actually use with the customer.
Prompt: I want a partner to sell [describe the commercial structure] to [account name]. Draft a short explanation they could use with the customer: what the structure is, what it gives the customer, what it requires from them, and the two questions the customer is most likely to ask. Write it for an audience outside Microsoft. Do not include internal margin or cost detail, seat counts, spend figures, personal data, or anything that reads as an export from our systems.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Check the draft against the CELA rules before it goes anywhere: no personal data, no seat or spend detail, nothing resembling an export.
3. Read it as the partner would - if it only makes sense with your explanation attached, it is not finished.
4. Send it through your normal partner channel.
RequiredContext: Your recommended commercial structure and the account. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
ExpectedOutput: A partner-usable explanation of the structure, checked against the data-sharing boundary before it leaves Microsoft.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE owns what crosses to the partner and checks the draft against the data rules before sending. A model asked to make a commercial structure persuasive will reach for the numbers that make it persuasive, and the sender is the only control on that.
WhyThisMatters: A structure a partner cannot explain will not be sold, whatever its merits. Enablement is the actual lever when somebody else transacts.

Name: Check what this deal sets up for the next one
Description: Test whether a structure that works here creates an expectation you will inherit across the book.
Prompt: I am considering [describe the commercial structure] for [account name]. Show me other accounts in my book with a similar agreement type, size band, or product mix. For each, show the current agreement position and whether anything similar has already been done. Do not conclude that a similar account implies a similar outcome; just show me where the comparison would be drawn.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your structure and account.
2. Look for accounts where a partner would notice the difference, not just the customer.
3. Decide whether you would be comfortable doing this for all of them.
4. If not, work out what makes this account genuinely different and write it down.
RequiredContext: Your proposed commercial structure and account. Your wider book of agreements.
ExpectedOutput: The accounts where this structure would set a comparison, with an explicit decision on whether it is repeatable.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE judges whether a structure is a precedent or an exception, and records the reason. In a segment with many similar customers and shared partners, an exception granted once and undocumented becomes the expected baseline within a quarter.
WhyThisMatters: Enterprise deals are large enough to be treated individually. Here the customers are numerous and similar, and partners talk, so a one-off shape propagates quickly.

Name: Scan the book for the gap between bought and used
Description: Find where deployed reality has drifted from the commercial commitment, across the whole book rather than one account.
Prompt: Across the accounts in my book, show each agreement with its type, end date, the products and quantities committed, and what is deployed against them. Identify the accounts where deployed quantities are materially below what was committed, and separately the accounts where they are above. Show the size of the difference for each. Do not interpret entitlement or compliance.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Treat the two lists as different problems: under-deployment is a renewal risk, over-deployment is an exposure.
3. Route anything that looks like a compliance question to the authoritative owner rather than resolving it.
4. Rank by the size of the difference against how close the agreement date is.
RequiredContext: Your book of agreements with committed quantities. Whatever deployment or usage view you have access to.
ExpectedOutput: The book split into under-deployed and over-deployed accounts with the size of each gap, ranked against agreement dates.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides which gaps are commercially real. A deployment gap can be a customer who over-bought deliberately, a rollout that is simply slow, or a genuine problem, and the record does not distinguish them. Compliance-shaped findings route to the authoritative owner rather than being resolved here.
WhyThisMatters: At this book size nobody finds a deployment gap by looking at an account. It is found by scanning for the difference, and it is the single most reliable early signal of a renewal in trouble.

Name: Find the exception you have granted more than once
Description: Identify where a one-off concession has quietly become the standing expectation across the book.
Prompt: Across my accounts, show the agreements carrying a recorded amendment, exception or non-standard term. For each, show what the variation is, when it was recorded, the agreement type and the account size band. Group them by the type of variation and show how many accounts each group covers. Do not judge whether any variation was appropriate.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Look at the group sizes before the individual accounts.
3. Any variation appearing across several accounts has stopped being an exception, whatever it is called.
4. Decide whether to standardize it, stop granting it, or escalate that the policy no longer matches practice.
RequiredContext: Your book of agreements including recorded amendments, exceptions and non-standard terms.
ExpectedOutput: Recorded variations grouped by type with the count of accounts affected, and a decision on the largest group.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides whether a repeated variation should be standardized, stopped, or escalated as evidence that policy no longer matches practice. That is a judgment about commercial consistency across a book, and no individual deal review will ever surface it.
WhyThisMatters: Exceptions are granted one deal at a time and reviewed one deal at a time, which is exactly why nobody notices when one has become the default.

Name: Tell an unattended agreement apart from a partner-covered one
Description: Work out whether an agreement with no activity behind it is genuinely abandoned or is being worked somewhere you cannot see.
Prompt: For the accounts in my book showing no recorded Microsoft activity in the last six months, show for each whether a partner is associated with the account, whether any co-sell or referral record exists and what status it carries, and whether any partner-attributed transaction has been recorded against the agreement. Group them into accounts with an active partner association, accounts with a lapsed or closed partner record, and accounts with no partner involvement recorded at all. Do not describe what any partner is currently doing.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt._x000D_
2. The third group is the genuinely unattended one. Start there._x000D_
3. For the first two groups, check Partner Center or the Partner Timeline view - the agent cannot see partner-side activity, so silence here means nothing on its own._x000D_
4. For anything in the second group, the partner record lapsing is the signal, not the silence._x000D_
5. Raise the third group with the account team this week.
RequiredContext: Your book of agreements with activity history. Partner association and co-sell records. Partner Center or the Partner Timeline view for partner-side status.
ExpectedOutput: Silent agreements separated into partner-covered, partner-lapsed, and genuinely unattended, with the third group escalated.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides which silence is real. An agreement being worked well by a partner and an agreement nobody has touched look identical from inside our systems, and treating the first as neglect damages the partner relationship that is actually delivering the account.
WhyThisMatters: Silence is the most misread signal in a partner-led segment. The distinction that matters is not how quiet an account is but whether anyone else is in it.

Name: Build the case that policy no longer matches practice
Description: Turn a repeated exception into evidence a policy owner can act on.
Prompt: I have found that [describe the variation] appears across [number] accounts in my book. Help me structure this as a case for a policy owner: what the variation is, how consistently it appears, what commercial pressure appears to be driving it, and what the options are. Frame the options as questions for the policy owner rather than recommendations. Do not state what the policy should be or assert that any variation is permitted.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed sections with your finding.
2. Check the account count yourself rather than accepting it.
3. Remove anything that reads as you deciding the policy - that is not your call and framing it that way gets it dismissed.
4. Send it to the policy owner with the evidence attached.
RequiredContext: Your grouped exception finding with the account count verified. The authoritative policy owner for this variation.
ExpectedOutput: A structured case for the policy owner with the pattern evidenced and the options framed as questions.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE presents evidence and does not propose the policy. A field observation carries weight precisely because it is an observation, and a case that arrives with the answer already written is read as advocacy and discounted.
WhyThisMatters: A repeated exception is either a policy that needs changing or a practice that needs stopping. Neither gets resolved while it stays visible only to the person granting it.

Name: Find out what the DAE has already promised
Description: Get the account history behind a conversation you did not arrange, so you do not contradict what has already been said.
Prompt: For [account name], show what has been recorded ahead of this conversation: the open opportunities and their stage, recent activity and who it was with, any commitment or next step logged, the products and workloads already in place, and any open support issue. Focus on anything that has already been said to this customer about my solution area. Where the record is thin, say so rather than filling it.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account.
2. Read the commitments first. Contradicting one in the meeting is the fastest way to lose the room.
3. Note what is thin - that is what you ask the DAE before the call, not the customer during it.
4. Send the DAE your two questions rather than arriving with them.
RequiredContext: One customer conversation you have been asked to join, and the account it concerns.
ExpectedOutput: The account history relevant to your solution area, with the commitments already made identified and the gaps turned into questions for the DAE.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what to check with the DAE before the conversation rather than discovering it in front of the customer. The record shows what was logged, and in a fast-moving territory the most important commitment is often one the DAE made verbally and has not written down yet.
WhyThisMatters: A specialist who contradicts what the account owner promised last month damages both the deal and the relationship with the DAE. It is entirely avoidable with ten minutes of preparation.

Name: Bring what you have learned elsewhere to this customer
Description: Use the objections you have already met across other territories to anticipate what this customer will raise.
Prompt: I am proposing [describe your solution-area proposal] at [account name]. First, show what is deployed at that account today. Then, across the other opportunities in my solution area, show any recorded objection, blocker or competitor associated with a similar deployed estate. For each, show the account, what was recorded, and how it was resolved if it was. Do not assume a similar estate means the same objection will arise.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections._x000D_
2. Read the objections from other accounts before the target account's estate._x000D_
3. Discard any that do not fit this customer's actual situation - a pattern is a prompt to check, not a prediction._x000D_
4. Prepare the answer you already gave successfully somewhere else.
RequiredContext: Your solution-area proposal and the target account. The other opportunities across the territories you support, including recorded objections.
ExpectedOutput: Objections seen elsewhere on similar estates, filtered to the ones plausible here, with a previously successful answer ready.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS judges whether an objection seen elsewhere actually applies here. The same deployed estate can produce completely different concerns depending on who operates it and what they were burned by last time, and a specialist arriving with a rehearsed answer to the wrong objection is worse than one arriving with none.
WhyThisMatters: The specialist advantage over an account owner is having met this workload at many customers. That only pays if you go and look at what happened rather than relying on what you remember.

Name: Agree the boundary with the DAE before you are in the room
Description: Settle who covers what, so the customer sees one team rather than two people negotiating live.
Prompt: I am joining a customer conversation at [account name] that the DAE is leading. The intended outcome is [describe the outcome]. Help me draft a short note to the DAE proposing the split: which parts I will cover, which parts they keep, and the two questions I need answered before we go in. Keep it to a few lines - this is a working note between colleagues, not a brief.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account and the intended outcome.
2. Cut anything that reads as telling the account owner how to run their meeting.
3. Send it far enough ahead that they can actually reply.
4. If they do not reply, assume they own everything commercial and stay in your lane.
RequiredContext: The conversation you are joining, the account, and the intended outcome. Your DAE.
ExpectedOutput: A short agreed split of the conversation with your two open questions sent ahead of it.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS proposes the split and the DAE owns the decision, because the account relationship is theirs. Which DAE wants a specialist to lead and which wants them to stay quiet until asked varies by person rather than by process, and the only way to know is to have worked with them.
WhyThisMatters: Two people improvising a division of labor in front of a customer reads as a team that has not spoken. It takes three lines to prevent.

Name: Name the solution decision the deal is waiting on
Description: Find the specific technical or solution decision blocking an opportunity, as distinct from the commercial ones.
Prompt: For [opportunity name or ID] in my solution area, show the current stage, when it last moved, the recorded next step and owner, any blocker or objection captured, and what has been proposed to the customer. Based on that, identify what appears to be blocking progress and separate anything that is a solution or technical decision from anything commercial or relationship-based. Where the record does not say, say so.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your opportunity.
2. Work only the solution column. The commercial one belongs to the DAE and the CE.
3. If the solution column is empty, the deal is not blocked on you and your time is better spent elsewhere.
4. Name the single decision that would move it.
RequiredContext: One opportunity in your solution area that is not moving.
ExpectedOutput: The blockers split into solution decisions and commercial ones, with the single solution decision named or the deal correctly identified as not yours.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether a blocker is genuinely a solution problem. Deals are often described as technical when the real issue is budget or sponsorship, and a specialist who accepts that framing spends weeks solving a problem that was never the obstacle.
WhyThisMatters: Specialist time is the scarce resource across a solution area. The most valuable output of this activity is sometimes discovering the deal is not blocked on you at all.

Name: Assemble the evidence that settles it
Description: Work out what would actually resolve the solution decision, and who has to produce it.
Prompt: A deal at [account name] is waiting on this solution decision: [describe the decision]. Based on what is recorded for this account, what evidence exists that bears on it, what is missing, and what would a customer need to see to decide? For each missing piece, state whether it would come from the customer, from a technical proof, from a reference, or from someone else at Microsoft. Do not assume a proof or reference exists.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections._x000D_
2. Separate evidence you can produce from evidence you have to ask for._x000D_
3. Pick the single piece most likely to settle it rather than assembling everything._x000D_
4. Start on that one and tell the DAE what you are doing and by when.
RequiredContext: The solution decision blocking the deal, and the account it concerns.
ExpectedOutput: The evidence that would settle the decision, split by who must produce it, with one piece started.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what evidence is proportionate. A full technical proof is sometimes the right answer and is frequently a way of delaying a decision the customer was ready to make, and only the specialist can judge which situation this is.
WhyThisMatters: The instinct on a blocked technical decision is to build a proof. At this deal size that often costs more than the deal is worth, and a reference or a short answer would have done.

Name: Check whether you have answered this before
Description: Look across the territories you support for the same solution decision, because you have probably already solved it.
Prompt: Across the opportunities in my solution area, show any where the recorded blocker, objection or open question resembles this one: [describe the decision]. For each match, show the account, the current stage, what was recorded, and how it was resolved if it was. Do not assume a similar description means the same underlying problem.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your decision.
2. Check whether the matches are genuinely the same problem or just similar wording.
3. If you resolved one before, reuse the answer rather than rebuilding it.
4. If several are open at once, this is a solution-area problem and needs a reusable answer, not three conversations.
RequiredContext: The solution decision you are working. The territories and opportunities in your solution area.
ExpectedOutput: Prior or parallel instances of the same decision, with a reusable answer identified or the pattern escalated.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether two similarly described blockers are actually the same problem. Blocker text is written by different people in different territories, and a vocabulary coincidence sends you reusing an answer that does not fit.
WhyThisMatters: A specialist covering many territories answers the same question repeatedly without noticing. Noticing is what converts repeated effort into a reusable asset.

Name: Find where your solution area can actually be evidenced
Description: Separate the accounts where the outcome is provable from the ones where it is merely believed.
Prompt: For these accounts in my solution area where the solution was deployed [list up to fifteen accounts], show for each what is recorded: what was deployed and when, any usage recorded, support issues raised and whether they were resolved, and any milestone or success activity logged. Group them into accounts with recorded evidence of use, accounts with deployment but no recorded use, and accounts where the record shows only the sale. Do not infer outcomes from deployment.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write down up to fifteen accounts where your solution area was deployed. Pull from more than one territory - comparing across DAEs is the point._x000D_
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list._x000D_
3. The second group matters most - deployed but not used is a story you must not tell as a success._x000D_
4. Compare across territories: if one DAE's accounts show use and another's do not, that is a coverage difference, not a product difference._x000D_
5. Pick the strongest evidenced account as a proof-point candidate.
RequiredContext: Up to fifteen accounts from more than one territory where your solution area was deployed.
ExpectedOutput: A bounded set of deployments grouped by whether outcome is evidenced, compared across territories, with a proof-point candidate identified.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what counts as evidence of an outcome, and reads the difference between territories rather than averaging it. Usage data shows a product being run rather than a customer getting value, and a solution that lands in one DAE's accounts and not another's is usually telling you something about support rather than about the product.
WhyThisMatters: Specialists are asked for proof constantly and reach for the customer they remember rather than the one they can evidence. The two are often not the same account.

Name: Build a proof point you can use with another customer
Description: Turn one evidenced deployment into something reusable, without carrying anything that should not travel.
Prompt: For [account name], where my solution area was deployed, draft a short proof point usable with a different customer: the problem, what was implemented, the outcome and how it is evidenced, and the conditions that made it work. Write it for an audience outside this account. Do not include the customer name, contact names, seat counts, spend figures, or anything that identifies them. Describe them by industry and size band only.
ActivitySteps:
1. Establish who actually led the delivery before you draft anything. If a partner led it, the outcome is theirs and the DAE cannot approve it on their behalf._x000D_
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [account name]._x000D_
3. Read it as though you were the customer being described. If they would recognize themselves, it is not anonymized._x000D_
4. Check the outcome claim is evidenced rather than asserted - that is the part a prospect will test._x000D_
5. Get approval from the account owner, and additionally from the partner if the partner led delivery. Anonymized is not the same as approved, and approved by us is not the same as approved by them.
RequiredContext: One account with an evidenced outcome in your solution area. The account owner, for approval.
ExpectedOutput: An anonymized, evidenced proof point, with account-owner approval sought before reuse.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS establishes who owns the outcome before seeking approval to reuse it. Where a partner led delivery, the account owner cannot consent on the partner's behalf, and a proof point built on somebody else's work and circulated without asking is the fastest way to lose a delivery partner. Customers also recognize themselves from far less detail than sellers expect.
WhyThisMatters: Reusable proof is the specialist's most valuable asset and the easiest to create carelessly. The anonymization is the technical part; the permission is the part that gets skipped.

Name: Work out whose evidence it actually is
Description: Establish where a partner led the delivery, because the proof sits with them and asking is a different conversation.
Prompt: For these accounts in my solution area with an evidenced or partial outcome [list the accounts], show what is recorded in MSX about partner involvement: whether a partner is associated with the account, any co-sell or referral record and its recorded status, and the dates on those records. Report only what the record contains. Do not infer or state who led the delivery - that is not determinable from MSX.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list._x000D_
2. Treat the output as a list of where to look, not as an answer._x000D_
3. For every account with a partner record, open Partner Center or the Partner Timeline view. Who led delivery is only determinable there._x000D_
4. Anything partner-led: the outcome evidence is theirs to share, not ours to assume._x000D_
5. If you want to use a partner-led outcome, ask the partner.
RequiredContext: Your evidenced accounts. Partner association and co-sell records in MSX. Partner Center or the Partner Timeline view, which is where delivery leadership is actually visible.
ExpectedOutput: The accounts carrying partner records, identified as requiring a Partner Center check before any outcome is claimed.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS establishes who led delivery in Partner Center rather than inferring it from our record, and decides on that basis whether an outcome is ours to claim. MSX shows that a partner was associated, never what they did, and presenting a partner's delivery as our proof point damages the relationship the moment they see it.
WhyThisMatters: Partner-led delivery is structural here, so a meaningful share of the best outcomes are not ours to tell. Knowing which is which prevents an avoidable conversation.

Name: Find out who has already spoken to this customer
Description: Establish what is already known about the estate and who holds the rest, before you take a single question to the customer.
Prompt: For [account name], show me what is already recorded about their technical estate: the products and workloads in place and when they were deployed, any open support or delivery issue, the opportunities open and what they are for, every recorded activity and which role it came from, and whether a partner or co-sell record exists on the account. Report only what the record contains. Do not describe what any partner has done - that is not in MSX.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your customer.
2. Read the activity list by role. Whoever has been active is the person who knows what is not written down.
3. If a partner record exists, check the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center - the partner may have run discovery of their own.
4. Write down what the record answers, and what it only appears to answer.
RequiredContext: One customer where you are about to start technical discovery.
ExpectedOutput: What the record already establishes about the estate, and the named colleagues or partners likely holding the rest.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what the record genuinely establishes versus what it merely mentions. A workload appearing in the record says it was bought rather than how it was configured, and the configuration is what you will be held to when you design against it.
WhyThisMatters: At this customer count you are arriving after a partner and a seller have both already been there. Starting from what they found is faster than starting again and does not spend the customer's patience.

Name: Test your criteria against what they already run
Description: Check draft decision criteria against the customer's recorded estate, and work out which ones a partner would have to satisfy.
Prompt: Here are the technical decision criteria I am proposing for [account name]: [paste your draft criteria]. Show me what that customer has deployed today and, for each criterion, whether anything in the record bears on it - an existing workload, an open support issue, a prior opportunity - or whether the record says nothing. Do not assess technical effort or judge whether a criterion is reasonable. I want to know which of these the record can already speak to.
ActivitySteps:
1. Draft your criteria first. This is your judgment, not the agent's.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
3. Criteria the record says nothing about are the ones you will have to establish with the customer or the partner.
4. Mark which of those a delivery partner would have to satisfy rather than you.
5. Agree the surviving set with the DAE before it reaches the customer.
RequiredContext: Your draft technical decision criteria, and the customer they are for.
ExpectedOutput: Your criteria split by whether the record already speaks to them, with the partner-satisfied ones marked.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE writes the criteria and decides which a partner could realistically meet. A criterion only the engineer can satisfy quietly commits you to every future deal of that shape, and at this customer count that is a commitment you cannot keep.
WhyThisMatters: Criteria written for yourself do not survive being handed to a delivery partner. Checking them against what the customer already runs is the cheap part; deciding who can meet them is the part that matters.

Name: Find where the technical record has gone quiet
Description: Rank the technical record by how long each part of it has gone without an update, then decide what you still have to verify yourself.
Prompt: For [account name], show me how current the technical record actually is. For each deployed product and workload give the date it was last updated, list any open support or service record with the date it last moved, and name the areas where nothing has been logged in the last [number] months. Sort by longest silence first, and lead with the gaps rather than a full inventory of the estate.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections - the account and the number of months you want checked.
2. Read the dates, not just the facts. Silence is not evidence either way: it means no entry was found in MSX for that period, not that nothing happened or that nobody recorded it somewhere you cannot see.
3. Now do the part the agent cannot: decide which of these facts you will confirm with a person before you design against them, and which are safe to take as read.
RequiredContext: The customer, and how far back you want the currency check to run.
ExpectedOutput: The technical record ranked by how long each part of it has gone untouched, with anything showing no entry inside the chosen period named separately.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE owns the design and therefore decides which recorded facts are safe to build on. A fact nobody has touched in a long time is not necessarily wrong, and the difference between an inaccuracy caught at design time and one found in production is entirely a matter of which fact it was.
WhyThisMatters: You cannot verify everything at this customer count. The record will not tell you what is true, but it will tell you which facts are fresh and which have gone untouched long enough to be worth checking before you design against them.

Name: Look for the proof before you build one
Description: Check whether you or a colleague have already proven this, at a customer with a comparable estate.
Prompt: I need to prove [describe what the customer doubts] for a customer running [describe their estate]. Across the opportunities in my patch, show me any where a similar workload or configuration was involved, what stage they reached, and any recorded notes, objections or outcomes. For each, show what the customer environment looked like. Do not assume a similar environment means the same proof will transfer.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Look for the closest environment rather than the closest product name.
3. If something transfers, find out who ran it before rebuilding it.
4. If nothing transfers, you now know why this one is genuinely new.
RequiredContext: The technical doubt to be settled, and the customer's environment as you understand it.
ExpectedOutput: Comparable prior work identified with an honest read on whether it transfers, or a clear statement that this proof is genuinely new.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE judges whether a prior proof actually transfers. Two customers on the same product can differ in the one respect the proof depended on, and a borrowed proof that quietly does not apply is worse than building a new one, because nobody re-examines it.
WhyThisMatters: A bespoke proof for every customer does not survive the customer count in this segment. Reuse is the constraint that makes the job possible, and it only works if somebody looks first.

Name: Cut your proof down before you build it
Description: State the proof you are considering, then test it against what comparable customers actually needed.
Prompt: A customer at [account name] is unsure about [describe the doubt]. I am considering this proof: [describe the proof you have in mind]. Across the opportunities in my patch, show me any where a similar doubt or objection was recorded, what was proposed, what stage the opportunity reached, and any note about what convinced the customer. Do not design a proof or judge whether mine is the right size.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write down the proof you have in mind first, including what it will not cover. That scoping is yours.
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace all three bracketed sections.
3. Look at what actually convinced comparable customers. It is frequently smaller than what was offered.
4. Cut yours to the smallest version that still settles the doubt, and write down explicitly what it excludes.
5. Get the customer to agree that this settles it, before you build anything.
RequiredContext: The customer, what they are unsure about, and the proof you are considering including its exclusions.
ExpectedOutput: Your proposed proof tested against what comparable customers actually needed, cut to the smallest sufficient version with exclusions stated.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what the customer is really doubting, which is frequently not what they asked to see. A request for a pilot is often a request for reassurance about operational effort, and building the pilot answers a question nobody had while leaving the real one open.
WhyThisMatters: Proof work expands to fill whatever time it is given, and at this customer count that time comes straight out of another customer. What convinced somebody comparable is the cheapest available check on your own scoping.

Name: Leave it in a state the next engineer can use
Description: Spend the extra hour that makes this proof reusable, rather than rebuilding it from memory next quarter.
Prompt: I have built a proof demonstrating [describe what it shows] for a customer running [describe the environment]. Help me write it up so another engineer could reuse it: what it demonstrates, what environment it assumes, what it deliberately does not cover, what would have to change for a different customer, and what someone should check before reusing it. Write it for an engineer who was not involved. Do not include the customer name, contact details, or anything identifying them.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the assumptions section as somebody who was not there. Anything implicit will be missed.
3. Remove anything identifying the customer.
4. Put it where your colleagues will actually find it, and tell the ones covering similar estates.
RequiredContext: The proof you built, what it demonstrates, and the environment it assumed.
ExpectedOutput: A reuse note covering what the proof shows, what it assumes, what it excludes, and what to check before reusing it, with the customer anonymized.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE states what the proof deliberately does not cover. A reuse note that lists only capabilities gets applied to a situation it was never valid for, and the engineer who inherits the failure will not know which assumption broke.
WhyThisMatters: Reuse only works if somebody wrote down the limits. The capabilities are obvious from the artifact; the boundaries exist only in the head of whoever built it.

Name: Work out what was actually asked
Description: Reconstruct the customer's real question from the version that reached you second-hand.
Prompt: A technical question has reached me through a partner or seller. Here is how it was relayed: [paste the question as you received it]. It concerns [account name]. Using what is recorded about that customer's estate, help me work out what they might actually be asking. Give the most likely readings, what each would imply about their concern, and the single clarifying question that would tell them apart. Do not answer the question yet.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the alternative readings against what the customer actually runs.
3. If two readings need completely different answers, ask the clarifying question before answering.
4. Answering the wrong reading confidently costs more than the delay of asking.
RequiredContext: The relayed question as you received it, and the customer it concerns.
ExpectedOutput: The plausible readings of the question with the one clarifying question that would resolve them.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether to answer or to ask. A relayed question has already lost the tone and the follow-up that would have disambiguated it, and answering the wrong reading with confidence is how a technically correct answer becomes a customer problem.
WhyThisMatters: You are not in the room in this segment, so every question arrives already translated once. Treating the relayed wording as the actual question is how engineers give confidently wrong answers.

Name: Write an answer that survives being forwarded
Description: Produce a technical answer for the person who will relay it, not for a technical peer.
Prompt: Here is a technical question about [account name]: [state the question you have established]. Here is my answer: [paste your answer in your own words]. Rewrite it for a partner or seller who will relay it to the customer and who is not a specialist in this area. Lead with the direct answer, then the conditions it depends on. Keep every qualification I have written - do not simplify one away. Mark clearly which parts must be passed on word for word and which can be summarized. Do not add technical claims I have not made.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write your answer first, in your own words. The technical content is yours.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace all three bracketed sections.
3. Check nothing has been added that you did not say, and no qualification has been softened.
4. Read it as the relayer. If a sentence needs you present to make sense, rewrite it.
5. Check the word-for-word section is genuinely short - if everything is marked critical, nothing is.
6. Check it against the CELA rules before it goes to a partner: no personal data, no seat or spend detail, nothing resembling an export.
RequiredContext: The question you have established, your own technical answer, and the account. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
ExpectedOutput: Your answer rewritten for relay, with qualifications intact, the must-not-paraphrase parts marked, and the data-sharing boundary checked.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE writes the technical answer and checks that nothing was added or softened in the rewrite. A model asked to make an answer clearer will drop the qualification that made it accurate, and the person relaying it has no way to know a sentence went missing.
WhyThisMatters: An answer written for a technical peer gets compressed by whoever passes it on, and the part they drop is the qualification. Having it rewritten for the relayer is useful; letting it be written from scratch is how a confident wrong answer reaches a customer.

Name: Work out what is not yours to answer
Description: Identify the parts of a technical question that belong to product, legal, security or commercial owners, and route them.
Prompt: Here is a technical question I have been asked about [account name]: [state the question]. Break it into its separate parts and, for each, say whether answering it needs current product behavior, an unreleased or roadmap capability, licensing or commercial terms, or a security, legal or compliance position. Do not answer any part and do not suggest who should own it.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. You route these, not the agent. Licensing and commercial go to your CE; security and compliance to the authoritative owner.
3. Anything touching roadmap goes nowhere near a customer until it has shipped.
4. Answer your part fully and name who is picking up the rest, so the question does not stall.
RequiredContext: The technical question and the account it concerns. Your CE for anything commercial, and the authoritative owner for security or compliance.
ExpectedOutput: The question split by the kind of answer each part needs, with your portion answered and the rest routed by you to a named owner.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE answers the technical part and routes the rest rather than being helpful across the boundary. An engineer's answer about licensing or a roadmap date is read as authoritative because it came from the technical person, and it is repeated long after it stops being true.
WhyThisMatters: A relayed question arrives as one question and unpacks into several. Splitting it is what stops an engineer accidentally giving a commercial commitment.

Name: Find who else is running the thing you know breaks
Description: Take a problem you have already met and find the other customers exposed to it.
Prompt: I have found a technical problem at one customer: [describe the configuration or workload and what goes wrong]. Across the accounts in my patch, show me which others have the same workload or product combination deployed, with what is recorded about their deployment and any open support issue. Do not conclude that a matching product list means the same problem is present.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your problem described.
2. Treat the output as a list of customers to check, not a list of customers affected.
3. Narrow it using what you know about the configurations rather than the product names.
4. Order the survivors by how visible the failure would be to the customer.
RequiredContext: A technical problem you have already diagnosed at one customer. The accounts in your patch.
ExpectedOutput: The customers plausibly exposed to the same problem, narrowed by configuration rather than product match, and ordered by customer-visible impact.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides which matches are genuinely exposed. A product list is not a configuration, and two deployments that share a product name can differ in exactly the setting that determines whether the problem occurs.
WhyThisMatters: You do not operate any of these environments and there are too many to inspect. The only scalable way to find a problem before the customer does is to already know its shape.

Name: Check whether the problem is already being worked
Description: Find out whether an exposed customer already has a support issue open on the problem, before you warn anyone about it.
Prompt: For these customers [list the exposed accounts], show every support or service issue recorded in the last six months: what it concerns, when it was raised, its current status, and whether it has been resolved. Show the deployed workloads alongside so I can see which issues touch the configuration I am worried about. Report only what is recorded and do not judge whether any issue relates to my problem.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list.
2. Read the open issues first. An issue already raised on the same workload means somebody found this before you.
3. A resolved issue on the same configuration is worth reading too - it may be the fix you were about to describe.
4. Only for accounts with nothing recorded should you check the Partner Timeline view, since a partner may be working it outside our systems.
5. Warn only the customers where nobody appears to be on it.
RequiredContext: Your list of exposed customers from the previous activity.
ExpectedOutput: The exposed customers split by whether an issue is already open, already resolved, or nothing is recorded at all.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether an existing issue is actually the same problem. Support records describe a symptom in the customer's words rather than the cause in yours, and a ticket that looks unrelated is often the same fault reported by someone who did not know what they were seeing.
WhyThisMatters: Most of these environments are operated by somebody else, so a problem you have just spotted has often already been raised by the people living with it. Warning them about it costs you standing you will need later.

Name: Send the fix to whoever can actually apply it
Description: Write the problem up so the person who operates the solution can act on it without needing you.
Prompt: I need to tell the people operating a solution about this problem: [describe the problem, the trigger, and the fix]. Draft a short technical note for whoever operates the environment: what the symptom looks like, what causes it, how to confirm whether they are affected, and what to do about it. Write it for a competent engineer who was not involved in the original design. Keep it to what is technically necessary and exclude customer names, personal data, seat counts and spend figures.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Check the confirm-whether-affected step is something they can actually run themselves.
3. Remove anything a partner should not receive under the CELA rules.
4. Send it, and record where you sent it so this does not come back to you as new in three months.
RequiredContext: The problem, its trigger and its fix. The partners or customer teams operating the affected environments. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
ExpectedOutput: A technical note the operating team can act on unaided, with the check they can run themselves and the customer detail removed.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether the note is genuinely actionable by somebody who was not there, and checks it against the data rules before it goes to a partner. A problem report that requires the author to explain it will sit unactioned, and the customer will find the problem first.
WhyThisMatters: You are not going to fix these yourself across this many customers. The work is making the fix travel, and a note that needs you attached to it does not travel.

Name: Find out what is actually behind each account
Description: Establish which accounts have a delivery partner genuinely engaged and which have a support agreement, because on these accounts one of those may be all there is.
Prompt: For these accounts [list up to fifteen accounts from your portfolio], show two things. First, whether any support or services agreement is recorded on the account, and of what kind. Second, whether a partner is associated, with any co-sell or referral record and its recorded status and dates. Report only what the record contains and do not describe what any partner is doing or infer what support entitlement implies.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list with up to fifteen of your accounts.
2. Read the support agreement column first. An account with neither an agreement nor an engaged partner has nothing behind it at all.
3. An association is not an engagement - check the dates before assuming anyone is active.
4. For anything that looks live, open the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center; partner-side progress is only visible there.
5. Rank by what would happen at each account if something broke tomorrow.
RequiredContext: Up to fifteen accounts from your portfolio.
ExpectedOutput: Your accounts sorted by what is actually behind them: an agreement, an engaged partner, both, or nothing.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what counts as an engaged partner and what an absent agreement really means for a given account. A referral accepted eight months ago and a partner deploying this week look identical in our record, and an account with neither is one where your own time is the entire coverage.
WhyThisMatters: At this coverage ratio you are not the delivery mechanism, the agreement or the partner is. Knowing which accounts have neither tells you where a problem becomes yours by default.

Name: Write a handover the partner can act on without you
Description: Turn your own technical assessment into something a partner engineer can execute, inside the rules that govern what may be shared.
Prompt: I need to hand technical work to a delivery partner at [account name]. Here is my assessment and what I want done: [paste your own technical assessment and the work required]. Restructure this for a competent engineer at the partner who was not in any of my conversations: what the situation is, what needs doing, what order, and what they should check to confirm it worked. Do not add technical steps or recommendations I have not written. Exclude contact names and details, seat counts, spend figures, and anything that reads as an export from our systems.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write your technical assessment and the required work first. That content is yours.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
3. Check nothing technical has been added that you did not write.
4. Read it as the partner engineer. Anything that assumes a conversation they were not in has to be spelled out.
5. Check it against the CELA rules before sending: no personal data, no seat or spend detail, nothing resembling an export.
RequiredContext: One account, and your own technical assessment of what needs doing. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
ExpectedOutput: A partner-executable technical handover derived from your own assessment, checked for added content and for the data-sharing boundary.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA owns the technical content and confirms nothing was invented in the restructuring, then checks it against the data rules before it goes out. A partner engineer will execute what is written without knowing which line came from you and which was generated to make the sequence read well.
WhyThisMatters: Without a Unified agreement there is no delivery manager to interpret your intent. The handover is the whole intervention, and if it needs you attached to it, nothing happens.

Name: Decide how you will know it worked
Description: Name the observable signal that would tell you the partner's work landed, before you stop thinking about the account.
Prompt: I have handed technical work to a partner at [account name]. The intended technical outcome is [describe what should change if it worked]. Show me what is currently recorded for that account that relates to it: deployed workloads, open or resolved support issues, recorded activity, and any usage or consumption figures held in the record. Show the current state only. Do not project what should happen or judge whether the work will succeed.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Take this as your baseline and write it down with today's date.
3. Decide which single observable would change if the work landed, and by when you would expect it.
4. Put that check in your calendar. Nothing else in the week will surface it.
5. If the observable is not visible in any record you can reach, you need the partner to report it - agree that now, not later.
RequiredContext: One account with work handed to a partner, and your own definition of what would change if it succeeded.
ExpectedOutput: A dated baseline of what is currently recorded, with one observable signal and a date to check it.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA defines what would count as success and whether it is observable at all. Some technical outcomes leave no trace in any system we can see, and finding that out now rather than in three months is the difference between a check you can run and a hope.
WhyThisMatters: Work handed to a partner without a check is work you have stopped tracking. At this account count nothing will bring it back to your attention until the customer escalates.

Name: Pick the one thing worth their attention
Description: Assemble what is known about the account and choose the single technical priority, on the assumption you get one conversation.
Prompt: For [account name], show me what is recorded: the products and workloads deployed and when, any open or recently resolved support issue, any usage or consumption figures held in the record, recent activity and which role it came from, and whether a partner is associated. Present it as a factual summary. Do not rank the findings by importance or recommend what to focus on.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account.
2. Read it for what is missing as much as for what is there.
3. Now do the part the agent cannot: decide the single technical thing that most needs to be right at this customer.
4. Build the conversation around that one thing and let the rest go.
RequiredContext: One customer with a technical conversation coming up.
ExpectedOutput: A factual account summary, with your own decision on the single technical priority for the conversation.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA chooses the priority. The record shows what was bought and what has broken, but which risk actually matters for this customer depends on what they are trying to do, and a summary that ranks findings would be ranking them on the wrong criteria.
WhyThisMatters: With one conversation available, covering everything means the customer leaves with nothing. Choosing is the work, and it is not something the record can do for you.

Name: Leave something behind that works without you
Description: Turn your technical guidance into a short written artifact the customer or their partner can act on after you have moved on.
Prompt: I am advising [account name] on [state the priority you have chosen]. Here is my guidance in my own words: [paste your guidance]. Turn it into a short written note for the customer's own technical people and whoever supports them, covering what to do, in what order, what to check afterwards, and what would indicate it is going wrong. Do not add recommendations I have not written. Keep it to one page and write it for someone who was not in the conversation.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write your guidance first, in your own words. The technical judgment is yours.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace all three bracketed sections.
3. Check nothing has been added, and that no caveat you wrote has been smoothed away.
4. Test it against the question: could they follow this in three months with you unavailable?
5. Send it to the customer and, if a partner supports them, to the partner as well.
RequiredContext: One customer, your chosen technical priority, and your own guidance written out.
ExpectedOutput: A one-page durable note the customer or their partner can act on without you, derived from your own guidance.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA owns the guidance and confirms nothing was added in the rewrite. Advice that gets acted on months later with nobody available to interpret it has to be right as written, and a generated clarification that changes the meaning will not be caught by the person following it.
WhyThisMatters: At this coverage the value you leave is more durable than the value you deliver in the room. A conversation with nothing written down is gone the week after.

Name: Name who has this account after you
Description: Establish which Microsoft roles have been active recently and who realistically holds the technical relationship next.
Prompt: For [account name], list every recorded activity in the last six months with the date and the role it came from, and show any open support issue with its recorded owner. Show the roles by how recently each was active. Do not include partner or co-sell records, and do not infer who is responsible for the account technically.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account.
2. If the only recent activity is yours, that is the finding.
3. Decide who realistically holds this next - the DAE, a partner you already identified, or nobody - and be honest about the last option.
4. Tell them, and tell the customer who to contact. An unnamed successor is the same as none.
RequiredContext: One customer you are unlikely to revisit soon.
ExpectedOutput: The Microsoft roles active on the account ordered by recency, with a named technical successor or an explicit acknowledgment that there is not one.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides who genuinely picks this up, including the honest answer that nobody does. Naming a successor who has not agreed is worse than admitting the gap, because the customer will call someone who is not expecting them.
WhyThisMatters: Accounts at this coverage ratio quietly lose their technical contact and nobody notices until something breaks. Saying out loud that there is no successor is what turns it into a decision somebody can make.

Name: Work out which accounts left any trace of delivery
Description: Establish which of your accounts have a delivery record behind them and which have nothing but telemetry, because that determines what you can ever evidence.
Prompt: For these accounts [list up to fifteen accounts where you believe the technical outcome was good], show for each whether a support or services agreement is recorded, any support issue raised and how it was resolved, any milestone or success activity logged, and any usage or consumption figures held in the record. Separate the accounts that produced some record of delivery work from those where the only thing recorded is the purchase and whatever usage figures exist. Do not infer an outcome from deployment or from usage.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list.
2. The accounts with no delivery record are the normal case here, not the failures. That is what non-Unified looks like.
3. For those, usage figures are the only evidence that will ever exist, so decide now whether they say anything useful.
4. For the accounts that did produce a record, check whether the work recorded is actually connected to the outcome you have in mind.
5. Pick the account with the strongest case and carry it into the attribution step.
RequiredContext: Up to fifteen accounts where you believe the technical outcome was good.
ExpectedOutput: Your accounts split by whether any delivery record exists, with an explicit read on what can be evidenced for those where none does.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides whether usage figures alone amount to evidence of an outcome. On an account with no delivery record they are all there is, and consumption showing a service running is a much weaker claim than a customer saying it solved something.
WhyThisMatters: A Unified engagement leaves milestones and hours behind it. Most of these accounts leave nothing, so knowing which ones produced any record at all tells you where a value story is even possible before somebody asks you for one.

Name: Separate what you did from what the partner did
Description: Establish who actually performed the delivery work, so that outcomes are described by whoever earned them.
Prompt: For these accounts [list your evidenced accounts], show what the record says about work performed: each recorded activity with its date and the role it came from, each support issue with who logged it and who resolved it, and the dates workloads were deployed.
