Report the recorded actors only. Do not infer who was responsible for any outcome and do not summarize contribution.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list.
2. Our record captures what Microsoft logged. On a partner-delivered account that is a fraction of what happened, and the gaps are the partner's work.
3. Where a partner delivered, the outcome is theirs to describe and yours to acknowledge.
4. If you want to use a partner-delivered outcome, ask them rather than reconstructing it from our record.
RequiredContext: Your evidenced accounts from the previous activity.
ExpectedOutput: Recorded delivery work attributed by actor, with the partner-delivered outcomes identified as theirs to describe.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what is honestly ours to claim. Our record shows what Microsoft logged, which on a partner-delivered account is a small fraction of what happened, and presenting that fraction as the whole story is visible to the partner immediately.
WhyThisMatters: On non-Unified accounts the partner may have done most of the delivery. Getting attribution right is not politeness, it is the thing that keeps the partner willing to do it again.

Name: Get the evidence to whoever owns the renewal
Description: Pass the technical evidence to the account and commercial roles before the renewal conversation happens without it.
Prompt: For [account name], I have technical evidence of the outcome delivered. Here is what I can evidence: [paste what you established]. Draft a short internal note for the account executive and the commercial executive covering what was delivered, what the evidence is, what the partner contributed, and what remains unproven. Keep it brief and factual. Do not add claims I have not made and do not characterize the commercial implications.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Check nothing has been added, particularly anything that reads as a commercial recommendation.
3. Say plainly what remains unproven. A note that only lists wins is discounted by whoever reads it.
4. Send it to the DAE and the CE, and note the renewal date so you know whether it arrived in time.
RequiredContext: One account with evidenced technical outcomes, your own summary of them, and the renewal date if known.
ExpectedOutput: A brief factual internal note for the account and commercial roles, stating what is evidenced, what the partner contributed, and what is not proven.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA states what is not proven alongside what is. A technical note that reads as advocacy gets discounted entirely by the people preparing a renewal, and the unproven items are exactly what they need to know before they meet the customer.
WhyThisMatters: Renewal conversations belong to the account and commercial roles. Technical evidence that stays with the architect does not reach them, and at this coverage nobody will come and ask for it.

Name: Separate what you know from what you were told
Description: Establish what our own record can independently confirm about an opportunity a partner brought you.
Prompt: A partner has brought me an opportunity at [account or company name]. Here is what they have told me: [paste what the partner told you]. Show me what our record independently contains about that customer: whether they exist as an account and under whose ownership, any products or workloads already in place, any prior or open opportunity, any recorded activity and from which role, and any existing partner association. State plainly which of the partner's claims our record can speak to and which it cannot. Do not assess whether the opportunity is likely to close.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the cannot-speak-to list first. That is the part you are taking on the partner's word.
3. If the account is owned by a DAE, tell them before you invest anything.
4. Decide how much Microsoft resource you will commit against the unverifiable portion, and be explicit that you are choosing to.
RequiredContext: One opportunity brought to you by a partner, and what the partner told you about it.
ExpectedOutput: The partner's claims split into what our record can confirm and what rests entirely on their word, with an explicit decision on what to invest against the latter.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides how much to invest against a claim only the partner can make. Their qualification bar is not ours and their incentive is to get Microsoft engaged, and a partner who is habitually right about this is a different proposition from one who is not, which is a judgment about the relationship rather than about the deal.
WhyThisMatters: Every other role in this segment sends work out to partners. You also receive it, and what arrives has been qualified by somebody with a different standard and a different interest in the answer.

Name: Check the conditions before anyone counts on it
Description: Establish whether a partner-originated deal meets the recorded conditions for registration, before it is treated as one.
Prompt: For [opportunity name or ID], show me what is recorded that bears on co-sell registration: the account and whether it is Microsoft-managed, the recorded deal value and currency, the solution area and products attached, the opportunity creation date, and the current stage and status. Also show any existing co-sell or referral record on the opportunity with its dates. Report only what is recorded and do not assess eligibility.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Home and paste the prompt with the opportunity.
2. Check the recorded facts against the conditions yourself: a Microsoft-managed account, Azure IP co-sell eligibility, a value of at least twenty-five thousand US dollars, and at least seventy-two hours between creation and being marked won.
3. Anything you cannot confirm from the record, confirm with the authoritative owner rather than assuming.
4. Tell the partner what is missing now. Finding out at close is too late for both of you.
RequiredContext: One partner-originated opportunity. The current co-sell registration conditions from the authoritative source.
ExpectedOutput: The recorded facts assembled against the registration conditions, with the gaps identified and raised with the partner early.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS confirms eligibility against the authoritative source rather than against a summary. Registration conditions change and a deal that fails one at close costs the partner real money, which is the kind of thing that ends a partnership rather than a deal.
WhyThisMatters: The conditions are checkable long before close, and nothing prompts anyone to check them until it is nearly there. The whole cost of getting this wrong lands on the partner, and they will remember.

Name: Find the partner who keeps letting things lapse
Description: Look across your partners for the ones whose referrals and co-sell records consistently stall, because that is a relationship problem rather than a record problem.
Prompt: For these partners [list three to five partners], show me the co-sell and referral records associated with each: the account, the recorded status, the date the record was created, and the date of the last recorded change. Group the output by partner. Report the recorded dates only - do not calculate elapsed time, judge which are close to expiring, or compare the partners.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Home, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list with three to five of your partners.
2. Do the arithmetic yourself against the windows: fourteen days for a partner to accept a referral before it expires, sixty days after acceptance to convert before it is marked lost.
3. Read down each partner rather than across all the records. One lapsed referral is an accident; a partner with several is a conversation.
4. Check anything near a boundary in the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center, since our recorded status can lag what the partner has already done.
5. Chase the individual items with days left, and raise the pattern with the partner who has one.
RequiredContext: Three to five partners from your portfolio. The Partner Timeline view or Partner Center for anything near a boundary.
ExpectedOutput: Records grouped by partner with the window arithmetic done by you, separating one-off lapses from a partner-level pattern.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides whether a pattern of lapsed records is a capacity problem, a fit problem, or a partner who was never going to work them. Those need completely different conversations, and the records look identical in all three cases.
WhyThisMatters: Individual expiring referrals are chased by whoever sent them. Nobody else is positioned to notice whether the lapses concentrate on one partner, and that is the finding worth having.

Name: Decide which partners need you this month
Description: Triage a portfolio of partners into the ones with something to decide and the ones that only need contact.
Prompt: For these partners [list three to five partners], show for each: the co-sell and referral records currently associated with them and the recorded status of each, and any opportunity where they are the associated partner along with its stage and the date it last moved. Group the output by partner. Do not rank the partners, compare them, or recommend where to spend time.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list with three to five partners.
2. Look for partners with something stalled or something approaching a decision - those need a meeting with an agenda.
3. Partners with everything moving need a check-in, not a meeting.
4. Separately, check your own cadence commitment: a minimum of monthly contact per partner seller. Anyone you have not spoken to in that window needs contact regardless of what the record shows.
5. Split the month into meetings that need preparation and contacts that satisfy the cadence.
RequiredContext: Three to five partners from your portfolio, and your own record of when you last spoke to each.
ExpectedOutput: Those partners split into meetings that need an agenda and contacts that meet the cadence commitment.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides which partner genuinely needs time this month. Activity in the record tracks how much business is flowing rather than how much attention the relationship needs, and meeting a cadence minimum is a floor rather than a plan.
WhyThisMatters: A minimum contact cadence is an obligation, not a strategy. Without a deliberate split the calendar fills with the partners who ask for time, and the meetings that needed preparation get none.

Name: Give the meeting something to decide
Description: Turn a recurring partner meeting into one with a decision attached, using what has actually moved.
Prompt: I have a partner meeting with [partner name]. Show me what has changed on their associated records since a month ago where the record supports that: opportunities that moved stage, co-sell or referral records created or changed status, and any new recorded activity. Also show what has not moved. Present the changes factually and do not propose an agenda or suggest what to discuss.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [partner name].
2. The things that have not moved are the meeting. The things that have moved are the update.
3. Pick one decision you want out of the conversation and build the agenda around it.
4. Send the partner the decision you want to reach beforehand, so they can arrive able to make it.
RequiredContext: One partner with a meeting coming up.
ExpectedOutput: A factual read on what has and has not moved for that partner, with one decision chosen and sent ahead as the agenda.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS chooses the decision the meeting is for. What has not moved may be a partner problem, a Microsoft problem or a customer problem, and walking in with the wrong attribution turns a working session into a defensive one.
WhyThisMatters: Recurring partner meetings drift into status reporting, which both sides can do by email. A meeting with a decision attached is the only kind worth the cadence.

Name: Find out who else is talking to your partner
Description: Establish which Microsoft roles are engaged with the same partner, so the partner is not receiving three different asks.
Prompt: For these accounts where [partner name] is engaged [list three to five accounts], show which Microsoft roles have recorded activity on each in the last quarter and the date of the most recent from each role. Present it account by account with the roles named. Do not infer coordination or judge whether the engagement is aligned.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your partner and three to five of the accounts they work.
2. Look for accounts where several roles are active - the partner may be receiving conflicting asks.
3. Look for accounts where only the partner appears and no Microsoft role does.
4. Raise the conflicts at the territory health review rather than by chasing each role individually.
RequiredContext: One partner, and three to five accounts where they are engaged.
ExpectedOutput: The accounts where your partner is engaged, showing which Microsoft roles are active on each and where nobody is.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides whether several roles engaging one partner is coordination or confusion. The record shows activity rather than intent, and a partner being asked for different things by three people will do the easiest one and tell nobody.
WhyThisMatters: Partners work with many people at Microsoft, and one receiving mixed messages does not necessarily say so; they prioritize. Seeing the overlap is the only way to find out it is happening.

Name: Find out what happened after one partner's deals closed
Description: Take a single partner and establish what our record knows about the customers they closed, and where it goes silent.
Prompt: For [partner name], show me the opportunities recorded as closed won where they are the associated partner, going back two quarters. For each, show the account, the close date, and then what has been recorded on that account since that date: any activity and from which role, any support issue, and any usage or consumption figures held in the record. Show the most recent record date for each account alongside the close date. Do not infer customer satisfaction or outcome from any of it.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [partner name] with one partner.
2. Look at the gap between each close date and the most recent record. That gap is what Microsoft cannot see.
3. Read it as a pattern for this partner rather than as a list of accounts. If every one of their customers goes silent immediately, that tells you something about how they work.
4. Long silence is not evidence of a problem or of success. It is the normal condition when a partner owns the relationship.
5. Pick the customer where not knowing would cost the most, usually one with a renewal ahead.
RequiredContext: One partner whose closed deals you want to understand.
ExpectedOutput: The visibility gap across one partner's closed customers, read as a pattern for that partner, with the customer where it matters most identified.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides where a gap in our visibility actually matters. Silence after a partner-led close is normal rather than alarming, and treating every quiet customer as a risk will exhaust both your time and the partner's patience.
WhyThisMatters: Our record ends roughly where the customer's experience begins on these deals. Looking partner by partner rather than account by account shows you whether the blind spot is about one customer or about how that partner works.

Name: Ask the partner something worth answering
Description: Draft the question that gets a partner to tell you how a customer is actually doing, without it reading as an audit.
Prompt: I want to ask [partner name] how a customer is getting on since they closed and delivered. Here is what I already know from our record: [paste what you found]. Draft a short message asking about the customer's experience and any difficulty they have hit. Write it as a colleague with a shared interest in the customer, not as an inspection. Keep it to a few lines. Do not request seat counts, consumption figures, financial detail or anything commercially sensitive, and do not imply any obligation to report to us.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read it as the partner. If it sounds like a request for a status report, it will be answered like one.
3. Check it against the CELA rules in both directions - what you are asking for as well as what you are sharing.
4. Send it, and be ready to offer something in return. A question with nothing behind it gets a short answer.
RequiredContext: One partner and one customer they closed, plus what our record already shows. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
ExpectedOutput: A short colleague-to-colleague question about a specific customer, checked against the data rules and with something offered in return.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS owns how this reads to the partner. A partner has no obligation to report customer outcomes to Microsoft, so the answer depends entirely on whether the question sounds like interest or like inspection, and only the person in the relationship can judge which.
WhyThisMatters: This is the only route Microsoft has back to a customer a partner owns. Getting the tone wrong does not just fail to get an answer, it makes the next question harder.

Name: Get what you learn back to the people who need it
Description: Pass what a partner tells you about a customer to the account and commercial roles, without overstating what you were told.
Prompt: A partner has told me about a customer they closed and delivered. Here is what they said: [paste what the partner told you]. Here is what our record shows: [paste the record position]. Draft a short internal note for the account executive and the commercial executive setting out what the partner reported, what our record independently shows, and where the two do not line up. Attribute the partner's account clearly as theirs. Do not resolve any discrepancy or add conclusions I have not drawn.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Check the partner's account is presented as their report rather than as established fact.
3. Leave any discrepancy visible. The gap between what a partner says and what the record shows is the useful part.
4. Send it to the DAE and the CE, and tell the partner you have passed it on.
RequiredContext: What the partner told you, and what our record shows for the same customer.
ExpectedOutput: A short internal note separating the partner's report from our record, with discrepancies left visible and attribution clear.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides what is safe to represent as fact when it came from a single partner conversation. A partner's read is genuine information and is also their interpretation, and a note that promotes it into a finding will be acted on by people who never spoke to them.
WhyThisMatters: What you learn from a partner is worthless if it stays with you. It is also dangerous if it travels as established fact, and the difference is entirely in how the note is written.

Name: List the questions this structure will have to answer
Description: Surface the policy, licensing and eligibility questions a deal will meet, before the structure is fixed.
Prompt: For [account name], show what is recorded that bears on commercial eligibility: the agreement type and its dates, the products and quantities involved, whether a partner is associated and any co-sell or referral record, and any amendment or exception already on the account. Also show whether the account transacts direct or through a partner where the record says so. Report what is recorded and do not interpret eligibility, licensing entitlement or policy.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account.
2. Read the agreement type and the transaction route first - both change which rules apply.
3. Write down each question the structure raises. That list is yours to produce, not the agent's.
4. Route every one to the authoritative owner rather than answering from a previous deal.
RequiredContext: One live deal where the commercial structure is not yet fixed.
ExpectedOutput: The recorded facts that bear on eligibility, with your own list of the questions the structure raises.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides which questions genuinely need an authoritative answer and routes them rather than answering from precedent. A structure that worked for a similar customer shows only that it was permitted once, on facts you have probably not seen, and reusing it quietly converts someone else's exception into your own assumption.
WhyThisMatters: Policy questions are cheapest at the point the structure is still a question. Asked at approval they cost weeks, and by then the customer may already have been told something that no longer holds.

Name: Route the question so it comes back usable
Description: Frame a policy question so the authoritative owner can answer it once, rather than starting a conversation.
Prompt: I need to ask an authoritative owner a policy question about [account name]. Here is the question and the context: [paste your question and the deal facts that bear on it]. Restructure this as a single question that can be answered without a follow-up: what is being asked, the specific facts that determine the answer, what I have already checked, and what decision the answer will drive. Do not answer the question or suggest what the answer might be.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write the question yourself first, including the deal facts that determine the answer.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
3. Check the restructured version still asks YOUR question rather than a cleaner adjacent one.
4. Send it, and record the answer against the account so the next person does not ask again.
RequiredContext: Your policy question and the deal facts that bear on it. The authoritative owner for that question.
ExpectedOutput: A single self-contained question that can be answered without a follow-up, with the answer recorded against the account.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE owns the question and confirms the rewrite did not change what is being asked. A model asked to make a question clearer will often make it more general, and a general answer to a specific eligibility question is worse than no answer because it feels like one.
WhyThisMatters: Most policy delay is not the owner being slow, it is the question arriving without the facts needed to answer it. One well-formed question beats three exchanges.

Name: Say out loud what you are relying on
Description: Make an inherited policy position explicit enough that its owner can confirm or correct it.
Prompt: For [account name], show every amendment, exception or non-standard term recorded against this account: what each one is, the date it was recorded, and which agreement it sits against. Report only what is recorded on this account. Do not compare it to other accounts, and do not judge whether any of it still applies.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write down the position you are about to rely on, in one sentence, before you look at anything. If you cannot state it, you do not yet know what you are assuming.
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [account name] with your deal.
3. Check whether the record actually says what you remember it saying. Often it says something narrower.
4. Send your one sentence and the relevant record to the authoritative owner and ask whether it still stands.
RequiredContext: One live deal and the policy position you intend to rely on.
ExpectedOutput: The position you are relying on stated in one sentence, with its recorded basis, sent to the authoritative owner for confirmation.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE states precisely what position they are relying on and has the owner confirm it before building on it. Reuse is invisible - a previous answer gets carried forward as an assumption rather than re-examined as a decision - and only the person relying on it can notice they are doing it. Whether it still stands is the owner's call, not a matter of how recent it looks.
WhyThisMatters: The most expensive policy error is not a wrong answer, it is a right answer that has expired. Nothing in the record marks a position as superseded, so the only reliable move is to name what you are assuming and have it confirmed.

Name: Establish what can be conceded without asking
Description: Fix the concession boundary from approved guidance before any pressure is applied to it.
Prompt: For [account name], show any discount, concession or non-standard term already in force on this account: what each one is, which agreement it sits on, and whether a partner transacts it. Report what is recorded. Do not advise what concession would be appropriate and do not propose a boundary.
ActivitySteps:
1. Set your concession boundary from current approved guidance before you look at anything. That anchor does not come from the record.
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [account name] with your deal.
3. Treat what is already in force as a constraint on the boundary, not as evidence for it. It may itself have been an exception.
4. Write the boundary down, with the existing concessions noted against it, before anyone asks you to move.
RequiredContext: One live deal heading toward a negotiation. Current approved commercial guidance for concession authority.
ExpectedOutput: A concession boundary set from approved guidance, with the concessions already in force on the account recorded as constraints on it.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE sets the boundary from current approved guidance rather than from what comparable deals happen to carry. What was granted elsewhere may have been an exception, may have been wrong, or may have been approved under guidance that has since changed, and inheriting it silently converts one exception into a standard.
WhyThisMatters: A boundary set before the pressure arrives is a decision. The same boundary set during the negotiation is a reaction, and it will be argued with.

Name: Test whether your briefing gives away the floor
Description: Check what a partner could infer from the boundary you are about to hand them.
Prompt: A partner will negotiate [describe the deal] with the customer. Here is the briefing I have written for them, covering what is fixed, what is theirs to use without asking, and what has to come back to me: [paste your briefing]. Read it as the partner would. Tell me what could be inferred from it about how much room exists beyond what I have stated, what is vague enough to be read as permission I did not intend, and anything in it resembling internal cost, margin, approval thresholds, seat counts, spend figures or personal data. Do not rewrite the briefing and do not tell me where the boundary should sit.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write the briefing yourself, in three parts: what is fixed, what is theirs to use without asking, and what must come back to you. All three are your decisions and none of them are delegated.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
3. Close anything that could be read as permission you did not intend to give. Vagueness reads as room.
4. Check it against the CELA rules yourself as well. The agent is a second reader, not the control.
5. Send it through your normal partner channel before the negotiation, not during it.
RequiredContext: The partner briefing you have written, setting out what is fixed, what is theirs to use, and what must return to you for approval. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
ExpectedOutput: A partner briefing whose stated limits cannot be read as more room than you intended, with everything inferable closed before it is sent.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides how much of the boundary the partner needs to see. Too little and they concede something they should have escalated; too much and your floor becomes their opening position with the customer. That judgment depends on the specific partner, and only the person in the relationship can make it.
WhyThisMatters: A boundary is only as good as what the other side can infer around it. Partners are commercially sophisticated and will read the shape of what you did not say.

Name: Decide now what would make you escalate
Description: Name the specific condition that would take a concession decision above you, before it arrives.
Prompt: For the deal at [account name], my concession boundary is [paste your boundary]. Help me think through what circumstances would put a decision beyond that boundary: what the customer might reasonably ask for, what a partner might commit to on their own, and what timing pressure might create. For each, frame it as a condition to watch for rather than a prediction. Do not recommend whether to escalate or what the answer should be.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Pick the one or two conditions most likely to actually occur.
3. Write the trigger as something observable - a specific ask, a specific number - not as a feeling.
4. Tell your approver now that it may be coming, so the escalation is expected rather than a surprise.
RequiredContext: Your concession boundary and the deal it applies to. Your approval route.
ExpectedOutput: One or two observable escalation triggers named in advance, with the approver forewarned.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides what genuinely warrants escalation. Escalating everything trains your approver to stop reading, and escalating nothing means the boundary was never real, and only you can judge where this deal sits between those.
WhyThisMatters: An escalation raised before the pressure is a decision with time attached. The same escalation raised during a negotiation is an emergency, and gets a worse answer.

Name: Find every approval this structure triggers
Description: Assemble the full set of approvals a commercial structure will need, rather than meeting them one at a time.
Prompt: For [account name] I am taking this commercial structure to approval: [paste the structure]. Show what is already recorded that an approver would need to see: any exception or non-standard term already approved on this account and when it was recorded, the current deal stage and value, and whether a partner is associated with the account. Report what is recorded. Do not determine which approvals are required or who approves them.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your deal.
2. Work out the required approvals yourself from current approved guidance - that mapping is yours and it changes.
3. For each, decide whether it is one you obtain, one you request, or one the partner obtains from their own organization.
4. Confirm current lead times rather than assuming last quarter's.
RequiredContext: One deal with an agreed commercial structure needing approval. Current approved guidance on approval requirements.
ExpectedOutput: The full approval set for this structure, each classified by whether you obtain it, request it, or the partner obtains it.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE determines which approvals are required, because that mapping changes with guidance and the record cannot know it. The classification matters more than the list: an approval you can obtain and one the partner must obtain from their own organization look identical on a plan and behave completely differently.
WhyThisMatters: Approvals met one at a time cost a week each. Mapping them together can show which ones run in parallel, and the sequence that looked fixed may be habit.

Name: Replace every implied owner with a named one
Description: Turn an approval path expressed in roles into one expressed in people who know it is coming.
Prompt: Here is the approval path I have mapped for [account name]. For each step I have listed the owning role and the evidence that approval requires: [paste your approval list]. Draft the short note I would send to secure each one: what is being asked, the evidence I have listed against it, the date it is needed by, and what happens if it slips. Keep each to a few lines. Do not add evidence I have not listed, do not invent approver names, and do not state who the owner is.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Put a real name against every role before you send anything. A role is not an owner.
3. For partner-side steps, send the note to your partner contact rather than assuming they will discover it.
4. Send them all now rather than in sequence. Most of these are not actually dependent on each other.
RequiredContext: Your mapped approval path, with the owning role for each step and the evidence that step requires taken from current approved guidance. The people who currently hold those roles.
ExpectedOutput: A named owner and a sent request for every approval step, with the partner-side steps raised with the partner.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE confirms who currently holds each approval and that the evidence listed against it is what that approver actually asks for. Both change without announcement - a role moves, or a threshold is revised - and a note sent to last quarter's owner citing last quarter's evidence is a week lost before anyone notices it went to the wrong place.
WhyThisMatters: The approval path can be entirely correct and still unowned. Naming people converts a diagram into something that moves.

Name: Find the approval that never landed
Description: Check the approvals you have already requested against what the record now shows, before a customer date makes it urgent.
Prompt: Here are the approvals I have outstanding and the date I requested each one: [paste your list with dates]. For each, show what is currently recorded on that opportunity: the current stage, the recorded next step and who owns it, and the close date. Report what is recorded and do not infer why anything is waiting.
ActivitySteps:
1. List your outstanding approvals and the date you asked for each. If you cannot produce that list, that is itself the finding.
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
3. Compare the recorded next step against what you actually asked for. Where they do not match, the request never landed.
4. Chase the ones you own with the named person rather than the queue. For partner-side approvals, ask your partner contact - our record will not show their progress at all.
RequiredContext: The approvals you have already requested, and the date you requested each one.
ExpectedOutput: Outstanding approvals separated into those that landed, those that never registered, and those sitting with a partner organization.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides which approvals have genuinely stalled and which are simply waiting their turn. An approval nobody ever submitted and one sitting correctly in a queue look identical from inside our systems, and a partner-side approval leaves no trace here at all - chasing that one through our own record costs the week you were trying to save.
WhyThisMatters: Approvals fail quietly. The request that was never registered looks exactly like the one being worked, and the difference only becomes visible when the close date arrives.

Name: State the decision you are asking someone to make
Description: Turn a commercial structure into an explicit decision, so the approver is not left to work out what is being asked.
Prompt: I am taking a commercial structure to approval. Here is the structure and what I am asking for: [paste the structure and the ask]. Restate this as a decision: what specifically is being approved, what the alternatives were and why they were set aside, what happens if it is declined, and what the approver is accepting responsibility for. Use only what I have given you. Do not add commercial detail, do not recommend a decision, and do not soften the ask.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write the structure and the ask down yourself first. If you cannot state the ask in one sentence, it is not ready to send.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
3. Check the alternatives are the ones you genuinely considered, not ones that make the recommendation look inevitable.
4. Confirm the responsibility line is accurate. That sentence is the one the approver will remember.
RequiredContext: One commercial structure you have agreed and intend to take to approval. The approval you are seeking.
ExpectedOutput: The structure restated as an explicit decision, with the alternatives, the consequence of declining, and what the approver is accepting.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides what the approver is actually being asked to accept. An approval request that understates what the approver is taking on gets granted quickly and withdrawn later, and the second conversation is far more expensive than the first.
WhyThisMatters: Approvers are sent structures and left to infer the decision. The ones that stall are the ones where the ask was never stated plainly, and nobody wants to admit they could not find it.

Name: Make the numbers checkable by someone else
Description: Lay out the economics so an approver can verify them rather than take them on trust.
Prompt: Here are the economics of the commercial structure I am proposing: [paste your figures and where each came from]. Lay them out so someone else can check them: what is committed, over what period, what the customer pays and when, and what varies from standard and by how much. Show each figure alongside the source I have given for it. Do not calculate anything I have not supplied, do not estimate missing values, and flag any figure I have given without a source.
ActivitySteps:
1. Assemble your figures first, and write the source next to each one as you go.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
3. Look at what it flags as unsourced. Those are the ones you will be asked about.
4. Replace any figure you cannot source with the range you can defend, and say it is a range.
RequiredContext: The economics of your proposed structure, with the source of each figure.
ExpectedOutput: The economics laid out with a source against every figure, and unsourced figures either sourced or stated as ranges.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE owns every number in the narrative and confirms each against where it came from. A figure that appears in an approval document becomes the figure everyone quotes afterwards, and the person who typed it is the only one who knows whether it was measured or estimated.
WhyThisMatters: A commercial narrative can fail review on one unsourced number rather than on the strength of the case. The figure nobody can trace is the one that stops the meeting.

Name: Find what you have asserted without showing
Description: Read your own narrative as someone who was not in any of the conversations behind it.
Prompt: Here is the commercial decision narrative I have written: [paste the narrative]. Read it as someone who was not part of any conversation behind it. List every claim asserted without evidence attached, every figure whose source is not stated, and every place where a judgment is presented as though it were a fact. Do not rewrite it, do not supply the missing evidence, and do not tell me whether the case is a good one.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Read the list before defending anything. The first reaction to most of these is that the context is obvious.
3. Close the gaps on the central commercial claim. Leave the peripheral ones open if closing them would bury the argument.
4. Where a judgment is being presented as a fact, say whose judgment it is.
RequiredContext: Your drafted commercial decision narrative.
ExpectedOutput: The narrative's unevidenced claims identified, with the central ones closed and the remaining judgments attributed.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides which gaps must be closed before this goes and which can stand. A narrative that evidences every claim is unreadable and a narrative that leaves the central commercial claim unevidenced is returned, and telling those apart is the whole skill.
WhyThisMatters: You cannot see the assumptions you carried into your own document. Everything in it was obvious to you at the time, which is exactly why it reads as unsupported to the person approving it.

Name: Compare the options on what happens when nobody tunes them
Description: Research architecture options for a customer with no platform team, judging them on how they behave unattended.
Prompt: I am designing [describe the workload] for a customer with [describe their technical capacity and who will operate it]. Using approved Microsoft and authoritative public sources, compare the architecture options on operational burden: what each requires someone to monitor, tune or intervene on; what each does when left alone; what skills each assumes the operator already has; and what the documented failure modes are. Cite each claim and name where guidance conflicts or is missing. Do not recommend an option.
ActivitySteps:
1. Write down who will operate this before you look at any options. That constraint decides the answer.
2. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
3. Check the citations. Guidance written for a customer with a platform team will not say so, and you have to notice.
4. Discard any option whose operational assumptions this customer cannot meet, however good it looks.
RequiredContext: The workload and the customer's technical constraints. What you know about who will operate it.
ExpectedOutput: Architecture options compared on unattended behavior and operator skill assumed, with sources cited and gaps named.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what this customer can realistically operate. Published guidance assumes a competent platform team because it is written for the general case, and a design chosen on capability alone will be technically correct and quietly abandoned within two quarters.
BestFitJob: Compare the options on what happens when nobody tunes them
WhyThisMatters: For a portfolio of non-unified customers there is no support relationship to absorb an operationally demanding design. The question is not which architecture is best but which one survives contact with the people who will actually run it.

Name: Write the design for the person who will build it
Description: Turn a chosen architecture into something a partner or customer team can implement without you present.
Prompt: Here is the architecture I have chosen and what I know about who will implement it: [paste the design, the constraints, and what the implementer has built before]. Turn this into an implementation-ready description covering the sequence and the dependencies, marking which dependencies are outside the implementer's control. Separately, list every configuration decision the implementer will have to make that my design does not already settle, and for each state what the design implies but does not say. Do not choose any of those configurations for me and do not add architectural decisions I have not made.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Read the unsettled configuration list. Those are the decisions the implementer will otherwise make for you, at the point you are least available.
3. Write your recommended choice against each one yourself. That is a design decision and it does not get delegated.
4. Send it to the implementer and ask which step they would want to talk through.
RequiredContext: Your chosen architecture and its constraints. Who will implement it and what they have built before.
ExpectedOutput: An implementation-ready design with the sequence and dependencies, plus the configuration decisions your design leaves open, each answered by you.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA answers every configuration decision the design leaves open. The implementer will resolve anything left silent using their own defaults, which are reasonable for their usual customer and may be wrong for this one - and the divergence only becomes visible when something behaves unexpectedly months later.
BestFitJob: Write the design for the person who will build it
WhyThisMatters: The design is not the artifact. What the implementer does with it is the artifact, and everything you left implicit becomes their judgment call.

Name: Find what your design assumes the customer has
Description: Read your own design for the support, skills and tooling it quietly takes for granted.
Prompt: Here is a design I am about to hand over: [paste the design]. Here is what I actually know about the customer's operating capability: [describe their team, skills, tooling and support arrangements]. Identify every point where the design assumes capability, tooling, support or availability I have not confirmed they have. For each, state what the design expects and what happens if it is absent. Do not redesign anything and do not tell me whether the design is good.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the list before defending it. Most of these assumptions felt obvious when you made them.
3. Confirm or close the ones that would cause a silent failure. An assumption that fails loudly is survivable.
4. Where you cannot close one, say so in the handover rather than leaving it to be discovered.
RequiredContext: Your implementation-ready design. What you actually know about the customer's operating capability and support arrangements.
ExpectedOutput: The design's unconfirmed assumptions listed with the consequence of each, and the silent-failure ones closed or disclosed.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides which unconfirmed assumptions are acceptable to hand over. Every design assumes something, and closing all of it is not possible in this segment - the judgment is which assumption fails quietly, because that is the one that turns into a consumption problem nobody traces back to the design.
BestFitJob: Find what your design assumes the customer has
WhyThisMatters: You cannot see what you assumed. Everything in the design was reasonable when you wrote it, which is exactly why the gaps are invisible to you and obvious to the customer six months later.

Name: Find the accounts where something technical has changed
Description: Scan the portfolio for the recorded signals that precede a consumption problem.
Prompt: Across the accounts in my portfolio, identify those where consumption or usage has moved against plan, and separately those with a support or service record raised in the period I specify but no recorded technical activity from us. For the accounts that match, show the recorded movement, the support activity and the date of our last recorded technical engagement. Use this period: [state the period]. Do not return the accounts that do not match and do not diagnose a cause.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Treat the two groups differently: movement against plan is a question, support activity with no engagement from us is a gap.
3. For each candidate, form your own technical hypothesis before opening the account. The record will not give you one.
4. Rank by how expensive the problem becomes if it is still there next quarter, not by size.
RequiredContext: Your portfolio of accounts. Whatever consumption, usage and support views you can reach. The period you want assessed.
ExpectedOutput: The portfolio split into accounts moving against plan and accounts with unattended support activity, ranked by cost of delay.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides which movement is technically significant. Consumption drops for reasons that have nothing to do with the technology - a project ending, a budget cycle, a seasonal workload - and spending your limited portfolio time on those is how the real problem stays undiscovered.
BestFitJob: Find the accounts where something technical has changed
WhyThisMatters: At this portfolio size you cannot inspect accounts individually, so the scan is the only way in. It will not tell you what is wrong; it tells you where to spend the attention you have.

Name: Raise a problem the customer has not noticed yet
Description: Prepare the conversation where you tell a customer about a technical risk they did not ask you to look for.
Prompt: I need to raise a technical risk with a customer who has not asked about it. Here is the risk and my evidence: [describe the risk and what supports it]. Here is who I would raise it with and our history: [describe the contact and the relationship]. Help me rehearse this conversation: how to open it without implying they have been negligent, what they are likely to push back on, how to respond if they say it is not a priority, and how to close with a specific next step. Do not tell me whether to raise it.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Rehearse the pushback you find hardest rather than the opening you find easiest.
3. Decide in advance what you will do if they decline to act. That answer is yours, not the agent's.
4. Have the conversation, and record what they said so the next person does not raise it cold again.
RequiredContext: The technical risk you have identified and the evidence for it. Who at the customer you would raise it with.
ExpectedOutput: A rehearsed conversation with the likely objections worked through and a specific next step prepared.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides whether the evidence is strong enough to raise unasked. A technical risk surfaced on partial evidence and then disproved by the customer's own team costs the standing you would need to raise the next one, and the record may not contain enough to settle it either way before the conversation.
BestFitJob: Raise a problem the customer has not noticed yet
WhyThisMatters: Finding the risk is the easy part. The conversation is where it either becomes an intervention or becomes a note nobody acted on, and in this segment you may get one attempt.

Name: Set a standing check so the next one finds you
Description: Put a recurring watch on the portfolio so technical movement reaches you when it happens rather than at the next review.
Prompt: Set up a recurring weekly check across the accounts in my portfolio. Each week, tell me where consumption or usage has moved against plan, where a new support or service record has appeared on an account with no recent technical engagement from us, and where something I flagged previously has not changed. For each one, state what the data shows, what it does not tell us, and the single technical question I should ask next. Remember what you reported before, so you can tell me what is genuinely new and what is unchanged.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Scout and set the check running against your portfolio.
2. Give it the period and the movement threshold you actually care about, so it does not report everything.
3. Read the first run against what you already believed about these accounts.
4. Keep only the accounts where the movement is technically explainable and worth a conversation.
5. Prune it after two weeks. A check that reports everything gets ignored exactly like a dashboard nobody opens.
RequiredContext: Your portfolio of accounts. The consumption, usage and support sources you can reach. The risks already on your list.
ExpectedOutput: A weekly check running across the portfolio, separating new movement from unchanged risk, with a next technical question for each.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA confirms the technical reading of each signal and decides what is worth acting on. A standing check makes the finding cheaper, not the judgment - and the failure mode of automation here is a weekly report that everyone stops reading by week three.
BestFitJob: Set a standing check so the next one finds you
WhyThisMatters: Manual portfolio scans do not survive a busy quarter, which is exactly the quarter you need them. The value is that it keeps running when you have forgotten about it.

Name: Find the workload that is genuinely working
Description: Identify where a customer is succeeding with something, as the only reliable starting point for expansion.
Prompt: For the accounts in my portfolio, show for each the workloads deployed, what usage is recorded against each, when each was deployed, and any support or service record raised against them. Identify the accounts where recorded usage has been stable or growing over the period I specify: [state the period you want assessed]. Report what is recorded and do not infer readiness or recommend anything.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Look for stable and growing, not just large. A big workload that has flattened is not a readiness signal.
3. Decide for yourself how long usage has to hold before it evidences adoption rather than a pilot. That depends on the workload and the customer.
4. Pick the one account where the succeeding workload is closest to something the customer has said they care about.
RequiredContext: Your portfolio of accounts and whatever deployment and usage evidence you can reach.
ExpectedOutput: Accounts where a workload has demonstrably held or grown over two quarters, with the strongest candidate chosen.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what counts as genuinely succeeding. Recorded usage can reflect one team, one automated process, or a workload nobody has switched off, and expanding from a false positive costs the credibility you would need for the real conversation.
BestFitJob: Find the workload that is genuinely working
WhyThisMatters: Expansion built on a workload that is merely deployed fails in a predictable way. Expansion built on one the customer is visibly getting value from is a conversation they will start themselves.

Name: Test what usually comes next after this
Description: Check an expansion hypothesis against documented adoption patterns rather than against what we would like to sell.
Prompt: A customer is running [describe the workload] successfully and I am considering whether [describe the expansion you have in mind] is the next logical step. Using approved Microsoft and authoritative public sources, show what the documented technical prerequisites are for that expansion, what the common adoption sequence is from the first workload, and what the documented reasons are for that sequence failing. Cite each claim. Do not tell me whether this customer is ready.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the failure reasons before the prerequisites. They are more useful and less often looked at.
3. Check the prerequisites against what you actually know this customer has, not what a customer of this size usually has.
4. If the documented sequence puts something else before your expansion, take that seriously rather than skipping it.
RequiredContext: The workload the customer is succeeding with, and the expansion you are considering.
ExpectedOutput: The expansion's documented prerequisites and common failure reasons, checked against what this customer actually has.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides whether the documented sequence applies to this customer. Adoption patterns describe the average case and this segment is full of customers who are not average - the judgment is which prerequisite genuinely blocks and which is an assumption from a larger deployment.
BestFitJob: Test what usually comes next after this
WhyThisMatters: The expansion that follows a documented sequence is the one the customer can absorb. Skipping a step is how a technically valid expansion turns into a stalled deployment that damages the workload it grew from.

Name: Hand it over in a form somebody can sell
Description: Turn technical readiness evidence into something the person who owns the commercial conversation can actually use.
Prompt: I have technical evidence that a customer is ready for [describe the expansion]. Here is the evidence: [paste what you found - the succeeding workload, the usage pattern, the prerequisites met and any not yet met]. Draft a short handover for the person who owns the commercial conversation: what the customer is already succeeding with, what that makes possible, what is technically confirmed and what is not, and what would need to be true before it could start. Keep it factual. Do not write a pitch and do not include commercial or pricing framing.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Check that what is unconfirmed is as prominent as what is confirmed. A handover that reads as certainty will be sold as certainty.
3. Send it to whoever owns the commercial conversation and say explicitly that the technical readiness is your view and the timing is theirs.
4. Record it against the account so the next person does not rediscover it.
RequiredContext: Your evidenced expansion hypothesis. Who owns the commercial conversation on this account.
ExpectedOutput: A factual technical handover separating confirmed readiness from open questions, with the commercial owner named.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA states what is technically evidenced and stops there. Technical readiness and commercial timing are different judgments owned by different people, and a handover that strays into whether the customer will buy undermines the person who has to have that conversation.
BestFitJob: Hand it over in a form somebody can sell
WhyThisMatters: Uncovering the next workload is the DCSA's accountability; selling it is not. The handover is where that boundary is either respected or quietly crossed.

Name: Package it with what it assumes
Description: Turn something you built into a reusable asset, with the constraints that decide whether it fits.
Prompt: Here is something I built and want to make reusable: [paste or describe the artifact - a script, design, demo, response or checklist]. It was built for this situation: [describe the customer context, constraints and what it assumed]. Produce a reusable package covering what it does, what it requires before use, the steps to use it, what someone would need to change for their own situation, how to check it worked, where it does not apply, and who owns it. Flag anything customer-identifying that should be removed. Do not add capability it does not have.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Check the removal flags yourself. The agent will catch names and identifiers; it will not catch a configuration that only one customer would ever run.
3. Write the "where it does not apply" section properly. It is the part that stops the asset being misused and the part everyone skips.
4. Check the community hubs before publishing. If something close already exists, improve that instead of adding a second.
RequiredContext: The artifact you want to make reusable. The customer situation it was built for. Your team's rules on what may be shared internally.
ExpectedOutput: A reusable package with prerequisites, adaptation points, validation steps and stated limits, sanitized for internal sharing.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what is safe to hand to someone who will not know what it assumed. Automated flagging may surface names and identifiers but cannot be relied on to catch a configuration that only made sense for one customer, so the review is the seller's and it is not delegable.
BestFitJob: Package it with what it assumes
WhyThisMatters: An artifact without its constraints is not reusable, it is just findable. The next engineer either rebuilds it or applies it somewhere it was never validated.

Name: Write the note that makes it findable
Description: Produce the description another engineer would search for and could judge fit from without opening it.
Prompt: Here is a reusable asset I am publishing: [paste the package]. Write the entry another engineer would find when searching: a one-line description of what it does, the problem it solves stated in the words somebody would actually search for, the prerequisites, one example of when to use it and one of when not to, and the owner. Keep it short enough to read in fifteen seconds. Do not restate the asset itself.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Check the search words are the ones a colleague would type, not the ones you used when you built it.
3. Make sure the "when not to use it" example is specific. A vague limitation gets ignored.
4. Publish it where the team already looks, and tell one person who has the problem it solves.
RequiredContext: Your sanitized asset package. Where it will be stored and who maintains it.
ExpectedOutput: A short findable entry with the problem stated in searchable terms, a fit example, a non-fit example and a named owner.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether the description matches how colleagues actually search. The test is not whether it reads well but whether it uses the words someone would type while looking for something they cannot name precisely, and only somebody who has failed to find things in this repository knows what those are.
BestFitJob: Write the note that makes it findable
WhyThisMatters: An asset nobody can find fails for a reason that has nothing to do with its quality. Something described in the language of the person who built it is invisible to the person who needs it.

Name: Catch the question that has started arriving
Description: Set a standing check that surfaces technical questions which have begun recurring since you last looked, rather than re-listing what you already know.
Prompt: Check my messages and meetings from the last [state a period] for technical questions I have answered more than once. Group them by the underlying technical problem rather than by wording, and show how many different people or customers each came from. On each later run, report only groups that are new since your previous report, or where the number of distinct askers has grown. Do not draft answers and do not repeat groups you have already reported unless they have grown.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Scout, run the prompt, and set your own lookback period for the first run.
2. Treat the first run as a backlog. Everything it finds is historical and most of it you already half-knew.
3. From the second run onward, the value is only in what is new or growing. That is a signal that something has changed in the product, the market or your patch.
4. Pick candidates by breadth of asker rather than by count, and judge for yourself what breadth means for your patch.
5. When you publish an asset, check the next report to see whether the question stopped arriving.
RequiredContext: Your mail, chats and meetings. The assets your team has already published.
ExpectedOutput: Technical question groups that are new or growing since the previous run, with the breadth of askers for each.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether a newly recurring question reflects a genuine change or a coincidence of timing. A question that starts appearing may mean a product update, a competitor claim or a shift in what customers are attempting - and only someone who knows what changed recently can tell which, or whether it is simply two customers who happened to ask in the same two weeks.
BestFitJob: Notice what you are answering repeatedly
WhyThisMatters: A one-off scan finds the backlog once. What is worth knowing afterwards is which questions have STARTED arriving, because that is a change in the field you would otherwise notice months later.

Name: Find where the same partner keeps needing you
Description: Look across partner-led opportunities for the technical dependency that keeps coming back to you.
Prompt: For the opportunities in my area where a partner is associated and that have been open during [state the period], group them by partner and return only the partners with more than one. For those partners only, show for each opportunity the current stage, how long it has been at that stage, the recorded next step and its owner, and any recorded technical activity from me. Report what is recorded and do not infer why anything has stalled.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Look at the grouping by partner before the individual deals. One deal needing you is normal; one partner repeatedly needing you is the finding.
3. For each recurring partner, work out what specific technical step they hand back. The record will not say - you know it from the asks.
4. Separate what they cannot do from what they simply prefer you to do. Those need different responses.
RequiredContext: The partner-led opportunities you support, which partner is associated with each, and the period you want to look at.
ExpectedOutput: Partner-led opportunities grouped by partner, with the recurring technical dependency identified for each.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether a partner is genuinely lacking capability or has learned that asking is faster than doing. Both look identical in the record and in the request, and enablement fixes only the first - offering it for the second is politely ignored.
BestFitJob: Find where the same partner keeps needing you
WhyThisMatters: One deal at a time, absorbing the technical step looks like helpfulness. Across a partner's portfolio it is the reason their capability never grows and your time never comes back.

Name: Have the capability conversation without causing offense
Description: Prepare the conversation that names a partner's technical gap and offers to close it rather than cover it.
Prompt: I need to raise a technical capability gap with a partner. Here is the gap and what makes me think it exists: [describe the gap and the evidence]. Here is my relationship with them and who I would speak to: [describe the contact and the history]. Help me rehearse this: how to open it as an offer rather than a criticism, what they may say to deflect it, how to respond if they say they have it covered when the evidence says otherwise, and how to close with a specific action they own. Do not tell me whether the gap is real.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Rehearse the deflection you expect, not the version where they agree with you.
3. Decide beforehand what you will do if they decline. Continuing to absorb the work is a decision too, and it should be a deliberate one.
4. Close with an action the partner owns and a date. Enablement you own is not enablement.
RequiredContext: The capability gap you have identified and the evidence for it. Your relationship with the partner and who you would raise it with.
ExpectedOutput: A rehearsed capability conversation opened as an offer, with the likely deflections worked through and a partner-owned action prepared.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what evidence is sufficient to call something a capability gap rather than a preference. Repeated requests can mean the partner cannot do the work, or that they have learned we will, and naming the wrong one produces enablement that is politely attended and never applied.
BestFitJob: Have the capability conversation without causing offense
WhyThisMatters: This conversation is the whole workflow. Everything before it is preparation, and the alternative to having it is doing the partner's technical work indefinitely.

Name: Leave them something that works when you are not there
Description: Turn a resolved technical gap into material the partner can use themselves next time.
Prompt: A partner had this technical gap and here is how it was resolved this time: [describe the gap and what was done]. Here is what the partner's team already knows and works with: [describe their technical background and tooling]. Draft something they could use to do this themselves next time: the steps, the decisions they will face and what to consider for each, how to check it worked, and when to come to us anyway. Write it for their engineers, not for ours. Do not include internal-only detail, customer-identifying information, or anything that reads as an export from our systems.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Check it against your data-sharing rules before it leaves Microsoft. This is going to another company.
3. Be specific about when they should still come to us. Material that implies they never need us again is inaccurate and will be trusted anyway.
4. Send it to the person who owns the action, not to the account contact, and ask them to try it on the next one.
RequiredContext: The capability gap and how it was resolved. What the partner already knows and what they use.
ExpectedOutput: Partner-usable technical material with the decision points explained and the escalation boundary stated, checked before it leaves Microsoft.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what is genuinely safe to hand to another company and where the boundary of self-service sits. Material that is too complete invites a partner to attempt something they should escalate, and the failure lands on a customer who never knew the difference.
BestFitJob: Leave them something that works when you are not there
WhyThisMatters: A gap closed in one conversation reopens on the next deal. Something the partner keeps is the only version of this that reduces your load permanently.

Name: Find out what the competitor actually does well
Description: Build an evidenced view of a competitor's real strengths in your solution area, from sources rather than from internal belief.
Prompt: A customer is comparing our [describe the solution area] against [name the competitor]. Using authoritative public sources and approved Microsoft material, set out what that competitor's offering does well in this area, what its documented limitations are, and where independent sources disagree with either vendor's marketing. Cite each claim and state where evidence is thin. Do not tell me how to position against them and do not characterize the competitor as weak.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the competitor strengths first. That is the part internal material will not give you honestly.
3. Check the citations. A claim about a competitor that turns out to be out of date loses a technical audience.
4. Mark anything you would be uncomfortable saying if the competitor were in the room. That is the material to drop.
RequiredContext: The competitor and the solution area. The customer's stated decision criteria if you have them.
ExpectedOutput: An evidenced view of the competitor's genuine strengths and documented limitations, with sources cited and thin areas flagged.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what is safe to assert. A competitive claim that a customer can disprove in one search costs the whole position, not just that point, and internal competitive material is written to persuade rather than to survive being checked.
BestFitJob: Find out what the competitor actually does well
WhyThisMatters: You will be positioned against a competitor the customer has already researched. Arriving with a view that is less accurate than theirs ends the technical credibility you need for everything else.

Name: Check what this competitor has actually cost you
Description: Look across your solution area for what happened in past opportunities where this competitor was involved.
Prompt: Across the opportunities in my solution area, show any where [name the competitor] is recorded as involved: the account, the stage reached, whether it closed and how, and any recorded objection, blocker or competitor note. Group them by outcome. Report what is recorded and do not infer why any of them went the way they did.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Home and paste the prompt with your competitor.
2. Look at the losses before the wins. The recorded objection on a loss is the most useful sentence in the system.
3. Where the record says nothing, treat that as unknown rather than as no objection.
4. Pick the objection that appears most often across different accounts. That is the one worth preparing properly.
RequiredContext: The competitor. Your solution-area opportunities.
ExpectedOutput: Past opportunities involving this competitor grouped by outcome, with the recurring objection identified.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides which recorded objection reflects a real competitive pattern. Notes are written by whoever was losing at the time and often record the last thing said rather than the actual reason, so the same words can mean several different problems.
BestFitJob: Check what this competitor has actually cost you
WhyThisMatters: The objection you will meet has almost certainly been met before somewhere in your solution area. It is written down badly, but it is written down.

Name: Write the position against their criteria, not ours
Description: Turn competitive evidence into a position expressed in the customer's decision criteria.
Prompt: Here is what I know about how we compare to a competitor in my solution area: [paste your evidence and the recurring objection]. Here are the customer's decision criteria as they have expressed them: [paste or describe the criteria]. Map each criterion to what we can evidence, what the competitor can evidence, and where neither of us has evidence. Identify the criteria where the comparison genuinely favors us and those where it does not. Do not write positioning language and do not resolve the criteria where we are behind.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Look at the criteria where we are behind. Deciding what to do about those is the actual work.
3. Concede the ones you cannot win rather than arguing them. A concession buys credibility for the criteria that matter.
4. Build the conversation around the two or three criteria where the advantage is both real and valued.
RequiredContext: Your competitive evidence and the recurring objection. The customer's decision criteria in their own words.
ExpectedOutput: Decision criteria mapped to what each side can evidence, with the winnable criteria separated from the ones to concede.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides which criteria to concede. Contesting everything reads as a vendor who has not listened, and choosing what to give up is a judgment about this customer's priorities that no comparison table contains.
BestFitJob: Write the position against their criteria, not ours
WhyThisMatters: Customers decide on their criteria, not on ours. A position organized around our strengths answers a question they were not asking.

Name: Work out what the opportunity is actually missing
Description: Establish what support an opportunity needs by looking at what is recorded rather than at what feels stuck.
Prompt: For [opportunity name or ID] in my solution area, show what is recorded: the current stage and when it last changed, the recorded next step and its owner, any recorded blocker or objection, whether a partner is associated, and what technical or specialist activity is recorded against it. Report what is recorded and do not infer what support is needed.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your opportunity.
2. Compare the recorded next step against what you believe the next step is. Where they differ, someone else is working from the record.
3. Decide what is genuinely missing: a person, a decision, or evidence. They are asked for in different ways.
4. Write the need down as a task somebody could do, not as a description of the situation.
RequiredContext: One opportunity in your solution area that is not moving as it should.
ExpectedOutput: The opportunity's recorded position with the missing support identified as a person, a decision or a piece of evidence.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what would actually unblock this rather than what would be useful to have. In a segment with no assigned v-team every ask spends credit with someone who has their own targets, and asking for the wrong thing costs the same as asking for the right one.
BestFitJob: Work out what the opportunity is actually missing
WhyThisMatters: Most support asks describe a situation and hope the reader works out the task. Naming the missing thing precisely is what separates an ask that gets actioned from one that gets acknowledged.

Name: Write the ask so it can be said yes to
Description: Turn a support need into a request with a task, a date and a consequence.
Prompt: I need support on an opportunity and here is what is missing: [describe what you need and the opportunity context]. I am asking [describe who you are asking and what they are accountable for]. I need it by [state your date] because [state what happens to the opportunity if it does not arrive]. Draft the request using those: what specifically I am asking them to do, by my stated date, what I have already done so they are not repeating it, and my stated consequence. Keep it to a few lines. Do not set a date I have not given you, do not invent a consequence, and do not pad it with background.
ActivitySteps:
1. Decide your date and your consequence first. Both are yours and neither can be worked out from the opportunity record.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace all four bracketed sections.
3. Check that the task is something a person could start without asking you a question first.
4. Send it to a named person. A request to a team is a request to nobody.
RequiredContext: The support you need and the opportunity it is for. Who you are asking and what they are accountable for. The date you need it by, and what happens to the opportunity if it does not arrive by then.
ExpectedOutput: A short request with a specific task, a date, what has already been done, and the consequence of it not arriving.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides how much of the consequence to state. Overstating it is noticed and quietly discounted from then on; omitting it leaves the reader to guess the priority, and they will guess low because everything else they have been sent also looked urgent.
BestFitJob: Write the ask so it can be said yes to
WhyThisMatters: The people you need are not assigned to you and are choosing between several asks. Yours is competing on how easy it is to act on.

Name: Notice when an ask has gone quiet
Description: Set a standing check that tells you which of your requests never got answered.
Prompt: Set up a recurring weekly check across my sent messages for requests I have made that have not received a reply. For each, show who it went to, when it was sent, what was being asked, and whether any date I set has now passed. Group them by how overdue they are. Remember what you reported before so you can tell me which are newly overdue and which I have already been told about. Do not draft follow-ups.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Scout and run the prompt.
2. Read the newly-overdue group first. The long-overdue ones need a different approach rather than another chase.
3. For anything twice reported and still unanswered, go to the person a different way rather than resending.
4. Prune what you are tracking every few weeks. A list that includes everything you ever sent stops being useful immediately.
RequiredContext: The support asks you have outstanding and who each went to.
ExpectedOutput: Outstanding requests grouped by how overdue they are, separating newly overdue from previously reported.
