HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides which silence needs chasing and which means the answer is no. Some unanswered asks are a queue and some are a declined request nobody wanted to say out loud, and chasing the second repeatedly costs the relationship you will need for the next one.
BestFitJob: Notice when an ask has gone quiet
WhyThisMatters: Support asks fail silently. Nobody tells you they are not doing it, and by the time you notice, the opportunity has moved past the point where it would have helped.

Name: Look at what the partner has actually delivered
Description: Establish a partner's delivery record from what is recorded, before deciding what to route to them.
Prompt: For [partner name], show what is recorded: the opportunities where they are associated and the stage each reached, any co-sell or referral record and its status, what closed and over what period, and the workloads or solution areas involved. Group by outcome and by solution area. Report what is recorded and do not assess their capability.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your partner.
2. Look at what they have delivered in the specific solution area you are considering, not their overall record.
3. Note where the record thins out. A partner with three closed deals and nothing recorded since is a different proposition from one with steady flow.
4. Treat this as the capability half only. Nothing here tells you whether they have anyone available.
RequiredContext: The partner you are assessing. The work you are considering routing to them.
ExpectedOutput: The partner's recorded delivery grouped by outcome and solution area, with the gaps in the record noted.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides what the delivery record actually evidences. A partner who closed several deals two years ago with a team that has since left looks identical in the record to one delivering now, and the record has no way of showing you the difference.
BestFitJob: Look at what the partner has actually delivered
WhyThisMatters: Capability is the half of partner readiness we have evidence for. Getting it from the record rather than from the relationship is what makes the routing decision defensible when it is questioned.

Name: Ask about capacity without implying doubt
Description: Prepare the conversation that establishes whether a partner actually has people available, which no system will tell you.
Prompt: I need to find out whether a partner genuinely has capacity to take on [describe the work], and our systems cannot tell me. Here is what I know about their delivery record: [paste your findings]. Help me prepare that conversation: how to ask about available people without implying I doubt them, what answers would tell me they are overcommitted, how to respond if they say yes when the evidence suggests otherwise, and how to leave the door open if the answer is no. Do not tell me whether to route the work.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Rehearse the case where they say yes and you do not believe them. That is the hard one and it is common.
3. Ask about named people and current commitments rather than about capacity in general. General questions get general reassurance.
4. Decide in advance what you will do with a no. A partner who can say no safely will tell you the truth next time.
RequiredContext: The partner and what you are considering routing to them. Your delivery-record findings.
ExpectedOutput: A prepared capacity conversation with the tell-tale answers identified and a safe route to no.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides whether a named-people answer is specific enough to route work on. A partner naming individuals and dates has given you something checkable; a partner describing capability in general has not, and accepting the second because the first felt intrusive is how work gets routed to a firm rather than to a team.
BestFitJob: Ask about capacity without implying doubt
WhyThisMatters: Nothing in our systems shows partner capacity. It only comes from a conversation, and how you ask determines whether the answer is real.

Name: Watch for the partner who has stopped moving
Description: Set a standing check across your partners for the delivery signals that appear before a partner-led engagement stalls.
Prompt: Set up a recurring check across the partners I work with. Each time, show me for each partner-associated opportunity and referral: its current status, the date that status was last recorded, and how long it has held. Show the same for any partner with no recorded activity in the period. Report the elapsed times and do not classify anything as stalled, at risk or normal. Remember what you reported before so you can tell me which elapsed times have grown since last time.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Scout and confirm which partner and opportunity sources it can reach.
2. Choose your own cadence. Partner rhythms differ and a frequency that suits one portfolio buries another.
3. Decide for yourself what counts as too long for each partner. A quiet period that is routine for one partner is a warning for another.
4. Remember our record shows nothing about partner-side activity. Silence here is a prompt to ask, not a finding.
5. Prune what you track once you can see which categories actually move.
RequiredContext: The partners you carry. The opportunities and referrals associated with each.
ExpectedOutput: Elapsed time against each partner-associated record, with the times that have grown since the previous run identified.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides what a gap in partner activity means. There is no general answer - partners work to their own cadence, and two weeks of quiet that is routine for one is a warning for another - so the elapsed time is a prompt to ask rather than a conclusion to act on.
BestFitJob: Watch for the partner who has stopped moving
WhyThisMatters: Elapsed time is a fact the record can supply. Whether a given elapsed time matters is a judgment about a specific partner relationship, and conflating the two produces either constant false alarms or a report nobody reads.

Name: Assemble what the partner already knows about themselves
Description: Build the performance picture the partner will recognize, before you ask them for anything.
Prompt: [Partner name]
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Know Your Partner and type the partner name or their PartnerOne ID.
2. Read the performance and program sections first. This is the version of the relationship they can also see.
3. Check the web-sourced context - recent news, acquisitions, expansion. That often explains a change in behavior better than any metric.
4. Note where it shows a placeholder rather than a figure. Missing data is not zero, and treating it as zero in front of a partner is expensive.
5. If you do not have access, assemble the same picture from partner performance reporting and continue with the rest of the workflow.
RequiredContext: The partner and the conversation you have coming up.
ExpectedOutput: A partner performance and context picture covering program participation, delivery and recent business developments.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides which of this the partner would recognize as their own view. Our reporting measures what matters to Microsoft, and opening a conversation with figures the partner does not use is how a business discussion turns into a data argument.
BestFitJob: Assemble what the partner already knows about themselves
WhyThisMatters: Partners experience the relationship through their own numbers. Arriving with only our version guarantees the first ten minutes are spent reconciling rather than deciding.

Name: Reframe the ask in what their business gains
Description: Turn a Microsoft priority into an ask expressed in the partner's own economics.
Prompt: I want a partner to [describe the one thing you want them to do]. Here is what I know about their business and performance: [paste your partner picture]. Here is what I know about how they make money, and what I do not know: [describe their model and state the gaps]. Set out the questions I would have to answer before I could claim this is good for their business: what it would cost them, what they would gain, and over what period. For each question, say whether what I have given you answers it. Do not estimate any figure I have not supplied, do not construct a return calculation, and do not use Microsoft targets or incentive language.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace all three bracketed sections, including what you do NOT know.
2. Look at which questions your material cannot answer. Those are what you ask the partner, not what you assert to them.
3. Do not fill a gap with an estimate. A partner will recognize a number you invented about their own business immediately.
4. Reduce it to one ask, framed by the questions you can actually answer.
RequiredContext: Your partner picture. The one thing you want the partner to do. Whatever you actually know about how they make money, including what you do not know.
ExpectedOutput: The economic questions the ask depends on, marked by whether your material answers them, with the unanswerable ones turned into questions for the partner.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides which economic claims can be made and which must be asked. A partner's cost base is not visible to us, and a return figure constructed from our side is both wrong and recognizably wrong to the person who runs the business - which costs the credibility the ask depends on.
BestFitJob: Reframe the ask in what their business gains
WhyThisMatters: Partners commit to things that improve their business. Claiming to know their economics when you do not is how you get treated as a vendor rather than a partner.

Name: Rehearse the part where they push back
Description: Prepare for the objection this partner will actually raise, rather than the conversation where they agree.
Prompt: I am asking a partner to [describe your reframed ask]. Here is our history: [describe what this partner has committed to before and what actually happened]. Help me rehearse the difficult part: what they are most likely to push back with, how to respond if they raise a past commitment we did not meet, what to do if they agree in the room but the history suggests they will not act, and how to close with something specific enough to follow up on. Do not tell me whether the ask is reasonable.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Rehearse the response to a past Microsoft failure honestly. Deflecting it is remembered longer than the original failure.
3. Prepare for agreement-without-action specifically - it is the most common outcome and the hardest to name politely.
4. Close on something checkable with a date, and put it in writing the same day.
RequiredContext: Your reframed ask and the partner picture. The history of what this partner has and has not done before.
ExpectedOutput: A rehearsed conversation covering the likely pushback, the history, and a close specific enough to follow up.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides which previous commitment is solid enough evidence to raise. A commitment that was implied, or made by someone who has since left, will be disputed and turns the conversation into a disagreement about history - so the judgment is whether this specific instance is documented well enough to survive being questioned.
BestFitJob: Rehearse the part where they push back
WhyThisMatters: The partner conversation that changes anything is the one where the difficult part was prepared. The rest is a status meeting with a friendlier name.

Name: Let the territory tell you when it moves
Description: Set a standing check across the territory so a change reaches you when it happens rather than at the next review.
Prompt: Set up a recurring weekly check across the accounts in my territory. Each week, show me where an opportunity has changed stage or close date, where a new signal or plan priority has arrived and how long it has before it expires, where a renewal date has moved inside twelve months, and where a partner referral has changed status. For each, state what changed and what the record does not tell us. Remember what you reported before so you can separate what is new from what I have already seen.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Scout and confirm which signal, opportunity and referral sources it can reach for your territory.
2. Run the prompt and set the cadence to land before your own pipeline review.
3. The first run reports everything. Read it once, then tune it to movement rather than inventory.
4. Act on expiring signals first - they are the only items on the list with a deadline you cannot negotiate.
RequiredContext: Your territory of accounts. The signal, opportunity and renewal sources you can reach.
ExpectedOutput: A weekly view of territory movement separating new changes from previously reported ones, with expiring items surfaced.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides which movement needs action this week. A territory of this size generates change constantly and most of it is noise, so the judgment is which change alters what you were going to do anyway.
BestFitJob: Let the territory tell you when it moves
WhyThisMatters: At this territory size nothing surfaces on its own. The choice is between a standing check and finding out at the review, and the review is always too late for the signals that expire.

Name: Keep watching the book between reviews
Description: Set a standing check across the agreement book so commercial exposure surfaces before it becomes a renewal problem.
Prompt: Set up a recurring check across the agreements in my book that runs every two weeks. Each time, show me where an agreement end date has moved, where a new exception or amendment has been recorded, and where a renewal date has come inside the window I specify. Report only what has changed since the previous run. Do not assess commercial risk and do not recommend action.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Scout and set the check running against your book of agreements.
2. Run the prompt and set it to repeat every two weeks. Commercial exposure moves more slowly than pipeline and a weekly check would mostly report nothing.
3. Read the first run in full, then read only the changes after that.
4. Decide which movements need a conversation and which are administrative.
RequiredContext: Your book of agreements. The consumption, amendment and renewal data you can reach.
ExpectedOutput: A change-only view, refreshed every two weeks, of agreement dates moving, new exceptions recorded, and renewals entering the window.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides which movement is commercially material. An exception recorded on one account is administration; the same exception appearing repeatedly is a policy signal, and only someone reading across the book over time can tell which one they are watching.
BestFitJob: Keep watching the book between reviews
WhyThisMatters: Commercial exposure in this segment accumulates quietly across many small agreements. Nobody discovers it in a single review, because no single account looks like a problem.

Name: Read what the guidance actually says
Description: Establish what published commercial and licensing guidance states on a question, before asking anyone to interpret it.
Prompt: I need to understand what published guidance says about [describe the policy, licensing or eligibility question]. Using approved Microsoft sources and authoritative public documentation, set out what the published position is, what conditions or exceptions the documentation names, what it explicitly does not cover, and where different sources say different things. Cite each source and give its date. Do not tell me whether it applies to my deal and do not resolve any conflict you find.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Check the dates before the content. Commercial guidance gets revised without being re-read.
3. Where sources conflict, that is your question for the authoritative owner - not something to resolve yourself.
4. Take the citations with you when you ask. A question that shows what you have already read gets a faster and better answer.
RequiredContext: The policy or licensing question your deal raises.
ExpectedOutput: The published position with its conditions, its explicit gaps, and any conflicts between sources, each cited and dated.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides which fact about this deal takes it outside the published general case. Guidance is written for the standard shape and commercial eligibility turns on the specifics that differ, so the judgment is which of your deal's particulars actually changes the answer - that is what determines whether you need a ruling or already have one.
BestFitJob: Read what the guidance actually says
WhyThisMatters: Arriving at the policy owner having read nothing wastes their time and yours. Arriving having read it and knowing exactly where it stops being clear is the difference between one exchange and four.

Name: Establish what the deal actually looks like
Description: Assemble the recorded facts that determine which investment routes are even open to this opportunity.
Prompt: For [opportunity name or ID] in my solution area, show what is recorded: the account, the products and workloads involved, the deal value and stage, any existing agreement and its type, whether a partner is associated and any co-sell or referral record, and any consumption or usage recorded on the account. Report what is recorded. Do not determine eligibility for any investment program and do not recommend a route.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your opportunity.
2. Note the partner association first. It changes which routes are even in scope.
3. Write down the barrier the investment would remove, in one sentence. If you cannot, investment is not the answer yet.
4. Take the facts and the barrier to the next step rather than deciding eligibility here.
RequiredContext: One solution-area opportunity where customer investment might remove a barrier.
ExpectedOutput: The recorded facts that bear on route selection, with the barrier the investment would remove stated in one sentence.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether there is a real barrier that money removes. Investment attached to a deal that is simply slow does not speed it up, and a request built on a barrier nobody can name is declined late, after the effort has been spent.
BestFitJob: Establish what the deal actually looks like
WhyThisMatters: Route selection depends on facts about the deal that are already recorded. Starting from the program rather than the deal is how sellers end up building a case for a vehicle the opportunity never fitted.

Name: Find out what the routes actually require
Description: Establish from published guidance what each candidate investment route requires, before choosing between them.
Prompt: I am considering customer investment for an opportunity with these characteristics: [paste the deal facts and the barrier]. Using approved Microsoft sources and authoritative internal documentation, set out what the published requirements are for each investment route that could apply, what evidence each requires, what each explicitly excludes, and where the documentation is silent. Cite each source and give its date. Do not tell me which route to use and do not assess whether my opportunity qualifies.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Read the exclusions before the requirements. That is where most requests fail and it is the part least often read.
3. Check the dates. Investment guidance changes between fiscal years and last year's version is still findable.
4. Where the documentation is silent, that is a question for the authoritative owner, not a gap for you to fill.
RequiredContext: Your deal facts and the barrier you named. The routes you are considering.
ExpectedOutput: Each candidate route's published requirements, evidence and exclusions, cited and dated, with the silent areas identified.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS confirms every eligibility reading with the authoritative owner rather than acting on the documentation alone. Published requirements describe the general case and investment decisions turn on specifics the documentation cannot see, so this shortens that conversation instead of replacing it.
BestFitJob: Find out what the routes actually require
WhyThisMatters: Sellers learn one route and apply it everywhere - the one that worked first. Reading what the alternatives actually require is the only way that habit gets corrected.

Name: Write the case against the route you chose
Description: Turn the barrier and the route requirements into a request that answers what that route actually asks.
Prompt: I am requesting customer investment through [name the route] for an opportunity. Here are the route's published requirements: [paste them]. Here is the barrier and the deal context: [paste them]. Draft the request so that it answers each requirement in turn: what is being asked for, the barrier it removes, the evidence for that barrier, what changes if it is approved, and how that change would be observed. Mark any requirement I have not evidenced. Do not assert eligibility, do not estimate any figure I have not supplied, and do not claim approval is likely.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace all three bracketed sections.
2. Look at what it marks as unevidenced. Those are the questions a reviewer will ask first.
3. Make the observable change specific. "Accelerates adoption" is not something anyone can check afterwards.
4. Send it through the route's own process rather than to whoever answered last time.
RequiredContext: Your chosen route and its published requirements. The barrier and the deal facts.
ExpectedOutput: A request answering each published requirement in turn, with unevidenced requirements marked and the observable change stated specifically.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS states what will be observably different if the investment is approved. A request that promises acceleration without naming what would be measured is approved on trust and cannot be defended at review, which is what makes the next request from your team harder.
BestFitJob: Write the case against the route you chose
WhyThisMatters: Investment requests are compared against each other, not judged in isolation. The one that answers the stated requirements in order is easier to approve than a better opportunity described loosely.

Name: Check what this partner has already signed up to
Description: Establish what program commitments a partner already carries before adding another one.
Prompt: For [partner name], show any co-sell or referral record currently open and the status and date of each, and any record showing a program or campaign this partner has been nominated into. For each, show whether it progressed after it was opened and the date of the last change. Report what is recorded. Do not assess their program eligibility and do not recommend an investment route.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your partner.
2. Look for records opened and never progressed. A partner carrying several of those has an acceptance habit rather than a delivery habit.
3. Check program participation in the partner reporting you have access to - our opportunity record shows nominations, not completions.
4. Decide whether this partner has room for another commitment before you offer one.
RequiredContext: The partner and the opportunity you are considering investment for. Whatever partner program reporting you can reach.
ExpectedOutput: The partner's open commitments with the ones that never progressed identified, and a view on whether they have room for another.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides whether this partner can absorb another commitment. Partners accept nominations readily and complete far fewer, so adding one to a partner already carrying unfinished commitments produces another unfinished commitment and makes the next conversation harder to have.
BestFitJob: See what this partner has already been nominated for
WhyThisMatters: A partner-led route only works if the partner does their part. What they have already agreed to and not delivered is the most direct evidence available, and it sits in a record nobody checks before nominating.

Name: Find out what the route asks of the partner
Description: Establish from published guidance what a partner-led route requires the partner to do, not just what it offers.
Prompt: I am considering [name the partner-led investment route] for a partner opportunity. Using approved Microsoft sources and authoritative internal documentation, set out what the route requires from the PARTNER specifically: what they must nominate, what activity they must complete, what evidence they must produce, over what period, and what they receive in return. Also show what it requires from Microsoft. Cite each source and give its date. Do not assess whether this partner qualifies.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Separate what the partner must do from what we must do, and list each partner obligation on its own line.
3. Note the period. A program requiring activity over two quarters is a different ask from one requiring a single nomination.
4. Take the partner-side obligations into the conversation with them rather than nominating first and explaining later.
RequiredContext: The route you are considering and the partner it would run through.
ExpectedOutput: The route's partner-side obligations, Microsoft-side obligations, timeframe and partner return, cited and dated.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS confirms the partner-side obligations with the authoritative owner before committing a partner to them. Program terms change between fiscal years and a partner told the wrong requirements will discover the real ones at the point they are being assessed, which costs the relationship rather than the program.
BestFitJob: Find out what the route asks of the partner
WhyThisMatters: Partner-led investment fails when the partner did not know what they had agreed to. The obligations are published, and nothing in the nomination flow requires anyone to read them.

Name: Get the partner to agree to their half
Description: Prepare the conversation where the partner commits to what the route requires of them, rather than simply accepting a nomination.
Prompt: I want a partner to take part in an investment route that requires this of them: [paste the partner-side obligations]. Here is their record of completing what they have started before: [describe it]. Help me prepare the conversation: how to present the obligations without making it sound like paperwork, what they are likely to agree to in the room and not do, how to raise a previous unfinished commitment without it becoming an argument, and how to close on something specific enough to check. Do not tell me whether to nominate them.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Rehearse raising the unfinished commitment. Avoiding it guarantees the same outcome.
3. Get agreement on a named person on their side, not on the firm. A firm cannot complete an activity.
4. Confirm in writing the same day, with what they agreed and by when.
RequiredContext: The route's partner-side obligations. The partner's record of completing what they start.
ExpectedOutput: A prepared conversation covering the partner's obligations, the previous record, and a close naming a person and a date.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS decides how directly to raise a partner's record of not finishing. Naming it risks the relationship; not naming it means nominating into the same outcome again, and only the person in the relationship can judge which this partner will take better.
BestFitJob: Get the partner to agree to their half
WhyThisMatters: A nomination is not a commitment. The conversation where the partner agrees to their specific half is the whole difference between a program that runs and one that appears in a report as unstarted.

Name: Tell a funding barrier from a decision barrier
Description: Assemble the recorded facts your role needs before contributing to an investment decision.
Prompt: For [account name], show what is recorded that would bear on whether investment could help: the open opportunities and their stage, any recorded blocker or objection, the existing agreement and its type, what is deployed against it, whether a partner is associated, and any recorded activity in the last six months. Report what is recorded and do not assess whether investment is appropriate.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account or opportunity.
2. Separate what the record shows from what you have been told. Where those two disagree is the barrier worth naming.
3. Form your own view before reading anyone else's assessment.
4. Route what you find to whoever owns the request rather than acting on it yourself.
RequiredContext: One account where something is blocked and money might move it.
ExpectedOutput: The account's recorded position with the barrier stated, and your own read on whether it is one funding removes.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides whether the barrier is one money removes. A customer who has not decided is not blocked by cost, and investment offered into indecision reads as discounting and is remembered as a price signal on the next deal.
BestFitJob: Tell a funding barrier from a decision barrier
WhyThisMatters: Investment is a lever for a specific class of barrier. Offering it against the wrong one trains the customer to wait for it.

Name: Route it to whoever owns the request
Description: Hand a recognized investment opportunity to its owner with enough evidence to be acted on.
Prompt: I have found an account where customer investment might remove a barrier. Here is what I found and the evidence: [paste your findings]. Draft a short note for whoever owns the investment request: the account, the barrier and what evidences it, what I have already confirmed, what I have not, and why I think investment is the lever rather than something else. Keep it brief. Do not assess eligibility and do not recommend an amount.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Check that what you could not determine is as visible as what you found. Silence on a gap reads as a clear result.
3. Say what your role would still have to do. Requests are approved without that and then stall on it.
4. Send it to the named owner, not to a distribution list.
RequiredContext: Your assessment and the evidence behind it. Who owns the investment request.
ExpectedOutput: A short handover naming the account, the barrier and its evidence, with what you confirmed separated from what you did not.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE hands over the barrier evidence and does not propose a figure. An amount suggested by the person who found the opportunity anchors the request before anyone has assessed eligibility, and a number that turns out to be wrong is remembered as the account team over-promising.
BestFitJob: Route it to whoever owns the request
WhyThisMatters: You see these barriers across more accounts than anyone. The value is only realized if the person who owns the request can act without a second conversation.

Name: Decide what would count as proof
Description: Assemble the recorded facts your role needs before contributing to an investment decision.
Prompt: A customer investment would fund this technical work: [describe the work and what the customer doubts]. Define what it would need to demonstrate for the customer's doubt to be resolved: the observable success criteria, what would constitute a clear negative result, the exit criteria that end the work either way, and the evidence a reviewer would need afterwards. Do not assume the investment is approved and do not estimate cost or duration.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account or opportunity.
2. Separate the recorded technical position from what you were briefed. The gap is where the success criteria will have to do their work.
3. Form your own view before reading anyone else's assessment.
4. Route what you find to whoever owns the request rather than acting on it yourself.
RequiredContext: One proposed piece of technical work that customer investment might fund.
ExpectedOutput: What the funded work would have to demonstrate, expressed as things somebody could observe happening.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE decides how much the funded work must prove before the customer would act on the result. Proving too little leaves the doubt intact and the funding spent; proving too much turns a bounded piece of work into a project, and where that line sits depends on what this specific customer said they doubted.
BestFitJob: Decide what would count as proof
WhyThisMatters: Funded technical work is assessed at closure against whatever criteria existed at the start. If none did, the assessment becomes a matter of opinion and the next request is harder.

Name: Write the criteria down before the work is funded
Description: Record the technical success and exit criteria in a form a reviewer can assess against afterwards.
Prompt: I have defined what an investment-funded piece of technical work must demonstrate. Here are my criteria: [paste them]. Write them up for the investment request: what will be demonstrated, how each will be observed, what would constitute a clear negative result, and the point at which the work stops either way. Mark anything I have written that could not actually be observed. Do not add criteria I have not stated and do not estimate effort or duration.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Check that what you could not determine is as visible as what you found. Silence on a gap reads as a clear result.
3. Say what your role would still have to do. Requests are approved without that and then stall on it.
4. Send it to the named owner, not to a distribution list.
RequiredContext: Your assessment and the evidence behind it. Who owns the investment request.
ExpectedOutput: Success and exit criteria written for the request, with anything unobservable marked before it is submitted.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSE owns which criteria survive into the request. Criteria are negotiated down when the request is assembled, and the ones removed are the ones that would have shown a negative result - which is exactly what makes the remaining set unfalsifiable.
BestFitJob: Write the criteria down before the work is funded
WhyThisMatters: Criteria that live only in your head are renegotiated at closure by people who were not there. Written into the request, they set the terms of the assessment before anyone has a stake in the answer.

Name: Check the environment, not the opportunity
Description: Assemble the recorded facts your role needs before contributing to an investment decision.
Prompt: An investment-funded engagement is proposed for [account name]: [describe the work]. Show me what is recorded about the account that bears on whether it could absorb this: the workloads deployed and what usage is recorded against them, any open or recently resolved support issues, whether a partner is associated, and the recorded technical activity in the last six months. Report what is recorded and do not assess readiness.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account or opportunity.
2. Separate what the record shows from what you have been told. On a non-unified account the record is thinner, so the difference matters more.
3. Form your own view before reading anyone else's assessment.
4. Route what you find to whoever owns the request rather than acting on it yourself.
RequiredContext: One proposed investment-funded engagement and the account it would run on.
ExpectedOutput: The account's recorded technical position, with your read on whether this customer could absorb the funded work.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides which customer-side dependency would genuinely block delivery. Every engagement depends on something the customer must provide, and the judgment is which of those this particular customer will actually struggle with - the record shows what they have, not what they can take on.
BestFitJob: Check the environment, not the opportunity
WhyThisMatters: Investment converts into consumption only if the customer can absorb the work. In a portfolio of non-unified customers that is the assumption the request does not test.

Name: Name the dependency that would stop it
Description: Set out the customer-side dependencies that would block funded delivery, and who would have to resolve each.
Prompt: I have assessed whether a customer could absorb investment-funded technical work. Here is what I found: [paste your findings]. Set out the customer-side dependencies that would have to be in place before the work could start or complete: what each is, who on the customer or partner side would have to provide it, and what happens to the engagement if it is not there. Separate the ones I have confirmed from the ones I am assuming. Do not assess whether the investment should proceed.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Check that what you could not determine is as visible as what you found. Silence on a gap reads as a clear result.
3. Say what your role would still have to do. Requests are approved without that and then stall on it.
4. Send it to the named owner, not to a distribution list.
RequiredContext: Your assessment and the evidence behind it. Who owns the investment request.
ExpectedOutput: The customer-side dependencies that would block delivery, separated into those confirmed and those assumed.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA distinguishes a dependency the customer has been told about from one they have agreed to. Those look identical in any write-up and behave completely differently at delivery, and only the person who had the conversation knows which one it was.
BestFitJob: Name the dependency that would stop it
WhyThisMatters: Funded work can stall on a customer-side dependency that no technical review would surface, and the stall is recorded as a Microsoft delivery failure regardless of whose dependency it was. Testing for them is separate work from testing the technical plan.

Name: Test whether the structure survives without the investment
Description: Check whether a commercial structure you are building depends on funding that has not been approved.
Prompt: For [account name], I am structuring a deal where customer investment is expected to form part of it. Show what is recorded: the existing agreement and its type, the products and quantities involved, any amendment or exception already recorded, the deal stage and value, and whether a partner is associated. Report what is recorded. Do not assess the investment, do not determine eligibility, and do not comment on approval.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account.
2. Describe the structure twice: once assuming the investment arrives and once assuming it does not.
3. If the second version does not work, the structure depends on a decision you do not own. Say so now rather than at approval.
4. Route any eligibility or investment question to the role that owns it rather than answering it.
RequiredContext: One deal you are structuring where customer investment is expected to be part of it.
ExpectedOutput: The structure described with and without the investment, and any dependency on an unapproved decision made explicit.
HumanCheckpoint: The CE decides whether a structure that depends on unapproved investment should be presented at all. A structure contingent on someone else's decision looks complete to a customer and to an approver, and the dependency only surfaces when the investment is declined and the commitment has already been made.
BestFitJob: Test whether the structure survives without the investment
WhyThisMatters: Investment decisions sit outside the CE's authority in this segment, but the commercial consequence of one not arriving lands entirely on the structure. That exposure is worth seeing before the customer does.

Name: Rehearse the objection you know you will get
Description: Prepare to meet the recurring competitive objection in the room, rather than only knowing what it is.
Prompt: I am going into a technical conversation where a competitor is in play. Here is the objection that comes up repeatedly: [paste the recurring objection you identified]. Here is what we can evidence and what I have decided to concede: [paste the criteria mapping]. Help me rehearse meeting it: how to acknowledge the part that is true without conceding the decision, what they are likely to say next, and how to respond if they press on something I have already decided to concede. Do not write competitive claims for me and do not tell me the competitor is wrong.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Agent J.ai and paste the prompt with the objection and your criteria mapping.
2. Practice the acknowledgment first. Decide how much of the objection you are willing to grant out loud.
3. Work the follow-up, not the opening. The opening is the part you have already thought about.
4. Say out loud the thing you decided to concede. If it sounds like a loss rather than a choice, it is not ready.
5. Take one sentence into the meeting, not a script.
RequiredContext: The recurring objection from your competitive review, and the criteria you decided to contest and concede.
ExpectedOutput: A rehearsed response to the recurring objection, with the acknowledgment and the concession both prepared as deliberate choices.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether the rehearsed response is accurate and which part of it to withhold. Rehearsal smooths an answer, and a smoothed answer can acquire confidence the underlying evidence does not support, so what gets said is a separate decision from what was practiced.
BestFitJob: Prepare to meet the objection you already know is coming
WhyThisMatters: Knowing the objection and being ready to meet it are different states. Rehearsal is where you find out which one you are in.

Name: Decide whether this partner is ready, and who closes the gap
Description: Put capability and capacity together into a readiness decision with a named owner and a date.
Prompt: Here is what the record shows about a partner's delivery capability: [paste your findings]. Here is what they told me about capacity: [paste what they said, including anything vague]. Bring these together into a readiness view for [describe the work]. Separate what they have demonstrated from what they have asserted. Set out the candidate gaps with the evidence for each, the possible impact of each on this work, and what is not known. Do not rank the gaps for me, do not decide whether to proceed, and do not assume any gap can be closed.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork and paste both halves - what the record showed and what the partner said.
2. Look first at anything demonstrated on one side and only asserted on the other. Demonstrated and asserted are different kinds of evidence and the difference is the point of this step.
3. Name one gap, not several. A readiness view with four gaps is a list, and lists do not get owned.
4. Decide who closes it and by when. If the honest answer is that you would close it yourself, that is a finding about this partnership rather than a plan.
5. Write down what happens to the work if the gap is not closed. That is the part that makes the date real.
RequiredContext: Your findings on the partner's delivery record, and what they said about capacity.
ExpectedOutput: A readiness view with demonstrated capability separated from asserted capacity, the candidate gaps evidenced, and the seller's chosen gap with a closing action, an owner and a date.
HumanCheckpoint: The PSS chooses which gap matters and names who closes it by when. The evidence supports several readings and selecting among them is the decision; an unowned gap has no date, and a readiness view without a date has not decided anything.
BestFitJob: Turn the two halves of partner readiness into one decision
WhyThisMatters: Capability and capacity are each half an answer. The decision that routes work needs both, joined, with somebody's name on what is missing.

Name: Check whether the technical explanation actually holds
Description: Test the most likely technical cause against documented behavior before raising it with anyone.
Prompt: I have a hypothesis about why a customer's workload is behaving the way it is. Here is what I observed and what I think is causing it: [describe the movement and your suspected technical cause]. Here is the configuration as far as I know it: [describe the workload and any relevant settings]. Using approved Microsoft and authoritative internal documentation, tell me whether this cause is consistent with documented behavior for this configuration. Give me at most three documented alternatives that would produce the same symptom on this configuration, and for each, what I would need to observe to tell them apart. Cite each claim. Where the documentation does not settle it, say so rather than choosing.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Researcher and paste the prompt with your observation and your suspected cause.
2. Read the alternative explanations before the confirming ones. You already believe your own.
3. Check the citations reach current documentation. A behavior that changed in a recent release is the case this step is for.
4. Note what you would need to observe to separate the explanations. That is your question for the customer's team.
5. Decide whether your hypothesis survived. If it did not, say so now rather than carrying it into the conversation.
RequiredContext: The account you ranked highest, what you observed, and your suspected technical cause.
ExpectedOutput: The hypothesis either retained or rejected, with up to three documented alternatives and the observation that would separate them, each claim sourced.
HumanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides whether the hypothesis survives contact with the documentation, and which observation would settle it. Documentation describes the general case and this customer is a specific one, so consistency raises confidence without confirming, and carrying an unrejected hypothesis forward as a finding is how a technical conversation goes wrong before it starts.
BestFitJob: Test the technical hypothesis before you take it to a customer
WhyThisMatters: A ranked list tells you which account to look at, not what is wrong with it. Testing the explanation is what turns a suspicion into something worth a customer's time.

Name: Check the renewals that arrived without you
Description: Work through renewal opportunities created automatically and decide which of them describe a renewal you would stand behind.
Prompt: Show me the renewal opportunities in my book that were created automatically rather than by me, using their creation date between [start date] and [end date]. For each, show the account, the recorded value and currency, the close date, the enrollment or agreement record it was built from, the product or SKU lines attached, and the forecast category currently set. Report what is recorded. Do not assess whether any value, date or line is correct.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your start and end dates.
2. For each opportunity, validate four things yourself against the agreement and the customer: the account it landed on, the value and currency, the close date, and the product or SKU lines attached.
3. Correct what is wrong and add what is missing - contacts, and any required field - before the opportunity progresses to the next stage.
4. Where the renewal should not exist at all, say so and route it rather than editing it into something plausible.
5. Set the forecast category yourself. The record existing is not the same as you committing to it.
6. Pick the one where what arrived differs most from what you would have entered, and work out why. That gap is the thing worth discussing.
RequiredContext: Your renewal book for the period, including opportunities you did not create. The underlying agreement or enrollment record for anything you intend to correct.
ExpectedOutput: Auto-created renewals reviewed with account, value, close date and product lines each confirmed or corrected, forecast category set by the CE, anything that should not exist routed rather than edited, and one flagged difference between what arrived and what was expected.
HumanCheckpoint: For each auto-created renewal the CE decides one of three things: accept it as it stands, correct it against the agreement, or reject it as a renewal that should not be in the book. The CE also decides whether and when to set a forecast category, which is the point at which the record becomes a commitment rather than a suggestion.
BestFitJob: Own the renewals that arrived in pipeline without you
WhyThisMatters: A renewal that appears in pipeline without anyone deciding it belongs there is a forecast entry nobody has stood behind. The work is no longer creating the record, it is deciding whether to own it.

Name: Find the closes you cannot account for
Description: List recent closed-won opportunities in your book and separate the ones you closed from the ones that closed some other way.
Prompt: Show me the opportunities in my book that were marked closed won with a close date in the last [state a short period, for example 30 days]. For each, show the account, the value, the close date, the products or SKU lines attached, and the recorded close reason or status if one is set. Report what is recorded. Do not assess whether any close was correct.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with a short recent period. Keep it small enough to read in one sitting.
2. Go down the list and mark the ones you do not remember closing. You are working from your own memory of the deal here, not from a field.
3. For each one you marked, ask whether you can account for the value, the products and the date. Mark anything you cannot.
4. Take the marked ones forward. If there are none, say so - that is a result worth the room hearing.
RequiredContext: Your own opportunities and the date range you want to review.
ExpectedOutput: Recent closed-won opportunities with the ones the seller cannot account for identified, or an explicit statement that there were none.
HumanCheckpoint: The seller decides which closes they can account for. A closed record can be well-formed and still describe something that did not happen, and the check is whether the value, products and date match what was actually sold.
BestFitJob: See which of your deals closed without you closing them
WhyThisMatters: A closed record carries your number whether or not you set it. A wrong one raises no error and blocks nothing, so it survives until somebody has to explain it.

Name: Work out what to do about the one you cannot explain
Description: Take a closed record you cannot account for and decide whether to accept it, correct it, or raise it.
Prompt: Here is a closed-won opportunity I cannot fully account for: [paste the record - account, value, close date, close reason, products]. Here is what I know was actually happening on this account: [paste what you know - what was sold, what was signed, what was delivered, what was still open]. Lay out where the record and my account knowledge agree, where they disagree, and what would settle each disagreement. Do not tell me whether the close was correct.
ActivitySteps:
1. Open Cowork and paste both the record and what you know about the account.
2. Work the disagreements, not the agreements. The agreements are why you did not notice sooner.
3. Decide which of four this is: the close is right and you had forgotten; it is wrong on detail you are able to correct yourself; it is wrong in a way that needs somebody else; or you cannot yet tell and need to check something first.
4. If it is yours to correct, correct it now while you still have the context.
5. If it needs somebody else or more evidence, write down what you checked and what you found, so the next person does not start from nothing.
RequiredContext: One closed record you could not account for, and what you know was happening on that account.
ExpectedOutput: One questionable close resolved into accepted, corrected by the seller, routed to whoever can act on it, or held pending a specific check.
HumanCheckpoint: The seller decides whether the record matches what was sold, and whether the correction is theirs to make or somebody else's. Account knowledge is one input rather than the deciding one, and a correction made without the contract in front of you replaces one wrong record with another.
BestFitJob: Decide what to do about a close you cannot account for
WhyThisMatters: A wrong close is easy to leave alone because nothing breaks. It shows up later as revenue that cannot be explained or a customer conversation that starts from a false position.

Name: Watch the satisfaction signals across a live delivery
Description: Gather the delivery signals that show how the customer is experiencing the work.
Prompt: For [Customer] and [delivery or engagement], set up a recurring check on the signals that show how the customer is experiencing this delivery: open issues and how long they have been open, escalations, missed or moved dates, response times, and questions left unanswered. Report what changed since the last check rather than restating everything. Separate what the record shows from what is inferred, and state what the record cannot see. My delivery context is [global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage]; reflect that in which signals you treat as material.
RequiredContext: Delivery status, open issues, escalation history, milestone dates; your delivery context, whether global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
ExpectedOutput: A recurring satisfaction signal watch showing what changed since the last check, separating evidence from inference.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA decides which signals reflect the customer's experience rather than internal process noise. A record with no open issues can still describe a customer who has stopped telling us about them.
WhyThisMatters: The signals are usually already in the record. The work is looking before the survey does.

Name: Rank the satisfaction risks by what the customer would say
Description: Turn the signals into a ranked view of what this customer would raise if asked today.
Prompt: Using the delivery signals for [Customer], rank what this customer would most likely raise if asked about their experience today. For each item give the specific moment behind it, who owns it, and whether it is still fixable within this delivery. Separate what is evidenced from what is inferred.
RequiredContext: Satisfaction signal summary, delivery timeline, role ownership; your delivery context, whether global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
ExpectedOutput: Ranked satisfaction risks with owner and a fixable or not-fixable call.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms each ranked item traces to a specific moment. A risk with no moment behind it is a feeling, and it will not survive the conversation with the account team.
WhyThisMatters: Ranking by what the customer would say, rather than by what is easiest to fix, is what makes this worth doing.

Name: Build the satisfaction recovery action
Description: Turn the top satisfaction risk into an action with an owner and a date.
Prompt: Take the top satisfaction risk for [Customer] and draft the recovery action: what will change, who owns it, what the customer will see and by when, and what we will say to them about it. Keep it to something deliverable inside this delivery.
ActivitySteps:
1. Take the highest-ranked satisfaction risk.
2. State what the customer would see change, not what we would do internally.
3. Name the owner and the date.
4. Decide what is said to the customer and by whom.
5. Route anything that is not yours.
RequiredContext: Ranked satisfaction risks, delivery timeline, account team roles; your delivery context, whether global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
ExpectedOutput: One satisfaction recovery action with owner, date and customer-visible change.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms the action is one the customer would notice. An internal process fix the customer never sees does not move satisfaction.
WhyThisMatters: A satisfaction risk without a customer-visible action is a note. This is the step that changes the score.

Name: Check the risk against what the record supports
Description: Test the satisfaction read against the evidence before taking it to the account team.
Prompt: Review this satisfaction read for [Customer]. For each claim, state whether the delivery record supports it, partly supports it, or does not support it. Identify anything asserted without evidence and anything the record cannot show either way.
RequiredContext: Satisfaction read, delivery record, escalation history; your delivery context, whether global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
ExpectedOutput: Evidence check with unsupported claims identified.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA decides what to take forward. Raising an unsupported satisfaction claim with the account team costs credibility on the ones that were real.
WhyThisMatters: Satisfaction claims get challenged. Checking them first is what lets you hold the position.

Name: Map what the customer's direction will demand of you
Description: Work out which technical topics this customer's roadmap will require you to be credible on.
Prompt: For [Customer], based on their stated technical direction, current estate and announced priorities, identify the technical topics they will need advice on over the next two to four quarters. Rank by how soon they will need it and how central it is to their direction. State what is known versus assumed.
RequiredContext: Customer technical direction, current estate, announced priorities; your delivery context, whether global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
ExpectedOutput: Ranked list of technical topics the customer will need advice on.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms this reflects the customer's direction rather than Microsoft's product roadmap. The two are not the same, and only one of them determines what the customer asks you.
WhyThisMatters: The list of things worth knowing is set by the customer. Starting anywhere else is how good effort gets spent on the wrong topic.

Name: Compare that against what you can defend today
Description: Set the customer's coming demands against what you could hold a conversation on now.
Prompt: Take this ranked list of technical topics for [Customer]. For each, help me separate what I could hold an advisory conversation on today, what I could speak to but not defend under challenge, and what I would have to route to a specialist. Ask me what I need to answer honestly rather than assuming.
RequiredContext: Ranked technical topics, your own recent customer conversations; your delivery context, whether global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
ExpectedOutput: Honest gap map across can defend, can discuss, and must route.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA answers this honestly rather than aspirationally. A gap map that flatters you produces a plan that closes nothing.
WhyThisMatters: Most credibility gaps are known and unstated. Writing them down is most of the work.

Name: Find where you were the bottleneck
Description: Look back at where a question had to go to someone else, and what that cost.
Prompt: Looking across my recent customer engagements, identify where a technical question had to be routed to someone else, where a decision waited on an answer I could not give, and where I deferred a topic more than once. Group them by topic and show which ones recur.
RequiredContext: Recent engagement history, meeting and escalation records; your delivery context, whether global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
ExpectedOutput: Recurring topics where you were the routing point rather than the answer.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA decides which routing was appropriate and which was a gap. Bringing in a specialist is often the right call, and treating every handoff as a personal shortfall points the plan at the wrong thing.
WhyThisMatters: The gaps that cost the most are the ones that recur. They are visible in your own history if you look.

Name: Build the credibility plan for one gap
Description: Turn the highest-value gap into a specific plan with a first step this week.
Prompt: Take the highest-value technical gap and build a plan to close it: what being credible on this looks like in a customer conversation, the smallest first step, what I will use to get there, how I will test whether it worked, and the date I will have it by. Keep it to one gap.
ActivitySteps:
1. Pick the gap the customer will hit soonest.
2. State what credible looks like in their words, not ours.
3. Name the smallest first step.
4. Decide how you will test it, ideally on a real conversation.
5. Put a date on it.
RequiredContext: Gap map, customer timeline, available time; your delivery context, whether global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
ExpectedOutput: A one-gap credibility plan with a first step and a date.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSA keeps this to one gap. A plan covering every gap is a plan that closes none of them before the customer needs the answer.
WhyThisMatters: One closed gap before the customer needs it beats a broad plan that arrives after they asked.

Name: Be told a signal is expiring instead of finding out
Description: Set a standing watch on the signal queue so the ones approaching expiry surface without anyone going to look.
Prompt: Watch my signal queue and tell me, on a schedule I set, which signals are approaching expiry, which have moved since the last check, and which have gone quiet after an initial response. Rank by how close they are to expiring and how warm the account looked. Carry forward what you told me last time so I can see what I acted on and what I let go.
ActivitySteps:
1. Set the cadence to match how fast your queue turns over, not how often you would like to look.
2. Say what counts as approaching expiry for your motion.
3. Ask it to report movement since the last check rather than the whole queue.
4. Check the first run before you trust the second.
5. After two weeks, look at what you consistently let go and decide whether that is a judgment or a capacity problem.
RequiredContext: Access to your signal queue, the expiry window that applies to your motion, and the cadence you want to be told on.
ExpectedOutput: A standing watch on the signal queue reporting what is close to expiry and what has moved since the last check, rather than a one-time list.
HumanCheckpoint: The DAE decides which expiring signals are worth the contact. A queue ranked by expiry date tells you what runs out first, not what is worth pursuing, and working the queue in date order is how the good accounts get the least attention.
WhyThisMatters: A signal you find on the day it expires is a signal you have already lost. Being told earlier is the whole difference.

Name: Watch for the engagement that turns into real intent
Description: Set a standing watch across your solution area so repeat engagement surfaces as it builds rather than after the window has closed.
Prompt: Watch engagement across the accounts in my solution area and tell me, on a schedule I set, where activity is repeating or building rather than one-off, where a signal has gone quiet after I responded, and where the same pattern is showing up across more than one account. Carry forward what you reported last time so I can see what built and what faded.
ActivitySteps:
1. Set the cadence and the accounts in scope.
2. Say what repeat engagement looks like in your solution area.
3. Ask for what changed since the last check, not the full picture.
4. Review the first run before relying on it.
5. Use the cross-account patterns to decide where your solution area is actually landing.
RequiredContext: The accounts in your solution area, access to the engagement signals for them, and the cadence you want to be told on.
ExpectedOutput: A standing watch across the solution area showing where engagement is building, where it went quiet after a response, and the patterns appearing across more than one account.
HumanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what repeat engagement means. Activity that repeats can be a buying signal or one person doing their research, and the difference is not in the count.
WhyThisMatters: A pattern across several touches says something a single event does not, and watching for it by hand is the part that does not get done.

Name: Pressure-test the options and tradeoffs with an executive
Description: Practice putting the real decision, its options and its tradeoffs to an executive.
Prompt: Use Agent J.ai to role-play the executive who has to make this decision. I will present the options and their tradeoffs rather than a recommendation. Push back where an option sounds like a pitch, where a tradeoff has been softened, or where what this executive is personally backing has not been named. Pause for my response before coaching me on whether the decision was put clearly and the tradeoffs stated honestly. Do not invent customer facts or commitments.
RequiredContext: The approved narrative; the decision being asked for; the options and their tradeoffs; who the executive is and what they are accountable for.
ExpectedOutput: A rehearsed decision conversation, the objections raised, and coaching on where an option was pitched rather than offered.
HumanCheckpoint: The ATS decides which tradeoffs are material enough to put in front of this executive. Review the downsides the rehearsal raises and add the material ones it missed, since not everything it raises bears on the decision being made.
WhyThisMatters: An executive decision put badly sounds like a pitch. Rehearsing it is how you hear the difference before they do.

Name: Rehearse the escalation conversation before you have it
Description: Practice telling a customer something has gone wrong, before the call.
Prompt: Use Agent J.ai to role-play the customer stakeholder I have to tell about this escalation. Use the approved status position, the validated escalation brief and the commitment boundaries I am pasting below, and ask me for anything missing before you begin. Play them as someone who is frustrated and wants a date I cannot yet give. Push back where I over-commit, where I soften the impact, or where I explain the cause instead of saying what happens next. Pause for my response before coaching me on whether I was clear about what is known, what is not, and when they will hear from me again. Do not invent facts about the incident.
RequiredContext: The validated escalation brief; the stakeholder and what they care about; the approved communication position; what you cannot yet commit to.
ExpectedOutput: A rehearsed escalation conversation, the objections raised, and coaching on where you over-committed or softened the impact.
HumanCheckpoint: The CSAM decides what can be said about cause and timing before the facts are settled. Rehearsal makes an answer fluent, and a fluent answer about an unresolved incident is easy to hear as a commitment.
WhyThisMatters: How an escalation is handled shapes the relationship long after the incident closes. Rehearsing it is cheaper than improvising it while they are angry.
